sourceLine: José de Acosta, Spanish Jesuit who lived in Peru and Mexico 1572–1587, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, 1590 (adapted)
text: I find there are three kinds of beasts at the Indies, whereof some have been carried from Spain; others are of the same kind we have in Europe, and yet not carried by the Spaniards; and others are proper to the Indies, whereof there are none in Spain. Of the first kind are sheep, kine [cattle], goats, swine, horses, asses, dogs, cats, and other such beasts, for there are of all these kinds at the Indies. … These wild kine have so multiplied in Santo Domingo and thereabouts, that they troop together in the fields and woods by thousands, having no master to whom they appertain. They hunt these beasts only for their hides … In the fleet, the year 1587, there came from Santo Domingo 35444 hides, and from New Spain 64350, which they value at 96532 pieces, so as when they discharge one of these fleets it is admirable to behold the river of Seville, and in the arsenal (where they unlade) so many hides …
original: I finde there are three kindes of beasts at the Indies, whereof some have been carried from Spaine ; others are of the same kinde we have in Europe, and yet not carried by the Spaniardes ; and others are proper to the Indies, whereof there are none in Spaine. Of the first kinde are sheepe, kine, goates, swine, horses, asses, dogs, cattes, and other such beasts, for there are of all these kindes at the Indies. … These wilde kine have so multiplied in Santo Domingo and thereabouts, that they troope together in the fields and woods by thousands, having no master to whom they appertaine. They hunt these beasts onely for their hides … In the fleet, the yere 1587, there came from Santo Domingo 35444 hides, and from New Spaine 64350, which they value at 96532 peeces, so as when they discharge one of these fleetes it is admirable to behold the river of Seville, and in the arsenall (where they vnlade) so many hides …
translation: Translated by Edward Grimston, 1604; edited by Clements R. Markham, The Natural & Moral History of the Indies, vol. 1, Hakluyt Society, 1880
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Adapted: compared text with original word by word against archive.org naturalmoralhist01acos, Book IV ch. xxxiii, pp. 270-271 (Grimston 1604, ed. Markham, Hakluyt Society, vol. I, MDCCCLXXX = 1880). Only spelling is modernised, and the bracket [cattle] clarifies "kine". Cuts keep the meaning.

sourceLine: José de Acosta, Spanish Jesuit who lived in Peru 1572–86 and visited Potosí, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, book 4, on refining silver with mercury, 1590 (adapted)
text: [Pedro Fernández de Velasco,] who offered to refine silver at Potosi with mercury; and having made trial thereof in the year of our redemption, one thousand five hundred seventy and one, performed it with credit; then began they to refine silver at Potosi with quicksilver, which they transported from Huancavilca, which was a goodly help for the mines; for by the means of quicksilver they drew an infinite quantity of metal from these mines, whereof before they made no account, the which they called scrapings. … The Catholic King draws from his quicksilver mines, without any charge or hazard, almost four hundred thousand pieces, the which are fourteen reals a piece, or little less, besides the rights that rise in Potosi, where it is employed, the which is a great riches. … for if there remained any fume or vapor, which should encounter them that unstopped the pots, they were in danger of death, or to be benumbed of their limbs, or at the least to lose their teeth.
original: who offred to refine silver at Potosi with mercury ; and having made triall thereof in the yeare of our redemption, one thousand five hundred seaventy and one, perfourmed it with credite ; then beganne they to refine silver at Potosi with quicksilver, which they transported from Huancavilca, which was a goodly helpe for the mines ; for by the meanes of quickesilver they drew an infinite quantity of mettall from these mines, whereof before they made no accompt, the which they called scrapings. … The Catholike King drawes from his quickesilver mines, without any charge or hazard, almost foure hundred thousand peeces, the which are fourteene rialls a peece, or little less, besides the rights that rise in Potosi, where it is employed, the which is a great riches. … for if there remained any fume or vapor, which should incounter them that vnstopt the pottes, they were in danger of death, or to be benummed of their limbes, or at the least to loose their teeth.
translation: Translated by Edward Grimston, 1604; edited by Clements R. Markham, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, vol. 1 (Hakluyt Society), 1880
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared original with Markham 1880 vol. 1, book 4 chs. 11-12, pp. 217-218 (leaves 285-286, page images): matches the print. Text vs original: spelling only (rialls->reals, vnstopt->unstopped, loose->lose etc.). Leading "[Pedro Fernández de Velasco,]" supplies the name the source gives immediately before "who offred" ("called Pedro Fernandes de Velasco") - a referent, not a paraphrase. Cut 1 drops one explanatory sentence; cut 2 drops the Huancavelica output figure and the description of distilling quicksilver in luted pots; the last piece (danger of mercury vapour on unstopping the pots, ch. 12) keeps its meaning. Edition/translator as for the other Acosta docs.

sourceLine: José de Acosta, Spanish Jesuit who lived in Peru 1572–86 and visited Potosí, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, book 4, 1590 (adapted)
text: They labour in these mines in continual darkness and obscurity, without knowledge of day or night. And forasmuch as those places are never visited with the Sun, there is not only a continual darkness, but also an extreme cold, with so gross an air contrary to the disposition of man, so as such as newly enter are sick as they at sea. … The metal is commonly hard, and therefore they break it with hammers, splitting and hewing it by force as if they were flints. … He that goes before carries a candle tied to his thumb, for, as it is said, they have no light from heaven, and so go they up the ladder holding it with both their hands; to mount so great a height which commonly is above a hundred and fifty estados [man-heights], a fearful thing and which breeds an amazement to think upon it, so great is the desire of silver, that for the gain thereof men endure any pains.
original: They labour in these mines in continuall darknes and obscuritie, without knowledge of day or night. And forasmuch as those places are never visited with the Sunne, there is not onely a continual darkness, but also an extreme colde, with so grosse an aire contrary to the disposition of man, so as such as newly enter are sicke as they at sea. … The mettall is commonly hard, and therefore they breake it with hammers, splitting and hewing it by force as if they were flintes. … He that goes before carries a candle tied to his thumb, for, as it is said, they have no light from heaven, and so go they vp the ladder holding it with both their handes ; to mount so great a height which commonly is above a hundred and fiftie estados, a fearful thing and which breeds an amazement to thinke vpon it, so great is the desire of silver, that for the gaine thereof men indure any paines.
translation: Translated by Edward Grimston, 1604; edited by Clements R. Markham, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, vol. 1 (Hakluyt Society), 1880
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared original with Markham 1880 vol. 1 (Hakluyt Soc.), book 4 ch. 8, pp. 207-208 (archive.org naturalmoralhist01acos leaves 275-276, page images): original matches the printed page word for word. Word diff text vs original: spelling only (continuall->continual, Sunne->Sun, vp->up, indure->endure etc.); "[man-heights]" is a pure gloss on estados. Cuts remove Acosta's own sickness in the mine/candle shifts and the ladder description; "He that goes before" is self-defining (the leading climber), meaning unchanged. Title page confirms "reprinted from the English translated edition of Edward Grimston, 1604 ... edited by Clements R. Markham, vol. I (books I-IV)", 1880. Role: Markham intro (pp. ii-ix) has Acosta leave Spain 1570, accompany Toledo in Charcas, reside in Mexico 1586 and sail home in the 1587 fleet; "Peru 1572-86" matches the standard biography; he says he entered a Potosí mine himself. Original Spanish 1590 (Seville).

sourceLine: José de Acosta, Spanish Jesuit who lived in Peru 1572–86, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, book 4, on the treasure fleet he sailed home with in 1587, 1590 (adapted)
text: In that fleet where I came in the year one thousand five hundred eighty seven, there were eleven millions transported in the two fleets of Peru and Mexico, whereof two thirds were in that of Peru, and almost the one half for the King. I thought good to set this down particularly, to show the power which his heavenly Majesty hath given to the Kings of Spain, heaping so many Crowns and Kingdoms upon them, who (by the especial favour of heaven) have joined the East with the West Indies, environing the whole world with their Power.
original: In that fleete where I came in the yeare one thousand five hundred eighty seaven, there were eleven millions transported in the two fleets of Peru and Mexico, whereof two thirds were in that of Peru, and almost the one halfe for the King. I thought good to set this downe particularly, to shew the power which his heavenly Maiestie hath given to the Kings of Spaine, heaping so many Crowns and Kingdomes vpon them, who (by the especiall favour of heaven) have ioyned the East with the West Indies, invironing the whole worlde with their Power.
translation: Translated by Edward Grimston, 1604; edited by Clements R. Markham, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, vol. 1 (Hakluyt Society), 1880
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared original with Markham 1880 vol. 1, book 4, p. 204 (leaf 272, page image): continuous passage, matches the print exactly; text differs by spelling only (ioyned->joined, invironing->environing etc.). Excerpt stops before Markham's bracketed passage "[It may be thought...]". Markham intro p. ix confirms Acosta went home in the fleet of 1587. Attribution, year and translation credit correct.

sourceLine: William Adams, English pilot shipwrecked in Japan in 1600 who became an adviser to Tokugawa Ieyasu, letter to his countrymen, 1611
text: So in process of four or five years the emperor [Tokugawa Ieyasu] called me, as divers times he had done before. So one time above the rest he would have me to make him a small ship. I answered that I was no carpenter and had no knowledge thereof. Well, do your endeavor, said he; if it be not good, it is no matter. Wherefore at his command I built him a ship of the burden of eighty tons or thereabout; which ship being made in all respects as our manner is, he coming aboard to see it, liked it very well; by which means I came in favor with him, so that I came often in his presence, who from time to time gave me presents, and at length a yearly stipend to live upon … Now being in such grace and favor by reason I learned him some points of geometry and understanding of the art of mathematics with other things, I pleased him so that what I said he would not contrary.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Fordham 1611adams-japan.asp ('My Coming to Japan, 1611'; from Tappan, ed., The World's Story, vol. I, 1914, pp. 325-331, modernised by Arkenberg; Tappan: 'The letter ... was written in 1611'). Pieces verbatim; '[Tokugawa Ieyasu]' glosses Adams's 'emperor'; cut drops only the stipend amount. Written in English, translation null correct. The letter ends asking that his being in Japan be made known to his friends and countrymen, matching 'letter to his countrymen'.

sourceLine: Lope de Aguirre, Basque conquistador who led a rebellion during an expedition down the Amazon, letter to King Philip II of Spain, 1561
text: I demand of you, King, that you do justice and right by the good vassals you have in this land, even though I and my companions (whose names I will give later), unable to suffer further the cruelties of your judges, viceroy, and governors, have resolved to obey you no longer. Denaturalizing ourselves from our land, Spain, we make the most cruel war against you that our power can sustain and endure. Believe, King and lord, we have done this because we can no longer tolerate the great oppression and unjust punishments of your ministers who, to make places for their sons and dependents have usurped and robbed our fame, life, and honor. … Look here, King of Spain! Do not be cruel and ungrateful to your vassals, because while your father and you stayed in Spain without the slightest bother, your vassals, at the price of their blood and fortune, have given you all the kingdoms and holding you have in these parts.
translation: Translated by Tom Holloway, Cornell University, from the text in A. Arellano Moreno, ed., Documentos para la historia económica de Venezuela, 1961; released 1994 (Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with the Fordham page: text matches; the cut drops his complaints about his war wounds and the viceroy's hangings; meaning kept. The page says 'The following translation is by Tom Holloway, History, Cornell University, from the version published in A. Arellano Moreno (org.), Documentos para la Historia economic de Venezuela (Caracas: Univ. Central, 1961)' and gives his 1994 permission note; the credit now uses the name and edition as the page gives them (the earlier 'Thomas H.' was not on the page). Aguirre's role (Basque conquistador, leader of the rebellion on Ursúa's Amazon expedition) and the 1561 date match the letter.

sourceLine: Afonso de Albuquerque, Portuguese governor of India, speech to his captains before the attack on Malacca, 1511, as recorded in the Commentaries compiled by his son (published 1557)
text: The first is the great service which we shall perform to Our Lord in casting the Moors out of this country, and quenching the fire of this sect of Mafamede so that it may never burst out again hereafter; and I am so sanguine as to hope for this from our undertaking, that if we can only achieve the task before us, it will result in the Moors resigning India altogether to our rule, … And the other reason is the additional service which we shall render to the King D. Manuel in taking this city, because it is the headquarters of all the spiceries and drugs … and I hold it as very certain that if we take this trade of Malaca away out of their hands, Cairo and Meca are entirely ruined, and to Venice will no spiceries be conveyed except that which her merchants go and buy in Portugal.
translation: Translated by Walter de Gray Birch, The Commentaries of the Great Afonso Dalboquerque, vol. 3 (Hakluyt Society), 1880
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org commentariesgre02unkngoog, pp. 116-118 (title page: Birch, Commentaries vol. III, Hakluyt Society; vol. III is 1880). Cuts skip supporting arguments within each of the two reasons; meaning kept. The sourceLine says honestly that the speech is as recorded in the Commentaries compiled by his son (1557); year 1511 is the date of the speech.

sourceLine: Commentaries of Afonso de Albuquerque, compiled by his son Bras de Albuquerque from his father's papers (published 1557), on the capture of Malacca in 1511
text: And when Afonso Dalboquerque found himself less troubled by the uproars which the Moors caused by day and night, and that there was no longer in the city any force which could resist them, and as a recompense for past labours, he gave permission to everyone to sack the city, and free power to keep or dispose of everything they took, … When the city had been sacked, certain merchants, who had fled away to their country houses, seeing the kind way in which Ninachatu [a Hindu who had been kind to the Portuguese captives] had been treated, sent and begged a safe-conduct from Afonso Dalboquerque that they might come to the city; and he granted this to all, except the Malays, who were natives of the country, for as to these he gave orders that all should be put to death wheresoever they were found. … In this second time of taking the city, many of our men were wounded, … and of the Moors, women and children, there died by the sword an infinite number, for no quarter was given to any of them.
translation: Translated by Walter de Gray Birch, The Commentaries of the Great Afonso Dalboquerque, vol. 3 (Hakluyt Society), 1880
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org commentariesgre02unkngoog, pp. 126-127 (Birch, vol. III, 1880). "Ninachatu" appeared with no introduction (the cut removed the order to spare his houses, and the earlier passage is outside the excerpt). Added the bracket [a Hindu who had been kind to the Portuguese captives], taken from p. 126 ("Ninachatu, a Hindoo by nation", who had shown "kindnesses" to Ruy de Araujo and the Christians "during their captivity"). Restoring the cut words was not possible because they run across a page break and running head. Year 1557 (publication of the Commentaries) matches the sourceLine.

sourceLine: Pope Alexander VI, papal bull Inter Caetera, addressed to Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain after Columbus's first voyage, May 4, 1493
text: Among other works well pleasing to the Divine Majesty and cherished of our heart, this assuredly ranks highest, that in our times especially the Catholic faith and the Christian religion be exalted and be everywhere increased and spread, that the health of souls be cared for and that barbarous nations be overthrown and brought to the faith itself. … In the islands and countries already discovered are found gold, spices, and very many other precious things of divers kinds and qualities. … Wherefore, as becomes Catholic kings and princes, after earnest consideration of all matters, especially of the rise and spread of the Catholic faith, as was the fashion of your ancestors, kings of renowned memory, you have purposed with the favor of divine clemency to bring under your sway the said mainlands and islands with their residents and inhabitants and to bring them to the Catholic faith.
translation: Translated in Frances Gardiner Davenport, ed., European Treaties Bearing on the History of the United States and Its Dependencies to 1648 (Carnegie Institution of Washington), 1917
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: The papalencyclicals.net page names no translator. Compared its text with Davenport, European Treaties vol. 1 (Carnegie Institution, 1917), archive.org europeantreaties01daveuoft, Doc. 7 (bull Inter caetera of May 4, 1493), English translation: same wording ("Wherefore, as becomes Catholic kings and princes ... mainlands and islands"), which differs from her translation of the May 3 bull of the same name. So the Davenport credit is correct and the date May 4 is right. Cuts skip the narrative of Columbus's voyage; meaning kept.

sourceLine: Francisco de Ávila, priest of San Damián and campaigner against Andean religion, report on the gods and rites of the Indians of Huarochirí, Peru, 1608
text: The above traditions are so rooted in the hearts of the people of this province at the present time that they preserve them most inviolably; and thus they hold the condors to be sacred, and never kill one, believing that he who kills one will die himself. I know that there was a condor in the ravine of San Damian, near the bridge, which was unable to fly from extreme old age; but there was not an Indian who would touch it, and it lived there for thirteen or fourteen years. … They also have a great horror of the small fox; and they do to the lion all that was ordained in the blessing of Coniraya, bringing out the skin on great occasions, while he who owns it kills a llama. I have often seen this done in my own parish in Huarochiri, on occasion of the drinking bouts called Huantachinaca.
translation: Translated by Clements R. Markham, Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, 1873
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Markham, Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (1873), Avila's narrative, pp. 130–131. Title on the page: 'collected by the Doctor Francisco de Avila, Presbyter (Cura of the parish of San Damian in the said province of Huarachiri…)'; Markham's introduction: 'It was written in 1608.' The cut removes Avila's remark that people asked how he dared kill condors; meaning kept. 'The above traditions' refers to the Coniraya story that precedes it (Coniraya is named in the excerpt). sourceLine accurate; the narrative itself denounces these 'errors, false gods … and diabolical rites', so 'campaigner against Andean religion' is fair.

sourceLine: Duarte Barbosa, Portuguese royal clerk and interpreter in India, The Book of Duarte Barbosa, on Kilwa (East Africa), c. 1518
text: Before the King our Lord sent out his expedition to discover India the Moors of Cofala, Cuama, Angoya and Mocambique were all subject to the King of Quiloa, who was the most mighty king among them. And in this town was great plenty of gold, as no ships passed towards Cofala without first coming to this island. … This town was taken by force from its king by the Portuguese, as, moved by arrogance, he refused to obey the King our Lord. There they took many prisoners and the king fled from the island, and His Highness ordered that a fort should be built there, and kept it under his rule and governance.
translation: Translated by Mansel Longworth Dames, The Book of Duarte Barbosa, vol. 1 (Hakluyt Society), 1918
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org bookofduartebarb0001mans, p. 18 (Dames, Hakluyt Society, 2nd series no. XLIV, issued for 1918; title page: "completed about the year 1518", which supports c. 1518). The cut skips a description of the Moors' dress and religion; meaning kept.

sourceLine: Duarte Barbosa, Portuguese royal clerk and interpreter in India, The Book of Duarte Barbosa, on Malindi (East Africa), c. 1518
text: Leaving Mombaca, and journeying along the coast towards India, there is a fair town on the mainland lying along a strand, which is named Melinde. … They are great barterers, and deal in cloth, gold, ivory, and divers other wares with the Moors and … Heathen of the great kingdom of Cambaya; and to their haven come every year many ships with cargoes of merchandize, from which they get great store of gold, ivory and wax. In this traffic the Cambay merchants make great profits, and thus, on one side and the other, they earn much money. … The king and people of this place ever were and are friends of the King of Portugal, and the Portuguese always find in them great comfort and friendship and perfect peace, …
translation: Translated by Mansel Longworth Dames, The Book of Duarte Barbosa, vol. 1 (Hakluyt Society), 1918
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org bookofduartebarb0001mans, pp. 22-23 (Dames 1918). The "…" between "the Moors and" and "Heathen" skips only footnotes and a page break; the other cuts skip description. The closing quoted variant reading, which Dames marks with quotation marks, is left out. Date as for barbosa-1518-kilwa.

sourceLine: John (Jean) Barbot, French Huguenot agent of the French Royal African Company who made slaving voyages to West Africa in 1678–82, A Description of the Coasts of North and South Guinea (passage on the Senegal coast), published 1732 (adapted)
text: Abundance of little Blacks of both sexes are also stolen away by their neighbours, when found abroad on the roads, or in the woods; or else in the Cougans, or corn-fields, at the time of the year, when their parents keep them there all day, to scare away the devouring small birds, that come to feed on the millet, in swarms. … In times of dearth and famine, abundance of these people will sell themselves, for a maintenance, and to prevent starving. … To conclude, some slaves are also brought to these Blacks, from very remote inland countries, by way of trade, and sold for things of very inconsiderable value; but these slaves are generally poor and weak, by reason of the barbarous usage they have had in traveling so far, being continually beaten, and almost famish'd; so inhuman are the Blacks to one another.

translation: No translator named: printed in English "from his original manuscript" in A. and J. Churchill, A Collection of Voyages and Travels, vol. 5, London, 1732; text as reproduced on a Vancouver Island University course page (HIST 320) and checked against the 1732 printing

The VIU page misprints one word: the printed text is "abundance of these people will sell themselves", not "those". sourceLine: John (Jean) Barbot, French Huguenot agent of the French Royal African Company who made slaving voyages to West Africa in 1678–82, A Description of the Coasts of North and South Guinea (passages on the Senegal coast, the Gold Coast and Whydah), published 1732 (adapted)
text: Those sold by the Blacks are for the most part prisoners of war, taken either in fight, or pursuit, or in the incursions they make into their enemies territories; others stolen away by their own countrymen; and some there are, who will sell their own children, kindred, or neighbours. … The kings are so absolute, that upon any slight pretense of offences committed by their subjects, they order them to be sold for slaves, without regard to rank, or profession. … The trade of slaves is in a more peculiar manner the business of kings, rich men, and prime merchants, exclusive of the inferior sort of Blacks. … If there happens to be no stock of slaves at Fida, the factor must trust the Blacks with his goods, to the value of a hundred and fifty, or two hundred slaves; which goods they carry up into the inland, to buy slaves, at all the markets, for above two hundred leagues up the country.
original: Those sold by the Blacks are for the most part prisoners of war, taken either in fight, or pursuit, or in the incursions they make into their enemies territories; others stolen away by their own countrymen; and some there are, who will sell their own children, kindred, or neighbours. … The kings are so absolute, that upon any slight pretense of offences committed by their subjects, they order them to be sold for slaves, without regard to rank, or possession. … The trade of slaves is in a more peculiar manner the business of kings, rich men, and prime merchants, exclusive of the inferior sort of Blacks. … If there happens to be no stock of slaves at Fida, the factor must trust the Blacks with his goods, to the value of a hundred and fifty, or two hundred slaves; which goods they carry up into the inland, to buy slaves, at all the markets, for above two hundred leagues up the country.
translation: No translator named: printed in English "from his original manuscript" in A. and J. Churchill, A Collection of Voyages and Travels, vol. 5, London, 1732; text as reproduced on a Vancouver Island University course page (HIST 320) and checked against the 1732 printing

M.DCC.XXXII") and checked every piece against the page images: pp. 47 (leaf 71, Book I, Senegal coast), 270 (leaf 408, Book III, Gold Coast) and 327 (leaf 465, Book IV, Fida). sourceLine: Andrew Battell, English sailor held by the Portuguese in Angola who lived among Imbangala (Jaga) warriors around 1600, account printed by Samuel Purchas, 1625
text: He [the Imbangala war leader] asked wherefore we came. We told him that we came to trade upon the coast. Then he bade us welcome, and called us on shore with our commodities. We laded our ship with slaves in seven days, and bought them so cheap that many did not cost one real, which were worth in the city [of Loanda] twelve milreis. … These Benguelas presently broke, and turned their backs, and a very great number of them were slain, and were taken captives, man, woman and child. The prince, Hombiangymbe, was slain, which was ruler of this country, and more than one hundred of his chief lords, and their heads presented and thrown at the feet of the great Gaga. … They settled themselves in this country and took the spoil of it.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg 41282 (Ravenstein, The Strange Adventures of Andrew Battell, Hakluyt Society 1901, pp. 19–21, "A Second Voyage to Benguella" / "Among the Jagas"). Words verbatim as printed in that edition. "[the Imbangala war leader]" replaces nothing: it names the referent of "He" (the source's "great Gaga, which is their general"); "[of Loanda]" is the editor's own bracket on the page. Cuts remove the battle narrative and the cannibalism passage; meaning kept. Attribution: Ravenstein's introduction says Battell's papers reached Purchas after his death and were first published in Purchas His Pilgrimes, 1625; he was a prisoner of the Portuguese in Angola from 1589 and among the Jagas c. 1600–01, so the sourceLine shows both dates.

sourceLine: Andrew Battell, English sailor held by the Portuguese in Angola who lived among Imbangala (Jaga) warriors around 1600, account printed by Samuel Purchas, 1625
text: I was so highly esteemed with the great Gaga, because I killed many negroes with my musket, that I had anything that I desired of him. He would also, when they went out to the wars, give charge to his men over me. By this means I have been often carried away in their arms, and saved my life. Here we were within three days’ journey of Massangano, before mentioned, where the Portugals have a fort: and I sought means, and got to the Portugals again with merchant negroes that came to the camp to buy slaves.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg 41282 (Ravenstein 1901), pp. 27–28: one continuous passage, verbatim; "He" refers to the great Gaga named in the first sentence. Attribution as for battell-1625-imbangala-captives (papers first printed by Purchas 1625; events c. 1600–01).

sourceLine: Sir William Berkeley, royal governor of Virginia, answers to the Lords Commissioners for Foreign Plantations, 1671 (adapted)
text: What obstructions do you find to the improvement of the trade and navigation of the plantations within your government? Answer. Mighty and destructive, by that severe act of parliament, which excludes us the having any commerce with any nation in Europe but our own, so that we cannot add to our plantation any commodity that grows out of it. … for it is not lawful for us to carry a pipe stave, or a barrel of corn to any place in Europe out of the king's dominions. If this were for his majesty's service or the good of his subjects, we should not repine, whatever our sufferings are for it; but on my soul, it is the contrary for both. And this is the cause why no small or great vessels are built here; for we are most obedient to all laws, whilst the New England men break through, and men trade to any place that their interest lead them.

Mighty and destructive, by that severe act of parliament, which excludes us the having any … mei'ce with any nation in Europe but our own, so that we cannot add to our plantation any commodity that grows out of it. … for it is not lawfull for us to carry a pipe stave, or a barrel of corn to any place in Europe out of the king's dominions. If this were for his majesty's service or the good of his subjects, we should not repine, whatever our sufferings are for it; but on my soul, it is the contrary for both. And this is the cause why no small or great vessells are built here ; for we are most obedient to all laws, whilst the New England men break through, and men trade to any place that their interest lead them,

sourceLine: Thomas Bluett, English lawyer, recording the account of Ayuba Suleiman Diallo (Job ben Solomon), a Muslim Fulbe scholar and trader from Bundu enslaved in Maryland, Some Memoirs of the Life of Job, 1734
text: In February, 1730. JOB's Father hearing of an English Ship at Gambia River, sent him, with two Servants to attend him, to sell two Negroes and to buy Paper, and some other Necessaries; but desired him not to venture over the River, because the Country of the Mandingoes, who are Enemies to the People of Futa, lies on the other side. … he crossed the River Gambia, and disposed of his Negroes for some Cows. … It happened that a Company of the Mandingoes, who live upon Plunder, passing by at that Time, and observing him unarmed, rush'd in, to the Number of seven or eight at once, at a back Door, and pinioned JOB, before he could get to his Arms, together with his Interpreter, who is a Slave in Maryland still.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with DocSouth (UNC) electronic edition of Bluett, Some Memoirs of the Life of Job (London: Richard Ford, 1734), Sect. II, pp. 16–17. Words verbatim; the two cuts remove the dispute with Captain Pike and the stop at a friend's house where Job hung up his arms; the remaining "rush'd in ... at a back Door ... before he could get to his Arms" still reads correctly. Attribution: title page "By Thomas Bluett, Gent. who was intimately acquainted with him in America"; Bluett met him in 1731 while "attending the Courts" in Kent County (consistent with "lawyer"); Job was born at Boonda (Bundu) in Futa.

sourceLine: Willem Bosman, chief merchant of the Dutch West India Company at Elmina on the Gold Coast, A New and Accurate Description of the Coast of Guinea, letter 11, Dutch original 1703, English translation 1705 (adapted)
text: The chief of these are Muskets or Carabins, in the management of which they are wonderful dextrous … you wonder how the Negroes come to be furnished with Fire-Arms, but you will have no Reason when you know we sell them incredible quantities, thereby obliging them with a Knife to cut our own Throats. But we are forced to it; for if we would not, they might be sufficiently stored with that Commodity by the English, Danes, and Brandenburghers … And since that and Gun-powder for some time hath been the chief vendible Merchandise here, we should have found but an indifferent Trade without our share in it.

sourceLine: William Bradford, governor of Plymouth Colony, Of Plymouth Plantation, entry for 1634 on the Native people near the colony's trading house on the Connecticut River, written c. 1640s (adapted)
text: This spring, also, those Indians that lived about their trading house there fell sick of the small pox, and died most miserably; … for usually they that have this disease have them in abundance, and for want of bedding and linen and other helps, they fall into a lamentable condition, as they lie on their hard mats, the pox breaking and mattering, and running one into another, their skin cleaving (by reason thereof) to the mats they lie on … and then being very sore, what with cold and other distempers, they die like rotten sheep. … But those of the English house, (though at first they were afraid of the infection,) yet seeing their woeful and sad condition, and hearing their pitiful cries and lamentations, they had compassion of them, and daily fetched them wood and water, and made them fires, got them victuals whilst they lived, and buried them when they died. … But by the marvellous goodness and providence of God not one of the English was so much as sick, or in the least measure tainted with this disease, though they daily did these offices for them for many weeks together.
original: This spring, also, those Indeans that lived aboute their trading house there fell sick of ye small poxe, and dyed most miserably; … for usualy they that have this disease have them in abundance, and for wante of bedding & lin̅ing and other helps, they fall into a lamentable condition, as they lye on their hard matts, ye poxe breaking and mattering, and runing one into another, their skin cleaving (by reason therof) to the matts they lye on … and then being very sore, what with could and other distempers, they dye like rotten sheep. … But those of ye English house, (though at first they were afraid of ye infection,) yet seeing their woefull and sadd condition, and hearing their pitifull cries and lamentations, they had compastion of them, and dayly fetched them wood & water, and made them fires, gott them victualls whilst they lived, and buried them when they dyed. … But by ye marvelous goodnes & providens of God not one of ye English was so much as sicke, or in ye least measure tainted with this disease, though they dayly did these offices for them for many weeks togeather.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Adapted: compared text with original against Gutenberg 24950 (images), Anno 1634. The existing modernisation is spelling only ("lin̅ing" = linning, i.e. linen; "could" = cold). The second cut removed the passage where the English at the trading house nursed the sick, so the closing "though they daily did these offices for them" had no referent. Restored it ("But those of ye English house ... to ye haszard of them selvs.") in "original", copied from the page (the page HTML has "&" in "wood & water"), and modernised only the spelling in "text". Year 1634 is the entry year; the sourceLine also says the history was written c. 1640s. Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: Jean de Brébeuf, Jesuit missionary among the Wendat (Huron) near Georgian Bay, Huron Relation of 1636, printed in the Jesuit Relations
text: Generally speaking they praise and approve the Christian Religion, and blame their wicked customs; but when will they leave them off entirely? … Some say to us: "Do you think … you are going to succeed in overturning the Country?" Thus do they style the change from their Pagan and Barbarous life to one that is civilized and Christian. … [One Wendat man] was willingly present at all our Assemblies, listening to our instructions; he was the first to make the sign of the Cross … but afterwards he tried to blend our creed with their superstitions and nonsense, and said that he wished to go with his Ancestors. … We went to see him, and he again sought our good offices—threatening that, if we did not satisfy him by singing in our way, he would overturn everything in our Cabin after his death, and even carry it away.
translation: Translated by Thwaites's staff (Finlow Alexander, Percy Favor Bicknell, William Frederic Giese, Crawford Lindsay, William Price; the translator of this document is not specified), The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, ed. Reuben Gold Thwaites, vol. 10, 1897
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Thwaites vol. 10 (contents: Document XXVI part II, 'Brebeuf's Relation of the Hurons', Ihonatiria, July 16, 1636), English pp. 25–27 and 61. Two of the '…' marks only bridge the page markers '[16]' and '[41]'; the long cut jumps from pp. 25–27 to p. 61, and '[One Wendat man]' replaces the pronoun 'He' (the source's 'an old man of our village', who died on 'the twentieth of October' (1635) 'in his unbelief'); the last cut omits his farewell feast before 'We went to see him'. Nothing kept is reversed or misleading. Translation credit changed to the translators the volume lists (no individual translator is given).

sourceLine: Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, Habsburg ambassador at the court of Sultan Suleiman, letter from Constantinople, 1556, on the rising of a man claiming to be the executed Prince Mustafa
text: At first he [the pretender] used this language privately, but afterwards he harangued in a similar strain the inhabitants of the places he visited; the men who were supposed to have been the companions of his flight supported his assertions by similar narratives; while persons of considerable position, who had been suborned by Bajazet [Suleiman’s son Bayezid], made statements to the same effect. … The Sultan, rightly surmising that one or other of his two sons was privy to the conspiracy, considered it a most serious matter, and sent despatches severely reprimanding the Sanjak-beys for their remissness in allowing the insurrection to assume such formidable proportions, instead of nipping it in the bud; moreover, he threatened to punish them severely if they failed to send him the impostor in chains at the very earliest date possible, and with him all the other ringleaders in this monstrous treason. … The rank and file of the Janissaries, excited by the idea of a revolution with Mustapha at its head, were well inclined towards the insurgents, and eager for the rising to become general.
translation: Translated by Charles Thornton Forster and F. H. Blackburne Daniell, The Life and Letters of Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, 1881
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Forster and Daniell, Life and Letters of Busbecq vol. 1 (Kegan Paul, 1881), Letter II, pp. 182-184; the letter is dated 'Constantinople, July 14, 1556' (p. 191, editors' correction of the Latin editions' 1555). Brackets '[the pretender]' and '[Suleiman’s son Bayezid]' are pure referent insertions (no source words replaced). Cuts (how the impostor won followers; Pertau Pasha's despatch) do not change meaning. Attribution (ambassador of the Habsburg Ferdinand I at Suleiman's court), year and translation correct. Confirmed.

sourceLine: Alvise Cadamosto, Venetian merchant sailing for Prince Henry of Portugal, account of his dealings in 1455 with Budomel, a Wolof ruler near Cape Verde, first printed 1507
text: As some Portuguese, who had dealt with Budomel, represented him as a very just person, who paid for any goods he might receive, and might therefore be confided in, I stopped at his country, that I might endeavour to dispose of some Spanish horses I had on board, which are in great request among the Negroes; besides which, I had some cloth, Moorish wrought silks, and other commodities for sale. … Not long afterwards Budomel came himself to the beach, attended by about fifteen horsemen and an hundred and fifty foot, … After some discourse, I delivered to him seven horses, with their furniture; and every other article for which he expressed an inclination, all of which had cost me 300 ducats, trusting to his honour for payment, which was to be in slaves, and which he promised to deliver at his own residence, which was twenty-five miles distant from the shore, whither he invited me to accompany him.
translation: English version in Robert Kerr, A General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels, vol. 2, 1824 (from Astley's translation and Ramusio's Italian text)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg 10803 (Kerr vol. 2, 1824), first voyage, Section V (Budomel). Words verbatim; the two cuts remove only the anchoring/interpreter and the landing courtesies and do not change the meaning. sourceLine: as for the other Cadamosto document, Kerr gives the voyages as 1455–56 and the first printing as Venice 1507, so the line now shows both (year 1455 kept = date of the events). Budomel is in the first (1455) voyage.

sourceLine: Alvise Cadamosto, Venetian merchant sailing for Prince Henry of Portugal, account of his 1455 voyage to the Senegal River and the Jolof kingdom, first printed 1507
text: The Arabs of this coast have many Barbary horses, which they carry to the country of the Negroes, which they barter with the great men for slaves, receiving from ten to eighteen men for each horse, according to their goodness. … The king [of the Jalofs] has no settled revenue; but the lords of the country court his favour, by making him yearly presents of horses, which being scarce, are in high estimation, together with horse furniture, cows, and goats, pulse, millet, and other things. He likewise increases his wealth by means of robbery, and by reducing his own subjects, and those of neighbouring provinces to slavery, employing a part of these slaves to cultivate the lands which are assigned to him, and selling the rest to the Arabs and Azanhaji traders, who bring horses and other things for sale; as likewise to the Christians, since they have established a trade in these parts.
translation: English version in Robert Kerr, A General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels, vol. 2, 1824 (from Astley's translation and Ramusio's Italian text)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg 10803 (Kerr, General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels, vol. 2, Edinburgh 1824, ch. on Cada Mosto, sect. on Arguin and the Jalofs). Words verbatim. The cut is long (c. 4,000 words) and jumps from the Arabs of the Arguin coast to the kingdom of the Jalofs, so "The king" had no referent: added "[of the Jalofs]" (the page's spelling; the source paragraph just before is about "the king who reigned in Senegal ... Zukholin"). sourceLine: Kerr's introduction says the voyages were made in 1455 and 1456 and were "first printed at Venice in 1507"; the account was not written in 1455, so the line now says "account of his 1455 voyage ..., first printed 1507" (year 1455 kept = date of the events). sourceLine: Francisco Hernández Arana Xajilá, Kaqchikel Maya noble who lived through the Spanish conquest (Brinton's edition credits this early part to his father), The Annals of the Cakchiquels (written c. 1560s–1580s), on the Kaqchikel revolt of 1524
text: Then Tunatiuh [Pedro de Alvarado] began to ask the chiefs for money. He wished that they should give him jars full of precious metals, and even their drinking cups and crowns. Not receiving anything, Tunatiuh became angry and said to the chiefs: “Why have you not given me the metal? If you do not bring me the precious metal in all your towns, choose then, for I shall burn you alive and hang you.” Thus did he speak to the chiefs. … Thus it was that our city was abandoned on the day 7 Ahmak on account of a priest of the Demon, O my children. … But what the chiefs did was soon known to Tunatiuh. Ten days after we had left the city, war was begun by Tunatiuh. On the day 4 Camey began our destruction. Then began our misery. We scattered in the forests; all our towns were taken, O my children; we were slaughtered by Tunatiuh. The Castilians entered the city and they arrived as to a deserted spot. From that time the Castilians were hated by the Cakchiquels. They made trenches, they dug pitfalls, that the horses might be killed, and war was waged by their men.
translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Annals of the Cakchiquels, 1885
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Brinton, The Annals of the Cakchiquels (Philadelphia, 1885), §§152 and 156 (English). Text matches; the cut (§§153–155: more gold demands, the chiefs' payment and their flight from Iximche on a priest's advice) is marked, and '[abandoning their capital, Iximche]' is a pure insertion clarifying 'what the chiefs did' (it summarises §155, which says the city of Iximche was deserted); '[Pedro de Alvarado]' glosses Tunatiuh. Attribution: Brinton's introduction (pp. 57–58) says the writer first names himself as Francisco Ernantez Arana in 1582, but argues the part up to 1559 (which includes 1524) was written by his father, an adult at the conquest, and that Francisco continued it 1560–1583; the sourceLine now says so rather than giving one author as settled. Year 1575 kept as an estimate for a text compiled between c. 1559 and 1583 (Brinton's dates). Lead verifier override: the bracket "[abandoning their capital, Iximche]" summarised the cut §155 rather than naming a referent, so it is removed and the last sentence of §155 is restored from the page instead ("Thus it was that our city was abandoned on the day 7 Ahmak on account of a priest of the Demon, O my children."); "But what the chiefs did was soon known to Tunatiuh" (§156) follows; the "…" between them spans only the Kaqchikel-language text of §156 and the section number on the bilingual page, no English words. Now 197 words.

sourceLine: Canassatego, Onondaga speaker for the Six Nations (Haudenosaunee), reply to the governor of Maryland at the Treaty of Lancaster, 1744, from the treaty minutes printed by Benjamin Franklin (adapted)
text: When you mentioned the Affair of the Land Yesterday, you went back to old Times, and told us, you had been in Possession of the Province of Maryland above One Hundred Years; but what is One Hundred Years in Comparison of the Length of Time since our Claim began? since we came out of this Ground? For we must tell you, that long before One Hundred Years our Ancestors came out of this very Ground, and their Children have remained here ever since. You came out of the Ground in a Country that lies beyond the Seas, there you may have a just Claim, but here you must allow us to be your elder Brethren, and the Lands to belong to us long before you knew any thing of them. … During all this Time the New-comers, the Dutch, acknowledged our Right to the Lands, and solicited us, from Time to Time, to grant them Parts of our Country, and to enter into League and Covenant with us, and to become one People with us.
original: WHEN you mentioned the Affair of the Land Yefterday, you went back ‘to old Times, and told us, you had been ‘in Poffeffion of the Province a Maryland above One Hundred Years; but what is One Hundred Years in ‘Comparifon of the Length of Time fince our Claim began? fince we came out of this Ground? -For we muft tell you, that long before One Hundred Years our Anceftors came out of this very Ground, and their Children have yemained here ever ‘fince. You came out of the’Ground in a Country that lies beyond the Seas, there you may have a juft Claim, but here you muft allow us to be your elder Brethren, and the Lands to belong to us long before you knew any thing of them. … During all this Time the New-comers, the Dutch, acknowledged our Right to the Lands, and follicited us, from Time to Time, to grant them Parts of our Country, and to enter into League and Covenant with us, and to become one People ‘with us.
translation: Interpreted by Conrad Weiser; English minutes printed by Benjamin Franklin, Philadelphia, 1744
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with the page image of Franklin's 1744 printing (archive.org treatyheldattown00unse, leaf 13): Canassatego's speech of June 26, 1744, P.M., 'Conrad Weiser, Interpreter', 'Printed and Sold by B. Franklin'. The OCR corrections are confirmed on the image: 'Province of Maryland' (OCR 'a'), 'remained' (OCR 'yemained'); all other differences are long-s spelling. The cut drops the Dutch ship-and-rope story; 'During all this Time the New-comers, the Dutch' still reads correctly. Translation credit and sourceLine are accurate.

sourceLine: Chanchian, Ming military official of Fujian sent as envoy of the emperor, letter to Pedro de Acuña, Spanish governor of the Philippines, about a rumoured "mountain" of gold and silver near Manila, 1603
text: Because Tio Heng, who is considered a reputable man, has gone to the king of China [the Wanli emperor] and told him that from this kingdom there could each year be taken for the king of China a hundred thousand taes of gold and three hundred thousand taes of silver at his expense, so that his vassals should not pay tribute or be molested, the king has sent a eunuch who is called Cochay to take charge of those who have said that there was gold. … The king gave permission that this should be done, and the eunuch named Cochay, with these mandarins, is accompanying Tio Heng to Luzon to reach the mine of gold and see whether there is or is not such a mine, when they will go back to the king and inform him. … I am quite certain that Tio Heng is lying.
translation: Translated from Chinese into Spanish by a Dominican friar in Manila; English translation by Robert W. Haight, in E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493–1898, vol. 12, 1904
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with B&R vol. 12 (1904), within "Three Chinese mandarins at Manila" (Salazar y Salcedo, 1603): verbatim. "[the Wanli emperor]" stands where the page has the footnote marker [16], and footnote 16 reads "The emperor of China at this time was Wanleh" - it clarifies the referent "king of China". The final piece stops at "Tio Heng is lying" where the source continues ", and command that they shall go..." - the clause stands on its own. Header: letter "wrote in the Chinese characters and tongue ... translated from the original of the said letter by a Dominican religious"; section note: "These documents are translated by Robert W. Haight" (except the second). Dated 31st year of Wanli ("Landec"), 4th moon = May 1603. Role ("who governs the warriors of the province of Hoquien, the envoy of the king") correct.

sourceLine: King Charles II of England, royal charter incorporating the Hudson's Bay Company, 2 May 1670 (adapted)
text: [We] do give, grant and confirm unto the said Governor and Company and their successors the sole Trade and Commerce of all those Seas, Straits, Bays, Rivers, Lakes, Creeks and Sounds in whatsoever Latitude they shall be that lie within the entrance of the Straits commonly called Hudson's Straits … We do give and grant unto the said Governor and Company and their Successors free Liberty and Licence in case they conceive it necessary to send either Ships of War, Men or Ammunition unto any their Plantations, Forts, Factories or Places of Trade aforesaid for the security and defence of the same, and to choose Commanders and Officers over them and to give them power and authority by Commission under their Common Seal or otherwise to continue or make peace or War with any Prince or People whatsoever that are not Christians, in any places where the said Company shall have any Plantations, Forts or Factories or adjacent thereunto as shall be most for the advantage and benefit of the said Governor and Company and of their Trade.
original: Doe give grant and confirme unto the said Governor and Company and theire successors the sole Trade and Commerce of all those Seas Streightes Bayes Rivers Lakes Creekes and Soundes in whatsoever Latitude they shall bee that lie within the entrance of the Streightes commonly called Hudsons Streightes … Wee doe give and grant unto the said Governor and Company and theire Successors free Liberty and Lycence in case they conceive it necessary to send either Shippes of War Men or Amunicion unto any theire Plantacions Fortes Factoryes or Places of Trade aforesaid for the security and defence of the same and to choose Commanders and Officers over them and to give them power and authority by Commission under theire Common Seale or otherwise to continue or make peace or Warre with any Prince or People whatsoever that are not Christians in any places where the said Company shall have any Plantacions Fortes or Factoryes or adjacent thereunto as shall bee most for the advantage and benefitt of the said Governor and Company and of theire Trade
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Wikisource 'Charter of Hudson's Bay' (granted 2 May 1670, 22 Charles II). A word diff of text against original shows spelling modernisation only (Doe→do, theire→their, Streightes→Straits, Shippes→Ships, Amunicion→Ammunition, Plantacions→Plantations, Factoryes→Factories, Warre→War, benefitt→benefit, etc.), plus punctuation. No words changed. '[We]' supplies the grant's subject, the King's royal 'Wee' that opens the clause in the source ('Wee have given granted and confirmed ... Doe give grant and confirme'). It does not change the meaning. The ~2,600-word cut joins the trade-monopoly grant to the clause allowing war and peace with non-Christian peoples, and both are genuine grants of the charter.

sourceLine: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor and king of Spain, the New Laws for the government of the Indies and the good treatment of the Indians, 1542
text: Item, We ordain and command that from henceforward for no cause of war nor any other whatsoever, though it be under title of rebellion, nor by ransom nor in other manner can an Indian be made a slave, and we will that they be treated as our vassals of the Crown of Castile since such they are. No person can make use of the Indians by way of Naboria or Tapia or in any other manner against their will. … Because report has been made to us that owing to the pearl fisheries not having been conducted in a proper manner deaths of many Indians and Negroes have ensued, We command that no free Indian be taken to the said fishery under pain of death … Moreover, We ordain and command that from henceforward no Viceroy, Governor, Audiencia, discoverer, or any other person have power to allot Indians in encomienda by new provision … neither by vacancy nor inheritance, but that the person dying who held the said Indians, they revert to our Royal Crown.
translation: Translated in Henry Stevens, ed., The New Laws of the Indies, 1893
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1542newlawsindies (source: The New Laws of the Indies, ed. Henry Stevens, London: Chiswick Press, 1893). Cuts skip the pearl-fishery provisions for the bishop and judge and a list of ways of transferring encomiendas; the remaining clauses keep their sense. The New Laws were issued in 1542 (Barcelona, November 20); attribution to Charles V (Charles I of Spain) is correct.

sourceLine: Maya chronicle of the katuns (twenty-year periods) from the Book of Chilam Balam of Tizimin, a community record kept in Yucatec Maya by unnamed Maya scribes; the book is dated by its editor to about 1600, and this chronicle's last entries are for 1610 and 1611
text: The fourth ahau; the pestilence, the general death, took place in the fortress. The second ahau; the smallpox took place. … 14. The eleventh ahau; foreigners arrived—mighty men from the east; they came, they arrived here in this land. The ninth ahau; Christianity began; baptism took place; also in this katun came the first bishop Toral; the year which was passing was—1544. 15. The seventh ahau; bishop Landa died in this katun. 16. The fifth ahau; the Fathers settled at Mani; the year that was passing was 1550; in the year 1552 they settled upon the water. 17. 1559; this year came the auditor and built the Hospital. 18. 1560; this year arrived Doctor Quixada, the first governor here in this land. 19. 1562; this year took place the hanging. 20. 1563; this year came Mariscal. 21. 1569; this year smallpox occurred.
translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Maya Chronicles, 1882
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 20205 (Brinton, The Maya Chronicles, 1882), "The Series of the Katuns", sec. 13-21; text correct. Date (flagged): Brinton says this book "appears to have been written about the close of the sixteenth century", which supports year 1600 as an estimate. But the same chronicle on the page continues to "22. 1610; this year those of Tekax were hanged. 23. 1611; ...", so "late sixteenth century" was not accurate for the text as preserved. Brinton notes that the copyists added current items. Kept year 1600 and changed the sourceLine to give both facts.

sourceLine: Pedro de Cieza de León, Spanish soldier and chronicler who saw Potosí in 1549, Chronicle of Peru, part 1, 1553
text: This wealth became so famous, that Indians came from all parts to extract silver from the hill. The climate is cold, and there are no inhabited places in the vicinity. When the Spaniards had taken possession, they began to extract the silver, and he who had a mine gave each Indian who entered it a marc, or, if he was very rich, two marcs every week. So many people came to work the mines, that the place appeared like a great city. … The Indians, who were so ingenious, found that in some parts the silver could not be extracted with the aid of bellows, as was the case at Potosi. They, therefore, made certain moulds of clay, in the shape of a flower-pot in Spain, with many airholes in all parts. Charcoal was put into these moulds, with the metal on the top, and they were then placed on the part of the hill where the wind blew strongest, and thus the metal was extracted, which was then purified and refined with small bellows.
translation: Translated by Clements R. Markham, The Travels of Pedro de Cieza de León, A.D. 1532–50 (Hakluyt Society), 1864
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg #48770 (Markham, Hakluyt Society 1864), ch. CIX: both pieces verbatim. The cut (~366 words: royal fifths 1548-51, failure of bellows) does not alter meaning; piece 2 begins a new paragraph. Cieza himself writes "I will say what I saw in the year of our Lord 1549 in this place", supporting "saw Potosí in 1549". Part 1 of the Crónica del Perú was published 1553; translator Markham named on the title page.

sourceLine: Christopher Columbus, Genoese navigator sailing for Spain, journal of his first voyage (known from Bartolomé de las Casas's abstract), 1492
text: Moreover, Sovereign Princes, besides describing every night the occurrences of the day, and every day those of the preceding night, I intend to draw up a nautical chart, which shall contain the several parts of the ocean and land in their proper situations; and also to compose a book to represent the whole by picture with latitudes and longitudes, on all which accounts it behooves me to abstain from my sleep, and make many trials in navigation, which things will demand much labor. … Sunday, 9 September. Sailed this day nineteen leagues, and determined to count less than the true number, that the crew might not be dismayed if the voyage should prove long. … Monday, 17 September. Steered west and sailed, day and night, above fifty leagues; wrote down only forty-seven; the current favored them. They saw a great deal of weed which proved to be rockweed, it came from the west and they met with it very frequently. They were of opinion that land was near. The pilots took the sun's amplitude, and found that the needles varied to the northwest a whole point of the compass; the seamen were terrified, and dismayed without saying why.
translation: Translated by Samuel Kettell, Personal Narrative of the First Voyage of Columbus to America, 1827, as given in the Internet Medieval Sourcebook
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham columbus1 (Kettell 1827 translation; see columbus-1492-journal-prologue). The bracket "[17 September:]" stood in for cut source words; replaced it with the whole 17 September entry from the page ("Monday, 17 September. Steered west ... without saying why."). sourceLine: the daily entries survive only in Las Casas's abstract, which is largely his paraphrase (Ford 1892, p. 27: "the bulk of it is in no sense the latter's writing"), so added "(known from Bartolomé de las Casas's abstract)".

sourceLine: Christopher Columbus, Genoese navigator sailing for Spain, prologue to the journal of his first voyage (known from Bartolomé de las Casas's abstract), addressed to Ferdinand and Isabella, 1492
text: … and in the present month, in consequence of the information which I had given your Highnesses respecting the countries of India and of a Prince, called Great Can, which in our language signifies King of Kings, how, at many times he, and his predecessors had sent to Rome soliciting instructors who might teach him our holy faith, and the holy Father had never granted his request, whereby great numbers of people were lost, believing in idolatry and doctrines of perdition. Your Highnesses, as Catholic Christians, and princes who love and promote the holy Christian faith, and are enemies of the doctrine of Mahomet, and of all idolatry and heresy, determined to send me, Christopher Columbus, to the above-mentioned countries of India, to see the said princes, people, and territories, and to learn their disposition and the proper method of converting them to our holy faith; and furthermore directed that I should not proceed by land to the East, as is customary, but by a Westerly route, in which direction we have hitherto no certain evidence that any one has gone.
translation: Translated by Samuel Kettell, Personal Narrative of the First Voyage of Columbus to America, 1827, as given in the Internet Medieval Sourcebook
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Translation checked: Fordham credits Olson & Bourne 1906, but Bourne's volume (archive.org northmencolumbus00olso, p. 88) says it uses Markham's translation, and its wording differs ("Because, O most Christian, and very high ..."). The Fordham text matches Samuel Kettell, Personal Narrative of the First Voyage of Columbus (Boston, 1827; archive.org personalnarrati00casagoog) word for word, and Ford 1892 also identifies the prologue as Kettell's. So the Kettell credit is right. Removed a "…" between "our holy faith;" and "and furthermore", where the page has no cut.

sourceLine: Christopher Columbus, letter to Raphael Sanchez, treasurer of Ferdinand and Isabella, reporting his first voyage, March 14, 1493
text: The trees, herbage, and fruits of Espanola are very different from those of Juana, and moreover it abounds in various kinds of spices, gold, and other metals. … Finally, to compress into few words the entire summary of my voyage and speedy return, and of the advantages derivable therefrom, I promise, that with a little assistance afforded me by our most invincible sovereigns, I will procure them as much gold as they need, as great a quantity of spices, of cotton, and of mastic (which is only found in Chios), and as many men for the service of the navy as their Majesties may require. … Let Christ rejoice on earth, as he rejoices in heaven in the prospect of the salvation of the souls of so many nations hitherto lost. Let us also rejoice, as well on account of the exaltation of our faith, as on account of the increase of our temporal prosperity, of which not only Spain, but all Christendom will be partakers.
translation: Translated (from the Latin version) by R. H. Major, Select Letters of Christopher Columbus (Hakluyt Society), 1847, as printed in Paul Leicester Ford, ed., Writings of Christopher Columbus, 1892
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1493-columbustosanchez (source given as Ford, Writings of Christopher Columbus, 1892). Ford's introduction (archive.org ofthenewworld00colurich, p. 33) says the English translation is by R. H. Major, Select Letters, 1847, from the Latin version, so the credit is right. Date "Lisbon, the 14th of March" [1493]. Cuts keep the meaning.

sourceLine: Christopher Columbus, letter to Raphael Sanchez, treasurer of Ferdinand and Isabella, on the fort he left at Navidad on Hispaniola, March 14, 1493
text: … yet there was one large town in Espanola of which especially I took possession, situated in a remarkably favourable spot, and in every way convenient for the purposes of gain and commerce. To this town I gave the name of Navidad del Senor, and ordered a fortress to be built there, which must by this time be completed, in which I left as many men as I thought necessary, with all sorts of arms, and enough provisions for more than a year. I also left them one caravel, and skilful workmen both in ship-building and other arts, and engaged the favor and friendship of the King of the island in their behalf, to a degree that would not be believed, for these people are so amiable and friendly that even the King took a pride in calling me his brother. But supposing their feelings should become changed, and they should wish to injure those who have remained in the fortress, they could not do so, for they have no arms, they go naked, and are moreover too cowardly; …
translation: Translated (from the Latin version) by R. H. Major, Select Letters of Christopher Columbus (Hakluyt Society), 1847, as printed in Paul Leicester Ford, ed., Writings of Christopher Columbus, 1892
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1493-columbustosanchez (Major 1847 via Ford 1892, confirmed as for the gold-spices excerpt). Removed a "…" between "gain and commerce." and "To this town", where only a paragraph break separates them. Final cut is at a semicolon; meaning kept.

sourceLine: Christopher Columbus, letter to Ferdinand and Isabella written from Jamaica during his fourth voyage, July 7, 1503
text: From hence [Veragua] they will obtain gold, and whereas if they should wish to become masters of the products of other lands, they will have to take them by force, or retire empty-handed, in this country they will simply have to trust their persons in the hands of a savage. … The Genoese, Venetians, and all other nations that possess pearls, precious stones, and other articles of value, take them to the ends of the world to exchange them for gold. Gold is the most precious of all commodities; gold constitutes treasure, and he who possesses it has all he needs in this world, as also the means of rescuing souls from purgatory, and restoring them to the enjoyment of paradise.
translation: Translated by R. H. Major, Select Letters of Christopher Columbus (Hakluyt Society), 2nd ed., 1870
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org selectlettersofc00colurich, pp. 202-203 (title page: Major, Select Letters, Hakluyt Society, 2nd ed., 1870, which matches the credit). Ford 1892 dates the letter Jamaica, July 7, 1503. "From hence" refers to Veragua ("this country", in the sentence before), not Jamaica, which the sourceLine names; added the bracket [Veragua] so students do not misread it. Cut skips Columbus's disclaimer; meaning kept. Final recheck: archive.org was temporarily offline (HTTP 500), so the corrected text was re-checked with checkText against verifier 1's saved copy of this sourceUrl (scratch pages/p8.txt, listed against this URL in its urls.txt), and it matches.

sourceLine: Hernan Cortes, Spanish conqueror of Mexico, second letter to Emperor Charles V, on his actions in Tenochtitlan, 1520
text: In these chapels are the images of idols, although, as I have before said, many of them are also found on the outside; the principal ones, in which the people have greatest faith and confidence, I precipitated from their pedestals, and cast them down the steps of the temple, purifying the chapels in which they had stood, … In the place of these I put images of Our Lady and the Saints, which excited not a little feeling in Moctezuma and the inhabitants, who at first remonstrated, declaring that if my proceedings were known throughout the country, the people would rise against me; … Moctezuma and many of the principal citizens remained with me until I had removed the idols, purified the chapels, and placed the images in them, manifesting apparent pleasure; and I forbade them sacrificing human beings to their idols as they had been accustomed to do; because, besides being abhorrent in the sight of God, your sacred Majesty had prohibited it by law, and commanded to put to death whoever should take the life of another.
translation: Translated by George Folsom, The Despatches of Hernando Cortes, 1843, as reprinted in Oliver J. Thatcher, ed., The Library of Original Sources, vol. 5, 1907, and modernized by J. S. Arkenberg for the Internet Modern History Sourcebook
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1520cortes. The page credits Thatcher 1907 and adds "The text has been modernized by Prof. Arkenberg". I checked the wording against Folsom, Despatches of Hernando Cortes (1843; archive.org despatchesofhern00cort, pp. 116-117): it is the same translation, with Folsom's "Muteczuma" changed to "Moctezuma" and similar touches. Added the modernization to the credit. The excerpt began "… the principal ones", whose noun (idols) had been cut; restored the clause before it from the page, "In these chapels are the images of idols, although, as I have before said, many of them are also found on the outside;". Date 1520 correct (second letter, October 30, 1520).

sourceLine: Frederick Coyett, last Dutch governor of Taiwan, and associates (published under the initials C.E.S.), 't Verwaerloosde Formosa (Neglected Formosa), 1675, reporting Koxinga's reply to Dutch envoys in 1661 (adapted)
text: To these requests Koxinga, without concerning himself much about the envoys' credentials, immediately replied that the friendship which the Company held towards him was of the same nature as that held towards other Indian Potentates and Princes: namely, that from their side, it lasted just so long as there was any advantage to be gained by it; for if they saw it to be to their advantage, no such friendship was observed, but they would not scruple in the least to throw a net over any one's head when it suited them to do so. … Hitherto this island had always belonged to China, and the Dutch had doubtless been permitted to live there, seeing that the Chinese did not require it for themselves; but requiring it now, it was only fair that Dutch strangers, who came from far regions, should give way to the masters of the island.
original: To these requests Koxinga, without concerning himself much about the envoys' credentials, immediately replied that the friendship which the Company held towards him was of the same nature as that held towards other Indian Potentates and Princes : namely, that from their side, it lasted just so long as there was any advantage to be gained by it ; for if they saw it to be to their advantage, no such friendship was observed, but they would not scruple in the least to throw a net over any one's head when it suited them to do so. … Hitherto this island had always belonged to Chi;ia, and the Dutch had doubtless been permitted to live there, seeing that the Chinese did not require it for themselves ; but requiring it now, it was only fair that Dutch strangers, who came from far regions, should give way to the masters of the island.
translation: Translated by William Campbell, Formosa under the Dutch, 1903
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared text vs original word by word: only change 'Chi;ia' -> 'China' (plus spacing before ; and :). Page image viewed (archive.org cu31924023514403 leaf 442 = Campbell, Formosa under the Dutch, 1903, p. 423): printed word is 'China'. OK under rule 6. Campbell (preface; p. 383 n.1) says the narrative is translated from 't Verwaerloosde Formosa 'which C. E. S. published in 1675' and does not name Coyett as author, so the sourceLine now states the C.E.S. imprint (the usual reading is Coyett et Socii). The cut drops Koxinga's further point that he took Formosa for his war with the Tartars; the excerpt does not contradict it. Translation credit (Campbell 1903) correct.

sourceLine: Charles Davenant, English writer on trade and public finance and former commissioner of the excise, An Essay on the East-India Trade, written in defence of the East India Company, 1697
text: Their [the English traders'] business in India cannot be managed without frequent gifts and presents to the rajas and governors, according to the practice in all the eastern countries. Forts and castles, with good garrisons, are there indispensably necessary for the preservation of the pepper-trade, and indeed needful upon many other accounts, … besides, they are a safety to our people from any insults of the natives, and a refuge upon any disorder, revolution, or other emergency in the Mogul's state and empire. … The Hollanders, at this time, are very powerful in India; they have many good forts and castles well provided, and large colonies of men; and they can, upon any occasion, call together there 40 strong frigates.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Avalon's text. 'Their' had no referent (in the source it refers back to 'the undertakers' who send large ships to India, i.e. the English traders), so a clarifying bracket was added. The first '…' marked only a paragraph break, so it was removed. The other cuts drop 'and magazines for naval provision...' (20 words) and ~1,400 words of profit figures before the passage on Dutch strength in India. Neither changes the meaning. The excerpt ends at a semicolon where the source goes on to say the Dutch could expel the English, which is consistent. Role corrected as for the other Davenant documents (former excise commissioner, not an official in 1697). 'written in defence of the East India Company' fits the essay, which argues against the bill banning East India silks and calicoes.

sourceLine: Charles Davenant, English writer on trade and public finance and former commissioner of the excise, An Essay on the East-India Trade, 1697 (adapted)
text: There is no trade so advantageous, especially to an island, as that of buying goods in one country, to sell them in another; and it is the original and chief article of the great wealth in Holland. There is gain by the freight; it occasions consumption of our home product; it breeds seamen, increases shipping, and improves navigation. … Our plantations (if we take care to preserve them from foreign insults and invasions) as they increase in people, will consume more of our home manufactures than we have hands to make: they produce commodities indispensably necessary to this part of the world, and not to be produced elsewhere, and, with industry and conduct, may be made an inexhaustible mine of treasure to their mother kingdom.
original: There is no trade so advantageous, especially to an island, as that of buying goods in one country, to sell them in another; and it is the original and chief article of the great wealth in Holland. There is gain by the freight; it occasions consumption of our home product; it breeds seamen, increases shipping, and improves navigation. … Our plantations (if we take care to preserve them from foreign insults and invasions) as they increase in people, will consume more of our home manufactures than we have hands to make: they produce commodities indispensably necessary to this part of the world, and not to be produced elsewhere, and, with industry and conduct, may be made an inexhastible mine of treasure to their mother kingdom.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Avalon's text. All words match. One cut (62 words, on discouraging home manufactures that hinder the carrying trade) does not change the meaning. 'inexhastible' is printed that way on the Avalon page (probably a transcription slip; the page has others, e.g. 'iwll', 'attempot'). It is kept, with [sic] added so students do not take it for our error. Role corrected as for the other Davenant documents. Lead verifier follow-up: found the first edition on archive.org (DAVENANTCharles1696AnEssayOnTheEastIndiaTrade, "London, printed anno MDCXCVI", p. 36, page image leaf 38 viewed): it prints "may be made an inexhaustible Mine of Treasure to their Mother Kingdom", so "inexhastible" is Avalon's slip, not Davenant's. "[sic]" would have pinned it on Davenant, so the document is now adapted: "original" keeps the Avalon wording, "text" has the printed "inexhaustible" (no [sic]); every other word of the excerpt matches p. 36 of the 1696 printing. Note: that imprint is 1696 (Old Style, so it may be Jan–Mar 1697); year 1697 is kept as Avalon gives it.

sourceLine: Charles Davenant, English writer on trade and public finance and former commissioner of the excise, An Essay on the East-India Trade, 1697
text: For Europe draws from thence nothing of solid use; materials to supply luxury, and only perishable commodities, and sends thither gold and silver, which is there buried and never returns. I have good grounds to think, that the silver and gold brought from America, the gold dust brought from Africa, and the silver produced from the European mines, in the 200 years last past, has not amounted to less, in the whole, than 800 millions.
