There is no appearance of this immense sum in any country of Europe. … The English and Dutch, which together are not 1/10th part of Europe, enjoy this traffic almost without any rivalship; and if it be a burthen, it lies not upon the one, but on the other 9 parts, so that if the East-India trade carry out the gold and silver from this side of the world, it is truly and properly, at the cost and expence of France, Germany, Spain, and the northern kingdoms, who have little or no opportunities of trading thither.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Avalon's text of An Essay on the East-India Trade ('by Charles D'Avenant, 1697', addressed to the Marquis of Normanby). All words match. The first two '…' marked only paragraph breaks: nothing is omitted there, so they were removed and the sentences run on as on the page. The third cut (~290 words, on the wear of coin and on why England should keep the trade) does not change the argument. Role corrected: in 1697 Davenant held no government post. He had been an excise commissioner until 1689 and became inspector-general of exports and imports only in 1703, so 'government revenue official' was wrong for the date. Year 1697 is as on the page.

sourceLine: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Spanish soldier with Cortes, True History of the Conquest of New Spain (written c. 1568), on the massacre at Cholula in 1519
text: To which Cortes answered, "That the Spanish laws did not allow such treachery to pass by unpunished, and that they would be punished for it with the loss of their lives." At this moment he ordered a cannon to be fired, which was the signal for us to fall upon them. A great number of these people were put to the sword, and some were burnt alive, to prove the deceitfulness of their false gods. Before a couple of hours had elapsed our friends of Tlascalla came storming out of their camp into the town, and fought courageously with the troops of Cholulla in the streets, who strove to drive them back. They then dispersed themselves about the town for the sake of plunder, and taking prisoners; nor were we able to prevent them. … if we had not made an example here, we should have lived in constant alarm, as we were completely surrounded by Mexican and Cholullan troops, who were everywhere lying in ambush.
translation: Translated by John Ingram Lockhart, The Memoirs of the Conquistador Bernal Diaz del Castillo, vol. 1, 1844
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 32474 (Lockhart, vol. 1, 1844), chapter on Cholula. The first segment is continuous on the page; the second is Diaz's later defence of the massacre against Las Casas ("and, indeed, if we had not made an example here ..."). The cut skips the aftermath, which does not change the meaning of either part. Attribution and date correct.

sourceLine: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Spanish soldier with Cortes, True History of the Conquest of New Spain (written c. 1568), on the Tlaxcalan general Xicotencatl making peace in 1519
text: Xicotencatl said, "He came, in the name of his father, of Maxixcatzin, and of all the caziques of the republic of Tlascalla, to beg of us to admit them to our friendship: he, at the same time, in their name, came to do homage, and promise obedience to our emperor and master, and to beg forgiveness for having taken up arms against us. … Hard experience at length taught them who we were, and they now desired to become our friends, and the vassals of the great emperor Don Carlos; for, they were convinced, that in alliance with us, they would be able to live in security and peace with their wives and children, and not be each moment exposed to the incursions of the treacherous Mexicans." … He [Cortes] then continued to address them in a harsher tone of voice, and mentioned the repeated attacks they had made upon us. He would certainly bear them no malice, and freely forgave all the past, but they must sacredly observe the peace which he had granted them, and show no inconstancy in their conduct. If they did he would assuredly destroy their town and put all the inhabitants to the sword, …
translation: Translated by John Ingram Lockhart, The Memoirs of the Conquistador Bernal Diaz del Castillo, vol. 1, 1844
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 32474 (Lockhart, vol. 1, 1844), ch. LXXIII. The bracket "[Cortes answered that]" stood in for cut source words (rule 5). Restored the source sentences "He [Cortes] then continued to address them in a harsher tone of voice, and mentioned the repeated attacks they had made upon us. He would certainly bear them no malice, and freely forgave all the past, but", keeping only a bracket naming Cortes. The first cut joins two speeches by Xicotencatl, as on the page. Date (written c. 1568, events of 1519) and translation correct.

sourceLine: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Spanish soldier in Cortés's army, The True History of the Conquest of New Spain, written c. 1568 about 1519–1521
text: But to return to Narvaez. He happened to have a negro servant with him ill with the smallpox, through whom this terrific disease, which, according to the accounts of the inhabitants, was previously unknown in the country, spread itself through New Spain, where it created the greater devastation, from the poor Indians, in their ignorance, solely applying cold water as a remedy, with which they constantly bathed themselves; so that vast numbers were cut off before they had the blessing of being received into the bosom of the Christian church. … About this time thousands of people were carried off by the smallpox, and among them numbers of caziques; and Cortes, as though he had been lord of the whole country, appointed the new caziques, but made a point of nominating those who had the best claim.
translation: Translated by John Ingram Lockhart, The Memoirs of the Conquistador Bernal Diaz del Castillo, vol. 1, 1844
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 32474 (images), pp. 332 and 376-377 of Lockhart vol. 1. Both segments are exact. Lockhart is loose (flagged): "before they had the blessing of being received into the bosom of the Christian church" expands Diaz's "sin ser cristianos", but the meaning matches. Only change: added "vol. 1" to the credit, to match the other Lockhart documents.

sourceLine: Anonymous "relation" of Frenchmen who returned to France in a ship of Dieppe from the East Indies, on wrongs done by the Dutch to English traders there, 1617 (adapted)
text: Two English ships coming to Banda, in course of trade and traffic, the Hollanders assaulted with certain of their ships, which English ships in their resistance and defense the said Hollanders took, slew seven or eight of their men (whereof one was a chief factor), chained the captain, merchants, and mariners, and put the mariners into their galleys. All the munition and victuals in the said English ships did the Hollanders take out and carried the same ashore, challenging all to be theirs as their proper inheritance, and therefore will be lords of the same. … At Bantam the English and Hollanders had great disputes, insomuch as it was verily thought they would have fought together in the road, … but they fought not, for the governor of Bantam forbade them to fight in his road, and threatened them that if they did fight contrary to his command he would cut the throats of all their men that he should find upon the land.
original: Two English ships coming to Banda, in course of trade and traffic, the Hollanders assaulted with certain of their ships, which English ships in their resistance and defense of the said Hollanders took, slew seven or eight of their men (whereof one was a chief factor), chained the captain, merchants, and mariners, and put the mariners into their galleys. All the munition and victuals in the said English ships did the Hollanders take out and carried the same ashore, challenging all to be theirs as their proper inheritance, and therefore will be lords of the same. … At Bantam the English and Hollanders had great disputes, insomuch as it was verily thought they would have fought together in the road, … but they fought not, for the governor of Bantam forbade them to fight in his road, and threatened them that if they did fight contrary to his command he would cut the throats of all their men that he should find upon the land.
translation: English text as printed in James Harvey Robinson, ed., Readings in European History, vol. 2, 1906; original language and translator not stated
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Fordham 1617englandindies credits Robinson, Readings in European History, vol. II (1906), pp. 333-335. I checked the printed page (archive.org readingsineurope02robiuoft, leaf n372, p. 335), which reads "which English ships in their resistance and defense the said Hollanders took": the Hollanders took the English ships. Fordham's transcription inserts "of" ("defense of the said Hollanders"), which garbles the sense. The document is now adapted: "original" keeps the page wording with "of", and "text" drops "of" to match the printed book. sourceLine: Robinson's heading reads "A relation of the Frenchmen which lately arrived into France in a ship of Dieppe out of the East Indies ... (1617)"; it does not call them sailors, so "French sailors returned to Dieppe" became "Frenchmen who returned to France in a ship of Dieppe". Original language and translator are not stated, which the credit says.

sourceLine: Jean-Baptiste du Halde, French Jesuit in Paris who compiled the reports of missionaries in China (not an eyewitness), Description of the Empire of China, 1735, on the Kangxi emperor (reigned 1661–1722)
text: This nation, naturally proud, looked upon themselves as the most learned in the world, and they enjoyed this reputation without disturbance because they were acquainted with no other people more knowing than themselves; but they were undeceived by the ingenuity of the missionaries who appeared at court. The proof which they gave of their capacity served greatly to authorize their ministry and to gain esteem for the religion which they preached. The late emperor, Cang hi [Kangxi], whose chief delight was to acquire knowledge, was never weary of seeing or hearing them. On the other hand, the Jesuits, perceiving how necessary the protection of this great prince was to the progress of the Gospel, omitted nothing that might excite his curiosity and satisfy this natural relish for the sciences.
translation: Translator not named; English version printed in Eva March Tappan, ed., The World's Story, vol. 1, 1914 (Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Fordham 1680halde1.asp ('Père du Halde: Teaching Science to the Manchu Emperor, c. 1680'; from Tappan, The World's Story, vol. I, 1914, pp. 155-162; no translator named): opening paragraph verbatim, '[Kangxi]' glosses 'Cang hi'. Rule 4: du Halde (1674-1743) never went to China; he edited missionaries' reports into the 1735 Description. It was written within 1450-1750 and by a contemporary of Kangxi's reign, so it stays as a period source of European (Jesuit) views, and the sourceLine now says plainly that he was a compiler in Paris, not an eyewitness. 'The late emperor' fits writing after 1722; year 1735 = publication, and sourceLine gives Kangxi's reign.

sourceLine: Sir Dudley North, London merchant who traded for years in the Ottoman Empire, later a commissioner of the Treasury, Discourses upon Trade, 1691
text: No Man is richer for having his Estate all in Money, Plate, etc. lying by him, but on the contrary, he is for that reason the poorer. That man is richest, whose Estate is in a growing condition, either in Land at Farm, Money at Interest, or Goods in Trade. … Silver and Gold, like other commodities, have their ebbings and flowings: Upon the arrival of Quantities from Spain, the Mint commonly gives the best price; that is, coyned Silver, for uncoyned Silver, weight for weight. … That Laws to hamper Trade whether Forreign, or Domestick, relating to Money, or other Merchandizes, are not Ingredients to make a People Rich, and abounding in Money, and Stock.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Avalon's Discourses upon Trade (London: Tho. Basset, 1691), 'A Discourse of Coyned Money' and its conclusion. The three pieces are verbatim. They are joined by long cuts (~2,100 and ~1,300 words) but each piece states North's own view and none reverses it. The last piece is his concluding 'uniform Sentiment' that laws hampering trade do not make a people rich. Role is right: a Levant (Turkey) merchant at Smyrna and Constantinople, knighted 1683, later a commissioner of customs and of the Treasury, all before 1691.

sourceLine: The States General of the United Provinces of the Netherlands, Act of Abjuration renouncing allegiance to King Philip II of Spain, 1581
text: As it is apparent to all that a prince is constituted by God to be ruler of a people, to defend them from oppression and violence as the shepherd his sheep; and whereas God did not create the people slaves to their prince, to obey his commands, whether right or wrong, but rather the prince for the sake of the subjects (without which he could be no prince), to govern them according to equity, to love and support them as a father his children or a shepherd his flock, and even at the hazard of life to defend and preserve them. And when he does not behave thus, but, on the contrary, oppresses them, seeking opportunities to infringe their ancient customs and privileges, exacting from them slavish compliance, then he is no longer a prince, but a tyrant, and the subjects are to consider him in no other view. And particularly when this is done deliberately, unauthorized by the states, they may not only disallow his authority, but legally proceed to the choice of another prince for their defense.
translation: Translator not named; reprinted in Oliver J. Thatcher, ed., The Library of Original Sources, vol. 5 (Milwaukee: University Research Extension Co., 1907), via the Internet Modern History Sourcebook
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with the Fordham Modern History Sourcebook page (from Thatcher, Library of Original Sources vol. V, 1907, pp. 189-197). The '…' between 'to defend and preserve them.' and 'And when he does not behave thus' marked no omission (the source runs straight on), so it was removed. Translation: the page names no translator (Thatcher reprints an unnamed English version), so the credit now says 'Translator not named; reprinted in…'. Attribution (States General, The Hague, 26 July 1581) and year correct.

sourceLine: Metacom (King Philip), Wampanoag sachem, and his council, grievances stated to Rhode Island officials in June 1675, as recorded by Deputy Governor John Easton, A Relacion of the Indyan Warre, 1675 (adapted)
text: They said they had been the first in doing good to the English, and the English the first in doing wrong; said when the English first came their king's father was as a great man and the English as a little child; he constrained other Indians from wronging the English and gave them corn and showed them how to plant and was free to do them any good and had let them have a 100 times more land than now the king had for his own people … now their kings were forewarned not for to part with land for nothing in comparison to the value thereof; now whom the English had owned for king or queen they would disinherit, and make another king that would give or sell them their land, that now they had no hopes left to keep any land … we endeavored that however they should lay down their arms, for the English were too strong for them; they said then the English should do to them as they did when they were too strong for the English.
original: Hhay saied thay had bine the first in doing good to the English, and the English the first in doing rong, saied when the English first Came their kings father was as a great man and the English as a Utell Child, he Constraened other indians from rouging the English and gave them Coren and shewed them how to plant and was free to dq them ani good and had let them have a 100 times more land, then now the king had for his own peopell, … now ther kings wear forewarned not for to part with land for nothing in Gumpareson to the valew therofj now home* the English had owned for king or queen thay^ wold disinheret, and make a nother king that wold give or seell them there land, that now thay had no hopes left to kepe ani land. … we indevered that however thay should lay doune ther arems for the English wear to strong for them, thay saied then the English should do to them as thay did when thay wear to strong for the english.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared word by word with the printed pages (Lincoln, Narratives of the Indian Wars 1675–1699, 1913, pp. 10–11; page images archive.org narrativesindia01mathgoog n28–n29). Every text/original difference is spelling modernisation of Easton's phonetic spelling or an OCR misreading confirmed on the image: printed 'thay' (OCR 'Hhay'), 'litell' (OCR 'Utell') → little, 'ronging' (OCR 'rouging') → wronging, 'do' (OCR 'dq'), 'Cumpareson' (OCR 'Gumpareson'), 'therof.' (OCR 'therofj'); 'home' is printed with the editor's footnote 'Whom', so → whom is spelling; 'then' → than. Cuts drop the grievances about testimony, drunkenness and cheating in land sales, and the cattle/liquor grievances, without changing what is kept. Easton was deputy governor of Rhode Island 1674–1676 (editor's introduction); the Relacion is dated '5th 12m: 1675' (Feb. 1675/6) and headed 1675; the meeting with Philip was in June 1675, a week before the war began.

sourceLine: Parliament of the English Commonwealth, An Act for increase of Shipping and Encouragement of the Navigation of this Nation (the Navigation Act), 9 October 1651
text: For the increase of the shipping and the encouragement of the navigation of this nation, … be it enacted by this present Parliament, and the authority thereof, that from and after the first day of December, one thousand six hundred fifty and one, and from thence forwards, no goods or commodities whatsoever of the growth, production or manufacture of Asia, Africa or America, or of any part thereof; … shall be imported or brought into this Commonwealth of England, or into Ireland, or any other lands, islands, plantations, or territories to this Commonwealth belonging, or in their possession, in any other ship or ships, vessel or vessels whatsoever, but only in such as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of this Commonwealth, or the plantations thereof, as the proprietors or right owners thereof; and whereof the master and mariners are also for the most part of them of the people of this Commonwealth, under the penalty of the forfeiture and loss of all the goods that shall be imported contrary to this act.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Wikisource 'Navigation Act (1651)' [Oct. 9, 1651, Scobell's Acts, pt. ii, p. 176]. Words match. The cuts drop a pious clause and 'or of any islands belonging to them...' and do not change the meaning. The excerpt ends before the further forfeiture of the ship, which is not misleading. The title 'An Act for increase of Shipping and Encouragement of the Navigation of this Nation', the Rump/Commonwealth Parliament and the date 9 October 1651 are right.

sourceLine: Parliament of England under Charles II, An Act for the Encouraging and Increasing of Shipping and Navigation (Navigation Act), 1660
text: Be it enacted by the King’s most excellent majesty, … That from and after the first day of December one thousand six hundred and sixty, and from thenceforward, no goods or commodities whatsoever shall be imported into or exported out of any lands, islands, plantations or territories to his Majesty belonging or in his possession, … in Asia, Africa, or America, in any other ship or ships, vessel or vessels whatsoever, but in such ships or vessels as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of England or Ireland, … and all governors of the said lands, islands, plantations or territories, and every of them, are hereby strictly required and commanded, and all who hereafter shall be governors of any such islands, plantations or territories, by his Majesty, his heirs and successors, shall before their entrance into their government take a solemn oath, to do their utmost, that every the aforementioned clauses, and all the matters and things therein contained, shall be punctually and bona fide observed according to the true intent and meaning thereof.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Wikisource 12 Car. II c. 18 (Pickering's Statutes at Large), assented 13 September 1660. The last cut ('are hereby strictly required and commanded, … shall before their entrance') removed the subject of 'shall' ('and all who hereafter shall be governors of any such islands, plantations or territories, by his Majesty, his heirs and successors,'). That left a broken sentence that read as if present governors were 'commanded … shall'. Those 21 source words are restored (now ~175 words). The other cuts (the Lords and Commons formula, 'or which may hereafter belong...', and ~490 words of penalties and the clause on aliens) keep the meaning. sourceLine and year are right.

sourceLine: Catalina de Erauso, Basque woman who fled a convent and lived as a man, serving as a soldier in Peru and Chile, memoir attributed to her, c. 1626 (authorship and date disputed: her 1908 translator thought another hand pieced it together from her own accounts; first printed 1829)
text: The lady was a half-breed, the daughter of a Spaniard and an Indian woman. She was a widow, a good-natured soul, who seeing me and hearing of my calamity and misery, took pity on me and received me kindly. … and had vast herds and flocks; and as, apparently, few Spaniards ever pass that way, it seems that she cast her eye on me for her daughter. … A few days later she gave me to understand that she would be willing for me to marry a daughter of hers who lived there with her, and who was very black and as ugly as the devil — the very opposite of my taste, which has always been for pretty faces. I vowed myself enchanted at a condescension so undeserved, and fell at her feet, declaring that she might command me as a creature of hers snatched from destruction. I continued to serve her to the best of my powers. She dressed me out like a beau, and confidingly entrusted me with her house and belongings.
translation: Translated by James Fitzmaurice-Kelly, The Nun Ensign, 1908
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org nunensign00erauuoft, ch. VII, pp. 45-47 (Fitzmaurice-Kelly, London: Fisher Unwin, MCMVIII = 1908). (1) Authenticity (flagged): the translator writes that "we have no evidence as to when, or by whom, the Historia was written", reports Serrano y Sanz's view that it is a forgery, and concludes it is "mainly pieced together by some deft hand from the genuine Relaciones" of Erauso. It was first printed by Ferrer in 1829 (pp. xxxiii-xxxix). The sourceLine now says so instead of implying a dated memoir; c. 1626 is kept as the date of her own accounts, which end with her 1626 stay in Rome. Under rule 4 it is a borderline case; I kept it because the edition judges it based on her first-hand accounts. (2) The cut after "who was very black" removed "and as ugly as the devil — the very opposite of my taste, which has always been for pretty faces.". Without it, "I vowed myself enchanted" reads as sincere, when the narrator is pretending; restored it. The racist language is the source's own.

sourceLine: Ferdinand and Isabella, monarchs of Castile and Aragon, grant of titles and privileges to Christopher Columbus before his first voyage, April 30, 1492
text: For as much of you, Christopher Columbus, are going by our command, with some of our vessels and men, to discover and subdue some Islands and Continent in the ocean, and it is hoped that by God's assistance, some of the said Islands and Continent in the ocean will be discovered and conquered by your means and conduct, therefore it is but just and reasonable, that since you expose yourself to such danger to serve us, you should be rewarded for it. … Our will is, That you, Christopher Columbus, after discovering and conquering the said Islands and Continent in the said ocean, or any of them, shall be our Admiral of the said Islands and Continent you shall so discover and conquer; and that you be our Admiral, Vice-Roy, and Governour in them, and that for the future, you may call and stile yourself, D. Christopher Columbus, and that your sons and successors in the said employment, may call themselves Dons, Admirals, Vice-Roys, and Governours of them …
translation: Early English translation as printed in Francis Newton Thorpe, ed., The Federal and State Constitutions, Colonial Charters, and Other Organic Laws (US Government Printing Office), 1909; translator not named
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Avalon (source: Thorpe, Federal and State Constitutions, 1909; no translator named, which the credit says). Dated Granada, April 30, 1492. The excerpt ended on a semicolon in mid-sentence; changed the final ";" to " …" so it is marked as cut. No words changed.

sourceLine: Thomas Gage, English Dominican friar who lived in Mexico and Guatemala 1625–1637 and later turned Protestant and wrote for an English readership hostile to Spain, The English-American, or A New Survey of the West-Indias, 1648
text: In all the Dominions of the King of Spain in America, there are two sorts of Spaniards more opposite one to another then in Europe the Spaniard is opposite to the French, or to the Hollander, or to the Portingall; To wit, they that are born in any parts of Spain and goe thither, and they that are borne there of Spanish parents, whom the Spaniards, to distinguish them from themselves, terme Criolio's, signifying the Natives of that Countrey. … The cause of this deadly hatred hath proceeded from a jealousie which the Spaniards have ever had of the Criolio's, that they would faine withdraw themselves first from the commerce with Spain, and secondly, from the Government which is laid upon them; which is such, that the Criolio's must be alwaies under, and a subject, alwaies governed, but scarce any a Governour. Never yet was there seen any Criolio made Viceroy of Mexico, or Peru … And not onely thus are they kept from offices, but daily affronted by the Spaniards as uncapable of any Government, and termed halfe Indians by them.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 54425 (Gage, The English-American, London 1648), ch. IV, p. 9-10 of the edition. Cuts skip Gage's anti-Spanish aside and lists of offices; "this deadly hatred" follows from "two sorts of Spaniards more opposite one to another". The sourceLine's role (Dominican in Mexico and Guatemala 1625-1637, later Protestant, writing for an anti-Spanish English readership) is correct.

sourceLine: Thomas Gage, English Dominican friar who lived in Mexico and Guatemala 1625–1637 and later turned Protestant and wrote for an English readership hostile to Spain, The English-American, or A New Survey of the West-Indias, on Mexico City, 1648
text: Both men and women are excessive in their apparell, using more silkes then stuffes and cloth; pretious Stones and Pearles further much this their vaine ostentation; a hat-band and rose made of Diamonds in a Gentlemans hat is common, and a hat-band of Pearles is ordinary in a Tradesman; nay a Blackmore or Tauny young maide and slave will make hard shift but shee will bee in fashion with her Neckchaine and Bracelets of Pearls, and her Eare-bobs of some considerable Jewels. The attire of this baser sort of people of Blackmores and Mulatta's (which are of a mixt nature, of Spaniards and Blackmores) is so light, and their carriage so enticing, that many Spaniards even of the better sort (who are too too prone to Venery) disdaine their Wives for them.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 54425, ch. on Mexico City; one continuous passage with no cuts. Attribution correct.

sourceLine: Thomas Gage, English Dominican friar who lived in Mexico and Guatemala 1625–1637 and later turned Protestant and wrote for an English readership hostile to Spain, The English-American, or A New Survey of the West-Indias, on Guatemala, 1648
text: The Spaniards that live about that Country … alleadge that all their trading, and farming, is for the good of the Common-wealth, and therefore whereas there are not Spaniards enough … all are not able to buy slaves and Blackmores, they stand in need of the Indians help to serve them for their pay and hire; whereupon it hath been considered, that a partition of Indian labourers be made every Monday, or Sonday in the afternoon to the Spaniards … for every Indian delivered unto them, they give unto the Juez Repartidor or officer, halfe a Riall, which is three pence an Indian for his fees, … If complaint be made by any Spaniard that such and such an Indian did run away from him … the Indian must be brought, and surely tied to a post by his hands in the Market place, and there be whipped upon his bare backe. But if the poor Indian complaine that the Spaniards cousened and cheated him of his shovell, axe, bill, mantle, or wages, no justice shall be executed against the cheating Spaniard … Thus are the poore Indians sold for three pence a peece for a whole weeks slavery …
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 54425, Guatemala chapter, pp. 139-140 (flagged as cut to 180 words). The closing "Thus are the poore Indians sold for three pence a peece" depends on the cut description of the Juez Repartidor's fee. Restored the single source clause that explains it ("for every Indian delivered unto them, they give unto the Juez Repartidor or officer, halfe a Riall, which is three pence an Indian for his fees,") and added a closing "…" because the excerpt ends mid-sentence. The other cuts keep the meaning. Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: Journal of Vasco da Gama's first voyage, by a member of the crew (attributed to Alvaro Velho), reporting da Gama's words to the Zamorin (ruler) of Calicut, May 1498
text: And the captain-major told him he was the ambassador of a King of Portugal, who was Lord of many countries and the possessor of great wealth of every description, exceeding that of any king of these parts; that for a period of sixty years his ancestors had annually sent out vessels to make discoveries in the direction of India, as they knew that there were Christian kings there like themselves. This, he said, was the reason which induced them to order this country to be discovered, not because they sought for gold or silver, for of this they had such abundance that they needed not what was to be found in this country. … There reigned a king now whose name was Dom Manuel, who had ordered him to build three vessels, of which he had been appointed captain-major, and who had ordered him not to return to Portugal until he should have discovered this King of the Christians, on pain of having his head cut off.
translation: Translated by E. G. Ravenstein, A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama (Hakluyt Society), 1898, as reprinted in Oliver J. Thatcher, ed., The Library of Original Sources, vol. 5, 1907
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1497degama and Ravenstein (Gutenberg 46440): same translation. The cut skips one sentence about earlier captains returning without success. "him" is the king, named in the sourceLine. Date (late May 1498) correct.

sourceLine: Journal of Vasco da Gama's first voyage, by a member of the crew (attributed to Alvaro Velho), on dealings with the court and merchants of Calicut, May-June 1498
text: On Tuesday, May 29, the captain-major got ready the following things to be sent to the king, viz., twelve pieces of lambel, four scarlet hoods, six hats, four strings of coral, a case containing six wash-hand basins, a case of sugar, two casks of oil, and two of honey. And as it is the custom not to send anything to the king without the knowledge of the Moor, his factor, and of the bale [governor], the captain-major informed them of his intention. They came, and when they saw the present they laughed at it, saying that it was not a thing to offer to a king, that the poorest merchant from Mecca, or any other part of India, gave more, and that if he wanted to make a present it should be in gold, as the king would not accept such things. … On the following day, Saturday, June 2, in the morning, these gentlemen [i.e., the bale and others] came back, and this time they wore better faces. They told the captain-major that as he had informed the king that he intended to land his merchandise, he should now give orders to have this done, …
translation: Translated by E. G. Ravenstein, A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama (Hakluyt Society), 1898, as reprinted in Oliver J. Thatcher, ed., The Library of Original Sources, vol. 5, 1907
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1497degama (Ravenstein translation via Thatcher, checked against Gutenberg 46440). Each segment began "They ..." with no referent, because the sentences naming them were cut. Restored from the page "And as it is the custom not to send anything to the king without the knowledge of the Moor, his factor, and of the bale, the captain-major informed them of his intention." and "On the following day, Saturday, June 2, in the morning, these gentlemen [i.e., the bale and others] came back, and this time they wore better faces." (the bracket is on the page and in Ravenstein). Added [governor] after the first "bale", per Ravenstein's note 152 ("Bale in the Arabic Wali, governor"). The second sentence also shows that the June 2 terms came after the Portuguese had been detained. Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: Journal of Vasco da Gama's first voyage, by a member of the crew (attributed to Alvaro Velho), on arrival at Calicut, India, May 1498
text: On the following day (May 22) these same boats came again alongside, when the captain-major sent one of the convicts to Calicut, and those with whom he went took him to two Moors from Tunis, who could speak Castilian and Genoese. The first greeting that he received was in these words: "May the Devil take thee! What brought you hither?" They asked what he sought so far away from home, and he told them that we came in search of Christians and of spices. They said: "Why does not the King of Castile, the King of France, or the Signoria of Venice send thither?" He said that the King of Portugal would not consent to their doing so, and they said he did the right thing. … When he had eaten he returned to the ships, accompanied by one of the Moors, who was no sooner on board, than he said these words: "A lucky venture, a lucky venture! Plenty of rubies, plenty of emeralds! You owe great thanks to God, for having brought you to a country holding such riches!"
translation: Translated by E. G. Ravenstein, A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama (Hakluyt Society), 1898, as reprinted in Oliver J. Thatcher, ed., The Library of Original Sources, vol. 5, 1907
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Fordham 1497degama credits only Thatcher, Library of Original Sources vol. 5 (1907). Checked the text against Ravenstein's 1898 Hakluyt translation (Gutenberg 46440): same wording ("May the Devil take thee! What brought you hither?" ... "in search of Christians and of spices"), Thatcher lightly editing it ("captain" to "captain-major"). Credit is right. The cut skips one sentence (bread and honey); meaning kept. The quotation marks are on the page HTML.

sourceLine: Pero de Magalhães de Gândavo, Portuguese writer who had lived in Brazil, History of the Province of Santa Cruz (Brazil), 1576
text: Since these Indians covet certain things which come from the Kingdom of Portugal, namely, shirts, jerkins, iron tools, and similar things, they sell one another in exchange for these articles to the Portuguese; these, on the other hand, capture as many as they want and do them many injuries without any one's checking them [the Portuguese]. But now there is no longer this disorder in the land or the traffic in slaves as formerly. … the Fathers [Jesuits] ordered and arranged with the Governours and Captains of the land that there should be no more trading in slaves in the same way as in the past … whatever slaves are newly come out of the sertao … all go first to the custom house where they examine them and ask them questions: who sold them and what were the terms of purchase; for no one has the right to sell them save their fathers (if in case of dire necessity) or those who have captured them in a just war; those whom they find acquired illegally, they set at liberty.
translation: Translated by John B. Stetson Jr., The Histories of Brazil, Cortes Society, 1922
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org historiesofbrazi02ganduoft, ch. XIII "Of the results obtained there by the Fathers of the Company", pp. 113-115 (Stetson 1922). (1) The cut "save their fathers … or those who have captured them in a just war" removed the condition "(if in case of dire necessity)", making it seem fathers could sell their children freely; restored it. (2) Added [Jesuits] after "the Fathers" (the chapter's subject is the Fathers of the Company of Jesus). "[the Portuguese]" is Stetson's own bracket on the page. Role changed as for gandavo-1576-settlers-slaves.

sourceLine: Pero de Magalhães de Gândavo, Portuguese writer who had lived in Brazil, History of the Province of Santa Cruz (Brazil), 1576
text: …there are many others who are scattered about on the sugar mills and ranches, here [in Pernambuco] as in the other Captaincies, all the surrounding territory being settled. … for the inhabitants are much favoured and aided by the Indians of the land from among whom they get an infinite number of slaves with whom they work their farms. … The first thing they try to obtain is slaves to work the farms; and any one who succeeds in obtaining two pairs or a half-dozen of them (although he may not have another earthly possession) has the means to sustain his family in a respectable way; for one fishes for him, another hunts for him, and the rest cultivate and till his fields, and consequently there is no expense for the maintenance of his slaves or of his household. … one may infer how very extensive are the estates of those who own two hundred or three hundred slaves, for there are many colonists who have that number or more.
translation: Translated by John B. Stetson Jr., The Histories of Brazil, Cortes Society, 1922
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org historiesofbrazi02ganduoft, pp. 33-34 and 41 (Stetson, Cortes Society, vol. II, 1922; History printed 1576). "here" pointed to Paranambuco (Pernambuco), named in a sentence the excerpt cuts; added the bracket [in Pernambuco]. Role: the edition's introduction describes him as a writer who went to Brazil and stayed long enough to collect his material; it names no office, so "Portuguese official" became "Portuguese writer who had lived in Brazil". The "…" before "one may infer" skips a footnote marker and "From this,".

sourceLine: Garcilaso de la Vega, "El Inca", son of a Spanish conquistador and an Inca noblewoman, raised in Cuzco and writing in Spain, Royal Commentaries of the Incas, 1609
text: One of the chief things that have happened in the Indies, which must not be forgotten, is the introduction of Negroes, whom the Spaniards have brought there as slaves to work for them ; … From these two races others have arisen, mixed in various ways, and they have given them different names for distinction. … The sons of a Spanish man and woman, born in the country, are called Creoles, which means that they are born in the country. … Thus both Spaniards and Negroes born in the Indies are called Creoles. … The sons of a Spaniard by an Indian woman, or of an Indian by a Spanish woman are called Mestizos, which means that we are a mixture of both nations. … and, being a name given by our parents, I call myself by it with open mouth, and pride myself upon it. But the Indians look upon it as an insult, if anyone calls them Mestizos. … All these names, … have been invented in my country to designate the generations that have risen up since the arrival of the Spaniards; …
translation: Translated by Clements R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, vol. 2, 1871
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org india.history.resource.85882 (Markham, Royal Commentaries vol. II, Book IX ch. XXXI, pp. 502-504; Hakluyt Society 1871). The excerpt kept only "Mestizos" and then closed with "All these names, and others which I do not mention ... have been invented", which had nothing to refer to, because every other name had been cut. Restored, from the same chapter, "From these two races others have arisen ... different names for distinction", the Creole definition and "Thus both Spaniards and Negroes born in the Indies are called Creoles", and the Quatralvo definition. I skipped the sentences where the OCR is unreliable ("Mulaito", "Meéstizo", "Montafies"). Attribution, date and translation correct. Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: Garcilaso de la Vega, "El Inca", son of a Spanish conquistador and an Inca noblewoman, raised in Cuzco and writing in Spain, Royal Commentaries of the Incas, 1609
text: Many cows were introduced soon after the conquest, and spread over the whole country. The same must have been the case with pigs and sheep; for I remember having seen them at Cuzco, when I was quite a child. … The first bullocks I saw at the plough were in the valley of Cuzco in the year 1550, one year more or less … A whole army of Indians took me to see them, who came from all parts, astonished at a sight so wonderful and novel for them and for me. They said that the Spaniards were too idle to work, and that they forced those great animals to do their work for them. … When they began to sell cows, the prices were from two hundred pesos, lowering gradually as the beasts became more plentiful, until the price fell suddenly to what they now sell at. … In 1559 I saw cows bought at Cuzco for seventeen pesos or twenty and a half ducats, rather less than more.
translation: Translated by Clements R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, vol. 2, 1871
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org firstpartofroyal02vega, Book IX ch. XVII, pp. 470-471 (Markham, Hakluyt Society, vol. II, M.DCCC.LXXI = 1871). Cuts skip names and anecdotes; meaning kept. Published Lisbon 1609; correct.

sourceLine: Garcilaso de la Vega, called "El Inca," son of a Spanish conquistador and an Inca noblewoman, Royal Commentaries of the Incas, 1609
text: My mother resided in Cuzco, her native town, and almost every week some of the few male and female relations, who escaped the cruelty and tyranny of Atahualpa … came to visit her. On the occasion of these visits their usual conversation was on the subject of the origin of the Yncas, of their majesty, of the grandeur of their empire, of their greatness, of their mode of government in peace and war, and of the laws which they ordained for the good of their subjects. In short, they omitted nothing relating to the flourishing period of their history in the course of these conversations. From their past greatness and prosperity, they went on to the present state of affairs; they mourned for their dead kings, their lost rule, their fallen state. Such and the like discourses were held by the Yncas and Pallas when they visited my mother, and, at the memory of their lost happiness, they always concluded their conversations with tears and mourning, saying “We are turned from rulers into vassals.”
translation: Translated by Clements R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, 1869
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Markham's translation, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, vol. 1 (Hakluyt Society, M.DCCC.LXIX = 1869), book I, ch. 15. Text matches; the one cut removes a parenthesis ('as we shall relate in the account of his life'). Garcilaso, son of a Spanish conquistador and an Inca noblewoman; Part 1 published Lisbon 1609. All consistent.

sourceLine: Garcilaso de la Vega, "El Inca", son of a Spanish conquistador and an Inca noblewoman, raised in Cuzco, Royal Commentaries of the Incas, book 8, 1609
text: They could not turn it [quicksilver] to any purpose, while they saw that it was injurious to the lives of those who worked to procure it, for it caused them to tremble, and lose their feeling. For this reason, being Kings who cared much for the welfare of their people, in accordance with their title of Lovers of the Poor, they prohibited its being extracted, by a law. The Indians, therefore, abominated it to such an extent that they even let its name drop from memory and from their language. Thus they have no name for mercury, except those that have been adopted since the Spaniards discovered it in 1567.
translation: Translated by Clements R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, vol. 2 (Hakluyt Society), 1871
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, vol. II (books V-IX), Hakluyt Society 1871, book 8 ch. XXV "Of the quicksilver", p. 413: verbatim continuous passage; "[quicksilver]" is a pure gloss on "it" (the Inca kings who are "They" are named in the next sentence). Running heads confirm the Eighth Book. Attribution and 1609 (Lisbon) correct.

sourceLine: Miantonomo, Narragansett sachem, speech to the Montaukett on Long Island in 1642, as reported to and recorded by Lion Gardiner, English settler and former commander of the fort at Saybrook, Relation of the Pequot Warres (written 1660)
text: [Miantonomo] gave them gifts, calling them brethren and friends, for so are we all Indians as the English are, and say brother to one another; so must we be one as they are, otherwise we shall be all gone shortly, for you know our fathers had plenty of deer and skins, our plains were full of deer, as also our woods, and of turkies, and our coves full of fish and fowl. But these English having gotten our land, they with scythes cut down the grass, and with axes felled the trees; their cows and horses eat the grass, and their hogs spoil our clam banks, and we shall all be starved; therefore it is best for you to do as we, for we are all the Sachems from east to west, both Mouquakues and Mowhauks joining with us, and we are all resolved to fall upon them all, at one appointed day.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with A History of the Pequot War (Cincinnati: J. Harpel for W. Dodge, 1860, per archive.org metadata; ahistorypequotw00dodggoog), Gardiner's Relation pp. 25–26, dated East Hampton, June 12, 1660. Text matches the page ('[Miantonomo]' replaces the pronoun 'he'; source spells him 'Miantenomie'). Role corrected: by 1642 Gardiner was no longer commanding Saybrook fort — the narrative has the Montaukett coming to him 'at my house' by 'my Island', and the editor's note says he left the fort and moved to Gardiner's Island; he was not present at the speech, which the Montaukett sachem Waiandance reported to him ('he came over to me and acquainted me'), so the sourceLine now says 'as reported to and recorded by'. The 1642 date is the usual dating (not stated on the page; Miantonomo died 1643).

sourceLine: Anonymous Genoese pilot on Magellan's fleet, narrative of the voyage (c. 1524), on events in Cebu and Mactan in the Philippines, 1521
text: … in this island [Cebu] Fernando de Magalhaes did what he pleased with the consent of the country, and in one day eight hundred people became Christian, … he sent to a village … which is named Matam [Mactan], and which is also an island, and ordered them to send him at once three goats, three pigs, three loads of rice, and three loads of millet for provisions for the ships; they replied that of each article which he sent to ask them three of, they would send to him by twos, and if he was satisfied with this they would at once comply, if not, it might be as he pleased, but that they would not give it. Because they did not choose to grant what he demanded of them, Fernan de Magalhaes ordered three boats to be equipped with a matter of fifty or sixty men, and went against the said place, … there they found many people, who might well be as many as three thousand or four thousand men, who fought with such a good will that the said Fernan de Magalhaes was killed there, with six of his men, in the year 1521.
translation: Translated by Lord Stanley of Alderley, The First Voyage Round the World by Magellan (Hakluyt Society), 1874, as reprinted in Oliver J. Thatcher, ed., The Library of Original Sources, vol. 5, 1907
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Translation checked: Fordham credits only Thatcher 1907, but the text matches Stanley of Alderley, The First Voyage Round the World by Magellan (Hakluyt Society, 1874; archive.org firstvoyageround00piga, p. 12) word for word, so the credit is right. The bracket "[the islanders]" stood in for cut source words (rule 5); restored the full passage "Because they did not choose to grant ... there they found many people, who might well be as many as three thousand or four thousand men, who fought ...". "this one" (the king who became Christian) had no context, so started the excerpt at "in this island [Cebu] Fernando de Magalhaes did what he pleased ... eight hundred people became Christian, on which account ..." (the page calls the island "Cabo"). Added [Mactan] after "Matam". Date c. 1524: the page says the pilot "went to Portugal in the year 1524", so the narrative dates from then. Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: Anonymous Genoese pilot on Magellan's fleet, narrative of the voyage (c. 1524), on trade with the king of Tidore in the Moluccas (Spice Islands), 1521
text: As soon as they arrived at the island of Tydor, which is in half a degree, the King thereof did them great honor, which could not be exceeded: there they treated with the King for their cargo, and the King engaged to give them a cargo and whatever there was in the country for their money, … there arrived the King of Baraham, which is near there, and said that he wished to be a vassal of the King of Castile, and also that he had got four hundred bahars of cloves, and that he had sold it to the King of Portugal, and that they had bought it, but that he had not yet delivered it, and if they wished for it, he would give it all to them; to which the captains answered that if he brought it to them, and came with it, they would buy it, but otherwise not. The King, seeing that they did not wish to take the cloves, asked them for a flag and a letter of safe conduct, which they gave him, signed by the captains of the ships.
translation: Translated by Lord Stanley of Alderley, The First Voyage Round the World by Magellan (Hakluyt Society), 1874, as reprinted in Oliver J. Thatcher, ed., The Library of Original Sources, vol. 5, 1907
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1519magellan (Stanley 1874 translation; see genoese-pilot-1524-cebu-mactan). The cut removed the captains' answer ("to which the captains answered that if he brought it to them, and came with it, they would buy it, but otherwise not."), which the next sentence ("seeing that they did not wish to take the cloves") depends on. Restored it. Date as for genoese-pilot-1524-cebu-mactan.

sourceLine: John Gerard, English herbalist and gardener, The Herball or Generall Historie of Plantes (first published 1597), chapter "Of Turkie Corne", from Thomas Johnson's enlarged edition (1633, reprinted 1636) as abridged by Marcus Woodward, Gerard's Herball, 1927
text: [T]hese kinds of grain were first brought into Spaine, and then into other provinces of Europe: not (as some suppose) out of Asia minor, which is the Turks dominions; but out of America and the Islands adjoining, as out of Florida, and Virginia or Norembega, where they use to sow or set it to make bread of it, where it growes much higher than in other countries. It is planted in the gardens of these Northern regions, where it commeth to ripenesse when the summer falleth out to be faire and hot; as my selfe have seen by proof in myne owne garden. … Turky wheat doth nourish far lesse than either wheat, rie, barly, or otes. The bread which is made thereof is meanely white, without bran: it is hard and dry as Bisket is, and hath in it no clamminesse at all … whereas we may easily judge, that it nourisheth but little, and is of hard and evill digestion, a more convenient food for swine than for man.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org gerardsherball0000gera, pp. 25-26. This is Marcus Woodward's selection "distilled ... from the Edition of Th. Johnson, 1636" (1927; this scan is the 1964 reprint). Woodward says "No word has been altered, though all that is tedious or gross has been omitted", so the excerpt may contain unmarked cuts. The sourceLine did not say so, and said Johnson revised the text "for the 1636 edition"; his enlarged edition appeared in 1633 and was reprinted in 1636. Corrected the sourceLine. Year 1636 kept, as the printing used. "[T]hese": I viewed the page image (leaf n48), where the chapter opens with a large printed initial T that the OCR dropped; the bracket supplies that printed letter. Text otherwise exact.

sourceLine: The House of Commons of England, the Grand Remonstrance presented to King Charles I, December 1641
text: The root of all this mischief we find to be a malignant and pernicious design of subverting the fundamental laws and principles of government, upon which the religion and justice of this kingdom are firmly established. The actors and promoters hereof have been: 1. The Jesuited Papists, who hate the laws, as the obstacles of that change and subversion of religion which they so much long for. 2. The Bishops, and the corrupt part of the Clergy, who cherish formality and superstition as the natural effects and more probable supports of their own ecclesiastical tyranny and usurpation. … And although all this [Tonnage and Poundage and other customs duties] was taken upon pretence of guarding the seas, yet a new unheard-of tax of ship-money was devised, and upon the same pretence, by both which there was charged upon the subject near £700,000 some years, and yet the merchants have been left so naked to the violence of the Turkish pirates, that many great ships of value and thousands of His Majesty's subjects have been taken by them, and do still remain in miserable slavery.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with constitution.org, Gardiner, Constitutional Documents of the Puritan Revolution, no. 43 ('Presented to the King, December 1, 1641'). Piece 1 is the 'root of all this mischief' paragraph and actors 1-2 (actor 3 omitted, marked by '…'); piece 2 is clause 20. Clause 20's 'all this' refers back to clauses 18-19 (Tonnage and Poundage, impositions, Book of Rates), which the cut removes, so it dangled after the list of actors; added the referent bracket '[Tonnage and Poundage and other customs duties]'. Attribution (House of Commons, December 1641), year 1641 correct.

sourceLine: Juan Grau y Monfalcón, procurator-general (official representative) of Manila at the Spanish court, Informatory Memorial to the King, on the decline of the Indies trade, 1637
text: So great was the abundance of these metals in the Indias, that one could say the same as of Jerusalem in the time of Solomon, that they were regarded as the stones of the street. Accordingly, articles were paid for at so exorbitant prices, as is apparent from the histories of their conquests. That region has failed, for the ores that yielded three hundred pesos per quintal by smelting, now yield eight or six by quicksilver, which costs more than smelting; and [such ores] are worked as good ones. Potosi, which is the heart of the Indias, is threatening to give out; for it alone yielded for forty years an amount that it cannot now yield, although aided by the opening of many mines … The cost of mining is greater, the mines are poorer, and, consequently, the gains less, and less the amount obtained.
translation: Translated by James A. Robertson, in E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493–1898, vol. 27, 1905
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with B&R vol. 27 (1905), Grau y Monfalcón, Memorial informatorio (Madrid, 1637), Number 68. "[such ores]" is the editors' own bracket in the source. The first "…" (after "good ones.") marked no omission - the source runs straight on to "Potosi, which is the heart" - so it was removed; the remaining cut drops "which sustain its reputation. The mines of Nueva Reino ... have lost a part of what they had" without changing the meaning. Translator: section heading says "Translation: This is made by James A. Robertson". Role: B&R calls him "procurator-general for Manila and the Philippines at the Spanish court"; the royal decree of 1636 calls him the city's procurator-general.

sourceLine: Juan Grau y Monfalcón, procurator-general (official representative) of Manila at the Spanish court, Informatory Memorial to the King, setting out the Seville merchants' case against the Manila trade, 1637
text: This commerce of the Indias with the Filipinas is to the prejudice of España for two causes or reasons, from which result great disadvantages. The first, because the silver is withdrawn and conveyed to the islands, whence it passes into the possession of the enemies of religion and of this crown, Moors and pagans; and finally remains in China—which, according to what we understand, is the general center for the silver of Europe and Asia. … The second cause is that, in addition to the aforesaid losses (which are obvious) from the withdrawal of silver, no less are the damages that are experienced on what is sent in return for it to Nueva España, and passes to Perú—namely, a great quantity of the merchandise of China in textiles of gold, silk, and cotton, and other articles. [These are sold] at so low prices that, when the merchandise of these kingdoms arrives (which is worth more, as it is of better quality), it is not sold and has no outlet.
translation: Translated by James A. Robertson, in E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493–1898, vol. 27, 1905
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with B&R vol. 27, Memorial informatorio, Number 64 ("Commerce of the islands: why it is injurious to España"): verbatim; "[These are sold]" is the editors' bracket. The cut drops the elaboration on silver enriching enemies; meaning unchanged. The sourceLine correctly flags that Grau is stating the opposing case: Number 65 is his "Reply to the damages of the commerce of Filipinas", and the memorial elsewhere describes the damage "to the commerce of Sevilla" that drove the restrictions. Translator Robertson as above.

sourceLine: Hugo Grotius, Dutch jurist writing at the request of the Dutch East India Company (VOC), Mare Liberum (The Freedom of the Seas), 1609
text: My intention is to demonstrate briefly and clearly that the Dutch—that is to say, the subjects of the United Netherlands—have the right to sail to the East Indies, as they are now doing, and to engage in trade with the people there. I shall base my argument on the following most specific and unimpeachable axiom of the Law of Nations, called a primary rule or first principle, the spirit of which is self-evident and immutable, to wit: Every nation is free to travel to every other nation, and to trade with it. … Wherefore since both law and equity demand that trade with the East Indies be as free to us as to any one else, it follows that we are to maintain at all hazards that freedom which is ours by nature, either by coming to a peace agreement with the Spaniards, or by concluding a treaty, or by continuing the war.
translation: Translated by Ralph Van Deman Magoffin, The Freedom of the Seas, 1916
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg #75962 (Magoffin translation, ed. James Brown Scott, Oxford University Press for the Carnegie Endowment, 1916). The first piece is the opening of chapter I and the second the opening of chapter XIII ('The Dutch must maintain their right of trade with the East Indies by peace, by treaty, or by war'), both verbatim. The long cut joins Grotius's thesis to his conclusion and does not distort it. Mare Liberum was published in 1609; the Latin title page reproduced in the edition says 1608, the year it was written as part of his brief for the VOC, so year 1609 is right.

sourceLine: Guru Gobind Singh, tenth Guru of the Sikhs, Zafarnama (Letter of Victory) to the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, 1705
text: I have no faith in thine oath to which thou tookest the one God as witness. I have not a particle of confidence in thee. Thy treasurer and thy ministers are all false. He who putteth faith in thine oath on the Quran is thereby a ruined man. The insolent crow cannot touch him who hath fallen under the shadow of the huma. He who taketh the protection of a powerful tiger cannot be approached by a goat, a buffalo, or a deer. Had I even secretly sworn on the volume of my choice faith to accept thy religion, I should not have had to withdraw my infantry and cavalry from Anandpur. … When an affair passeth beyond the region of diplomacy, it is lawful to have recourse to the sword. … What though my four sons were killed, I remain behind like a coiled snake. What bravery is it to quench a few sparks of life? Thou art merely exciting a raging fire the more. … Thou art monarch of the world, but far from thee is religion.
translation: Translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 5, 1909
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion vol. 5 (Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1909), pp. 202-205, 'Address to Aurangzeb' in the Zafarnama, which Macauliffe says the Guru wrote at Dina after Chamkaur. Pieces follow the source order; cuts (Chamkaur battle detail, long reproaches, praise of Aurangzeb before 'Thou art monarch of the world, but far from thee is religion') keep the meaning. Attribution, 1705 date (after the Chamkaur battle and the sons' deaths, 1704-05) and translation credit correct. Confirmed.

sourceLine: Richard Hakluyt, English clergyman and promoter of colonization, chapter headings of A Discourse of Western Planting, written for Queen Elizabeth I at the request of Walter Raleigh, 1584 (adapted)
text: That this western discovery will be greatly for the enlargement of the gospel of Christ whereunto the Princes of the reformed religion are chiefly bound amongst whom her Majesty is principal. … That all other English trades are grown beggarly or dangerous, especially in all the king of Spain his dominions, where our men are driven to fling their Bibles and prayer books into the sea, and to forswear and renounce their religion and conscience and consequently their obedience to her Majesty. … That this western voyage will yield unto us all the commodities of Europe, Africa, and Asia, as far as we were wont to travel, and supply the wants of all our decayed trades. … What special means may bring king Philip from his high throne, and make him equal to the Princes his neighbours, wherewithal is showed his weakness in the West Indies. … That this action will be greatly for the increase, maintenance and safety of our navy, and especially of great shipping which is the strength of our realm, …
original: That this westerne discoverie will be greately for the inlargement of the gospell of Christe whereunto the Princes of the refourmed relligion are chefely bounde amongest whome her Majestie is principall. … That all other englishe Trades are growen beggerly or daungerous, especially in all the kinge of Spaine his Domynions, where our men are dryven to flinge their Bibles and prayer Bokes into the sea, and to forsweare and renownce their relligion and conscience and consequently theyr obedience to her Majestie. … That this westerne voyadge will yelde unto us all the commodities of Europe, Affrica, and Asia, as far as wee were wonte to travell, and supply the wantes of all our decayed trades. … What speciall meanes may bringe kinge Phillippe from his high Throne, and make him equal to the Princes his neighbours, wherewithall is shewed his weakenes in the west Indies. … That this action will be greately for the increase, mayneteynaunce and safetie of our Navye, and especially of greate shippinge which is the strengthe of our Realme, …
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Adapted: compared text with original word by word against the chapter list on the Wayback copy of the let.rug.nl page; only spelling is modernised (westerne->western, Phillippe->Philip, shewed->showed, etc.), no word changes. Heading: "Written In the yere 1584 by Richarde Hackluyt ... at the requeste and direction of ... Mr. Walter Raghly". Written in English, so translation null. Cuts skip whole chapter headings only.

sourceLine: Hendrick Hamel, Dutch East India Company bookkeeper shipwrecked on Korea in 1653 and held there until 1666, narrative of his captivity, 1668
text: He [Jan Weltevree, a Dutch sailor held in Korea since 1627] added that during his long residence in Corea he had often asked leave of the king to go over to Japan, without ever obtaining any other answer than that he must never expect it, unless he had wings and could fly thither — that the custom of the country was to detain strangers that came thither, but that they wanted for nothing, being provided with diet and clothes as long as they lived. … The king [of Korea] told us it was not the custom of Corea to suffer strangers to depart the kingdom—that we must resolve to end our days in his dominions, and he would provide us with all necessaries.
translation: Translator not named; English version from Churchill's Collection of Voyages, 1732, slightly modernised by William Elliot Griffis in Corea, Without and Within, 2nd ed., 1885
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Griffis, Corea, Without and Within, 2nd ed. (Philadelphia, preface note Oct. 1885), pp. 56-57 and 71. Griffis's note (ch. IV n.1) says he used the English version in Churchill's Collection, London 1732, with 'substitution of modern for obsolete words' -- translator unnamed, so credit made explicit. First bracket names 'He' (John Wetterree; the page gives his 1627 wreck), fine. Second piece: '[The Korean king]' replaced the source words 'The king' (p. 71); restored the source words and made the bracket a pure insertion: 'The king [of Korea] told us'. Hamel, VOC bookkeeper/supercargo, wrecked 1653, escaped 1666, journal published 1668: sourceLine and year fine.

sourceLine: Thomas Hariot, English scientist with the Roanoke colony of 1585–1586, A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia, 1588 (adapted)
text: There was no town where we had any subtle device practised against us, we leaving it unpunished or not revenged … but that within a few days after our departure from every such town, the people began to die very fast, and many in short space; in some towns about twenty, in some forty, in some sixty, and in one six score, which in truth was very many in respect of their numbers. … The disease also so strange, that they neither knew what it was, nor how to cure it; the like by the report of the oldest men in the country never happened before, time out of mind. … Insomuch that when some of the inhabitants which were our friends and especially the Wiroans [chief] Wingina had observed such effects in four or five towns to follow their wicked practices, they were persuaded that it was the work of our God through our means, and that we by him might kill and slay whom we would without weapons and not come near them.
original: There was no towne where we had any subtile deuise practised against vs, we leauing it vnpunished or not reuenged … but that within a few dayes after our departure from euerie such towne, the people began to die very fast, and many in short space; in some townes about twentie, in some fourtie, in some sixtie, & in one sixe score, which in trueth was very manie in respect of their numbers. … The disease also so strange, that they neither knew what it was, nor how to cure it; the like by the report of the oldest men in the countrey neuer happened before, time out of minde. … Insomuch that when some of the inhabitantes which were our friends & especially the Wiroans Wingina had obserued such effects in foure or fiue towns to follow their wicked practises, they were preswaded that it was the worke of our God through our meanes, and that wee by him might kil and slai whom we would without weapons and not come neere them.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Adapted: compared text with original word by word against Gutenberg 4247 (the 1590 de Bry edition of the 1588 Briefe and True Report). Only spelling is modernised ("preswaded" to "persuaded", "&" to "and", etc.). The bracket [chief] after "Wiroans" clarifies the word. The cuts drop Hariot's parenthesis on winning the people "by gentlenesse" and a clause on where the deaths happened; meaning kept. Year 1588 is the first edition; the page reproduces the 1590 printing of the same text.

sourceLine: Henry Hawks, English merchant who lived five years in New Spain, report on New Spain written at the request of Richard Hakluyt of Eyton, Herefordshire (the elder Hakluyt, a lawyer, cousin of the editor of the Principal Navigations), 1572 (adapted)
text: There is in New Spain a marvellous increase of cattle, which daily do increase, and they are of a greater growth than ours are. You may have a great steer that hath an hundred weight of tallow in his belly for sixteen shillings; and some one man hath 2000 head of cattle of his own. They sell the hides unto the merchants, who lade into Spain as many as may be well spared. … They have many horses, and mares, and mules, which the Spaniards brought thither. … This Maize is the greatest maintenance which the Indian hath, and also all the common people of the Spaniards. And their horses and mules which labour, cannot be without the same. … If the Miners should be without it, they could not labour their mines: for all their servants eat none other bread, but only of this Maize, and it is made in cakes, as they make oaten cakes, in some places of England.
original: There is in New Spaine a maruellous increase of cattle, which daily do increase, and they are of a greater growth then ours are. You may haue a great steere that hath an hundred weight of tallow in his belly for sixteene shillings; and some one man hath 2000 head of cattel of his owne. They sell the hides vnto the merchants, who lade into Spaine as many as may be well spared. … They haue many horses, and mares, and mules, which the Spaniards brought thither. … This Maiz is the greatest maintenance which the Indian hath, and also all the common people of the Spaniards. And their horses and mules which labour, cannot be without the same. … If the Miners should bee without it, they coulde not labour their mines: for all their seruants eate none other bread, but onely of this Maize, and it is made in cakes, as they make oaten cakes, in some places of England.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Adapted: compared text with original word by word against Gutenberg 40803 (Hakluyt, Principal Navigations, ed. Goldsmid, vol. XIV): only spelling modernised ("Maiz" to "Maize", "then ours" to "than ours"); cuts keep the meaning. sourceLine: the heading on the page says Hawks drew up the relation "at the request of M. Richard Hakluyt Esquire of Eton in the county of Hereford, 1572", i.e. the elder Richard Hakluyt, the lawyer of Eyton. In 1572 the younger Hakluyt, compiler of the Principal Navigations and author of the 1584 Discourse in this bank, was about 19. "written for Richard Hakluyt" invited confusing the two, so I named him precisely.

sourceLine: Henry Hawks, English merchant who lived five years in New Spain, report on New Spain written at the request of Richard Hakluyt of Eyton, Herefordshire (the elder Hakluyt, a lawyer, cousin of the editor of the Principal Navigations), 1572 (adapted)
text: The Indians have the friars in great reverence: the occasion is, that by them and by their means they are free and out of bondage; which was so ordained by Charles the emperor: which is the occasion that now there is not so much gold and silver coming into Europe as there was while the Indians were slaves. For when they were in bondage they could not choose but do their task every day, and bring their master so much metal out of their mines: but now they must be well paid, and much entreated to have them work. So it hath been, and is a great hindrance to the owners of the mines, and to the king's quinto or custom. … A good owner of mines must have at the least an hundred slaves to carry and to stamp his metals … And the mines fall daily in decay, and of less value: and the occasion is, the few Indians that men have to labour their mines.
original: The Indians haue the friers in great reuerence: the occasion is, that by them and by there meanes they are free and out of bondage; which was so ordeined by Charles the emperor: which is the occasion that now there is not so much gold and siluer comming into Europe as there was while the Indians were slaues. For when they were in bondage they could not chuse but doe their taske euery day, and bring their master so much metall out of their mines: but now they must be well payed, and much intreated to haue them worke. So it hath bene, and is a great hinderance to the owners of the mines, and to the kings quinto or custome. … A good owner of mines must haue at the least an hundred slaues to cary and to stampe his metals … And the mines fall dayly in decay, and of lesse value: and the occasion is, the few Indians that men haue to labour their mines.

Richard Hakluyt Esquire of Eton in the county of Hereford, 1572", i.e. the elder Richard Hakluyt, the lawyer of Eyton.
