"written for Richard Hakluyt" invited confusing the two, so I named him precisely.

sourceLine: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, chief imperial regent and unifier of Japan, edict expelling Christian missionaries, posted at Hakata, 1587
text: Having learned from our faithful councillors that foreign religieux [members of Catholic religious orders] have come into our estates, where they preach a law contrary to that of Japan, and that they had even had the audacity to destroy temples dedicated to our Kami and Hotoke: although this outrage merits the most extreme punishment, wishing nevertheless to show them mercy, we order them under pain of death to quit Japan within twenty days. During that space no harm or hurt will be done them. But at the expiration of that term, we order that if any of them be found in our States, they shall be seized and punished as the greatest criminals. As for the Portuguese merchants, we permit them to enter our ports there to continue their accustomed trade, and to remain in our estates provided our affairs need this. But we forbid them to bring any foreign religieux into the country, under the penalty of the confiscation of their ships and goods.
translation: Translated in James Murdoch and Isoh Yamagata, A History of Japan, vol. 2, 1903 (from a European version of the edict)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Murdoch, History of Japan [During the Century of Early Foreign Intercourse 1542-1651], Kobe 1903 (archive.org historyofjapan02murd, catalogued as vol. 2), p. 243: text is continuous and verbatim; Murdoch introduces it as the Edict 'published and posted up in Hakata' on 25 July 1587. Bracket only glosses 'religieux'. The version is the one given by the Jesuit historians (Murdoch cites Charlevoix/Crasset in the same passage), so the credit's 'from a European version of the edict' is accurate. Hideyoshi was kampaku (imperial regent) in 1587. 1450-1750 primary source; reads on its own.

sourceLine: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, ruler of Japan, letter to the Portuguese Viceroy of the Indies at Goa, 1591
text: With respect to what regards religion, Japan is the realm of the Kami, that is to say of Shin, which is the origin of all things. … The ‘Fathers of the Company,’ as they are called, have come to these islands to teach another religion here; but as that of the Kami is too surely founded to be abolished, this new ‘law’ can only serve to introduce into Japan a diversity of cults prejudicial to the welfare of the State. It is for this reason that by Imperial Edict I have forbidden these foreign Doctors to continue to preach their doctrine. I have even ordered them to quit Japan, and I am resolved no longer to allow any one to come here to spread new opinions. I nevertheless desire that trade between You and Us should always be on the same footing (as before). I shall have care that the ways are free by sea and by land; I have freed them from all pirates and brigands. The Portuguese will be able to traffic with my subjects in all security.
translation: Translated in James Murdoch and Isoh Yamagata, A History of Japan, vol. 2, 1903 (from a European version of the letter)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Murdoch 1903, pp. 375-376 ('To the Viceroy of the Indies the Regent wrote as follows', dated 1591 by Murdoch). Words verbatim; the one cut removes the Confucian-order sentence ('the good order of the government ... tranquillity abroad'), which does not alter the religious argument; excerpt ends at 'in all security' where the source has a semicolon. Murdoch gives no source for this version; credit says honestly it comes from a European version. Year 1591 matches.

sourceLine: Jahangir, Mughal emperor of India, letter to King James I of England, sent to the English ambassador Sir Thomas Roe from Ahmedabad, February 1618
text: When your Majesty shall open this letter let your royal heart be as fresh as a sweet garden. … Upon which assurance of your royal love I have given my general command to all the kingdoms and ports of my dominions to receive all the merchants of the English nation as the subjects of my friend; … and at what port soever they shall arrive, that neither Portugal nor any other shall dare to molest their quiet; and in what city soever they shall have residence, I have commanded all my governors and captains to give them freedom answerable to their own desires; to sell, buy, and to transport into their country at their pleasure. … For confirmation of our love and friendship, I desire your Majesty to command your merchants to bring in their ships of all sorts of rarities and rich goods fit for my palace; …
translation: Contemporary English version (a copy in Sir Thomas Roe's hand survives), translator not named; modernised text as printed in James Harvey Robinson, ed., Readings in European History, vol. 2, 1906
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1617englandindies, with Robinson vol. II (1906) p. 334, and with Foster, The Embassy of Sir Thomas Roe, vol. II (Hakluyt Society 1899; archive.org embassysirthoma01fostgoog, pp. 557-558). (1) Fordham's transcription drops a line. Robinson and Roe's copy read "that in what place soever they choose to live, they may have reception and residence to their own content and safety; and what goods soever they desire to sell or buy, they may have free liberty without any restraint", but Fordham joins the start of this sentence to its end. So the excerpt's clause misstated the grant. I cut that clause ("…") rather than keep the garbled version. The remaining words are the same in Robinson and, spelling aside, in Roe's copy. (2) Date: Roe's note at the end of the letter (Foster p. 558) says it was "sent to the Ambassador the 20 day feb. 1617[-18]" from Ahmedabad. 1617 is the Old Style year, so I set year 1618 and changed the sourceLine to February 1618. (3) Translator: the English text survives in a copy in Roe's handwriting (Foster p. 557n); no translator is named, which the credit now says.

sourceLine: Articles of Pacification concluded by John Guthrie and Francis Sadler for the British colonial government of Jamaica with the Maroons of Trelawny Town led by Captain Cudjoe, 1 March 1739 (dated 1738, Old Style), as printed in R. C. Dallas, The History of the Maroons, 1803 (adapted)
text: Whereas Captain Cudjoe, Captain Acompong, Captain Johnny, Captain Cuffee, Captain Quaco, and several other negroes, their dependants and adherents, have been in a state of war and hostility, for several years past, against our sovereign Lord the King, and the inhabitants of this island; … First, That all hostilities shall cease on both sides for ever. Second, That the said Captain Cudjoe, the rest of his captains, adherents, and men, shall be for ever hereafter in a perfect state of freedom and liberty, … Third, That they shall enjoy and possess, for themselves and posterity for ever, all the lands situate and lying between Trelawny Town and the Cockpits, to the amount of fifteen hundred acres, bearing north-west from the said Trelawny Town. … Ninth, That if any negroes shall hereafter run away from their masters or owners, and fall into Captain Cudjoe’s hands, they shall immediately be sent back to the chief magistrate of the next parish where they are taken; and those that bring them are to be satisfied for their trouble, as the legislature shall appoint.

Second, That the faid Captain Cudjoe,^ the reft of his captains, adherents, and men, ihall be for ever hereafter in a perfeA ftate of freedom and liberty, … Thirds That they ihall enjoy and poffeifi, for themfelves and pofterity for ever^ all the lands fituate and lying between Trelawny Town and the Cockpits, to the amount of fifteen hundred aeres, bearing north-weft from the faid Trelawny Towai … Ninth, That if any negroes ihall hereafter run away frpm their mailers or owners^ and fall into Captain Cudjoe*s hands^ … they (hall immediately be fent back to the chief magiftrate of the next pariih where they are taken ; and thofe that bring them are to be fatisfied for their trouble, as the legiflature (hall appoint.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared word by word with the page images (Dallas, History of the Maroons, vol. 1, 1803, pp. 58–63; archive.org historymaroonsf01dallgoog n193–n198). Confirmed OCR corrections: 'Cuffee', 'cease' (OCR 'oeafe'), 'perfect' (OCR 'perfeA'), 'Third', 'possess', 'acres' (OCR 'aeres'), 'from' (OCR 'frpm'), 'masters' (OCR 'mailers'), 'shall'. Changes: (1) the printed name is 'Acompong', not 'Accompong', restored; (2) 'Trelawny [Town]' — 'Town' is printed (OCR 'Towai'), so it is no longer bracketed and the original carries the OCR word; (3) the Ninth article ended at 'taken.' though the printed sentence continues; the rest of it ('; and those that bring them are to be satisfied for their trouble, as the legislature shall appoint') is added from p. 63 so the article is complete (178 words). sourceLine: James I, king of England and Scotland, A Counterblaste to Tobacco, 1604 (adapted)
text: And now good countrymen let us (I pray you) consider, what honour or policy can move us to imitate the barbarous and beastly manners of the wild, godless, and slavish Indians, especially in so vile and stinking a custom? … Now how you are by this custom disabled in your goods, let the gentry of this land bear witness, some of them bestowing three, some four hundred pounds a year upon this precious stink, which I am sure might be bestowed upon many far better uses. … The public use whereof, at all times, and in all places, hath now so far prevailed, as divers men very sound both in judgement, and complexion, have been at last forced to take it also without desire … A custom loathsome to the eye, hateful to the Nose, harmful to the brain, dangerous to the Lungs, and in the black stinking fume thereof, nearest resembling the horrible Stygian smoke of the pit that is bottomless.
original: And now good Countrey men let vs (I pray you) consider, what honour or policie can mooue vs to imitate the barbarous and beastly maners of the wilde, godlesse, and slauish Indians, especially in so vile and stinking a custome? … Now how you are by this custome disabled in your goods, let the gentry of this land beare witnesse, some of them bestowing three, some foure hundred pounds a yeere[J] vpon this precious stinke, which I am sure might be bestowed vpon many farre better vses. … The publike vse whereof, at all times, and in all places, hath now so farre preuailed, as diuers men very sound both in iudgement, and complexion, haue bene at last forced to take it also without desire … A custome lothsome to the eye, hatefull to the Nose, harmefull to the braine, dangerous to the Lungs, and in the blacke stinking fume thereof, neerest resembling the horrible Stigian smoke of the pit that is bottomelesse.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Adapted: compared text with original word by word against Gutenberg 17008 (Goldsmid 1884 reprint of the 1604 edition "Imprinted at London by R.B. Anno 1604"). Only spelling is modernised (e.g. "vs" to "us", "Stigian" to "Stygian"); [J] in "original" is the reprint's footnote marker. Cuts keep the meaning; "whereof" refers to tobacco-taking. Published anonymously in 1604 and known to be by James I.

sourceLine: John Blande, London merchant, printed petition to King Charles II on behalf of the planters of Virginia and Maryland against the Navigation Act, c. 1661
text: Most humbly representing unto Your Majesty the inevitable destruction of those Colonies, if so be that the late Act for increase of Trade and Shipping [the Navigation Act] be not as to them dispensed with … Why these men [the Act's promoters] procured this Act, prohibiting the Hollanders trade into those Colonies at first, and its continuance now, was, and is, because they would keep still in their own hands that Trade which they had engrossed, and have no body come there to hinder them, and that for the following reasons. First, That for whatever goods they carried out of England to those Plantations, the Inhabitants should pay to them what prices and rates they pleased to require, else they should have nothing at all of them to supply their necessities. Secondly, To force the Planters to deliver them such Tobaccoes, which by the labour and sweat of their brows they had made, at the rates they themselves trading thither would have it, whereby they got that oftentimes of the poor Planters for a halfpenny, which they made us pay for here in England by Retale three or four shillings.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with the EarlyPrint text A28354 and with the EEBO-TCP original-spelling transcription (Wing B3157, ESTC R33225; '[London?, 1661?]', 'Place and date of publication suggested by Wing'), so 'c. 1661' is right. EarlyPrint only standardises spelling (encrease→increase, dispenc'd→dispensed, Majesties→Majesty's, browes→brows, ingrossed→engrossed). The words match the TCP text. The bracket '[The Act's promoters intended:]' stood in for a cut sentence, so it was replaced by restoring the source sentence: 'Why these men procured this Act... was, and is, because they would keep still in their own hands that Trade which they had engrossed... for the following reasons.' 'these men' gets a referent bracket using the source's own word 'promoters'. To stay under 200 words, the clause 'for it will not only ruinate the Inhabitants and Planters, but make desolate ... Dominion' after 'dispensed with' is now cut (marked …). The petition's claim of 'inevitable destruction of those Colonies' stays.

sourceLine: Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa, Spanish naval officers sent by the king to South America 1735–1744, A Voyage to South America, on the inhabitants of Quito, first published 1748
text: This city is very populous, and has, among its inhabitants, some families of high rank and distinction; though their number is but small considering its extent, the poorer class bearing here too great a proportion. The former are the descendants either of the original conquerors, or of presidents, auditors, or other persons of character, who at different times came over from Spain invested with some lucrative post … The commonalty may be divided into four classes; Spaniards or Whites, Mestizos, Indians or Natives, and Negroes, with their progeny. … The name of Spaniard here has a different meaning from that of Chapitone or European, as properly signifying a person descended from a Spaniard without a mixture of blood. Many Mestizos, from the advantage of a fresh complexion, appear to be Spaniards more than those who are so in reality; and from only this fortuitous advantage are accounted as such. … at Quito the degrees of Mestizos are not carried so far back; for, even in the second or third generations, when they acquire the European colour, they are considered as Spaniards.
translation: Translated by John Adams, A Voyage to South America, 1758 (fourth edition, 1806)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org voyagetosouthame00ullo, Book V ch. V, pp. 261-262 (John Adams's translation, fourth edition, vol. I, London: Stockdale, 1806; first English edition 1758; Spanish original 1748). Cuts keep the meaning. The credit matches the edition.

sourceLine: Engelbert Kaempfer, German physician with the Dutch embassy to the shogun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi at Edo in 1691, The History of Japan (written after his return to Europe, published in English 1727)
text: As for my own particular the following questions were put to me: What external and internal distempers I thought the most dangerous, and most difficult to cure? How I proceeded in the cure of cancrous humors and imposthumations of the inner parts? Whether our European Physicians did not search after some Medicine to render people immortal, as the Chinese Physicians had done for many hundred years? Whether we had made any considerable progress in this search, and which was the last remedy conducive to long life, that had been found out in Europe? … Then ’twas ask’d, whether it [the remedy] could be had at Batavia? and having return’d in answer, that it was to be had there, the Emperor [the shogun] desir’d, that it should be sent over by the next ships.
translation: Translated by J. G. Scheuchzer, The History of Japan, 1727 (reprinted Glasgow, 1906)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Kaempfer, History of Japan (Scheuchzer trans., Glasgow 1906), vol. III, pp. 91-92 (margin 'A.D. 1691'): pieces verbatim; '[the shogun]' glosses Kaempfer's 'Emperor'. The 239-word cut removes the naming of the medicine (Sal volatile Oleosum Sylvii), leaving 'whether it could be had' without a clear referent: added the clarifying bracket 'it [the remedy]'. sourceLine 'written in the 1690s' changed to 'written after his return to Europe' (as for kaempfer-1692-dejima). Year 1691 = audience at Edo (margin date). Lead verifier: added "in 1691" after "at Edo" so the sourceLine shows the date that "year" gives (the margin date of the audience).

sourceLine: Engelbert Kaempfer, German physician to the Dutch East India Company post at Nagasaki in 1690–92, The History of Japan (written after his return to Europe, published in English 1727)
text: So great was the covetousness of the Dutch, and so great the alluring power of the Japanese gold, that rather than to quit the prospect of a trade, indeed most advantageous, they willingly underwent an almost perpetual imprisonment, for such in fact is our stay at Desima, and chose to suffer many hardships in a foreign and heathen country, to be remiss in performing divine service on Sundays and solemn festivals, to leave off praying and singing of psalms in publick, entirely to avoid the sign of the cross, the calling upon Christ in presence of the natives, and all the outward marks of Christianity … Some few paces off the Island, in the water, are thirteen very high posts standing at proper distances, with small wooden tables at the top, upon which is written, in large Japanese characters, an order from the Governors, strictly and under severe penalties forbidding all boats or vessels, to come within the said rails, and to approach the Island.
translation: Translated by J. G. Scheuchzer, The History of Japan, 1727 (reprinted Glasgow, 1906)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Kaempfer, History of Japan, trans. J. G. Scheuchzer, Glasgow: MacLehose 1906, vol. II, pp. 173-175 (margin 'A.D. 1692'): both pieces verbatim (1727 spellings 'publick' etc. as printed); the cut skips the description of the island's layout and does not change the meaning. Title page: 'Physician to the Dutch Embassy to the Emperor's Court', translated by Scheuchzer -- credit fine. sourceLine said 'written in the 1690s'; Kaempfer left Japan in 1692 and wrote the work afterwards in Europe (it appeared only posthumously in 1727), which the page does not date to the 1690s, so changed to 'written after his return to Europe'. Year 1692 = the time described (margin date), and both dates now show.

sourceLine: The Kangxi emperor of the Qing dynasty, edict of toleration for Christianity (a ruling of the Board of Rites issued with his approval), 1692
text: The Europeans are very quiet; they do not excite any disturbances in the provinces, they do no harm to anyone, they commit no crimes, and their doctrine has nothing in common with that of the false sects in the empire, nor has it any tendency to excite sedition … We decide therefore that all temples dedicated to the Lord of heaven, in whatever place they may be found, ought to be preserved, and that it may be permitted to all who wish to worship this God to enter these temples, offer him incense, and perform the ceremonies practised according to ancient custom by the Christians. Therefore let no one henceforth offer them any opposition.
translation: Translator not named; quoted in Stephen Neill, A History of Christian Missions, Penguin, 1964, pp. 189-190 (Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Fordham page 1715chineserites.asp, 'From Decree of K'ang-hsi (1692)': text verbatim; the '…' corresponds to the page's own '. . .'. Page credits 'From S. Neill, A History of Christian Missions (Harmondsworth: Penguin Books 1964), pp. 189-190' -- Neill quotes an existing English version and is not named as translator, so 'Translated in Stephen Neill' changed to an honest 'translator not named; quoted in'. sourceLine: the 1692 toleration edict was the Board of Rites' deliberation ('We decide therefore...') approved by the emperor; added that so the 'we' voice is not read as the emperor's own words. Year 1692 matches.

sourceLine: The Kangxi emperor of the Qing dynasty, comment on the papal decree that forbade Chinese Christians to honour Confucius and their ancestors, 1721
text: Reading this proclamation, I have concluded that the Westerners are petty indeed. It is impossible to reason with them because they do not understand larger issues as we understand them in China. There is not a single Westerner versed in Chinese works, and their remarks are often incredible and ridiculous. To judge from this proclamation, their religion is no different from other small, bigoted sects of Buddhism or Taoism. I have never seen a document which contains so much nonsense. From now on, Westerners should not be allowed to preach in China, to avoid further trouble.
translation: Translated by Dan J. Li, China in Transition, 1517–1911, 1969 (Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Fordham page 1715chineserites.asp, 'From Decree of Kangxi (1721)': excerpt is the whole passage, verbatim, no cuts; credit on page: Dan J. Li, trans., China in Transition, 1517-1911 (Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1969), p. 22 -- matches the translation field. Kangxi's comment on Clement XI's decree (Ex illa die) as brought by the legate in 1720-21; year 1721 matches page.

sourceLine: Kiotseaeton, Mohawk (Haudenosaunee) speaker, peace speech to the governor of New France at Three Rivers, 1645, as recorded by the Jesuit Barthélemy Vimont in the Relation of 1644–45 (adapted)
text: Kiotsaeton, who was high in stature, rose and looked at the Sun, then cast his eyes over the whole Company; he took a collar of porcelain beads in his hand and commenced to harangue in a loud voice. “Onontio, lend me ear. I am the mouth for the whole of my country; thou listenest to all the Iroquois, in hearing my words. There is no evil in my heart; I have only good songs in my mouth. We have a multitude of war songs in our country; we have cast them all on the ground; we have no longer anything but songs of rejoicing.” … The tenth was given to bind us all very closely together. He took hold of a Frenchman, placed his arm within his, and with his other arm he clasped that of an Alguonquin. Having thus joined himself to them, “Here,” he said, “is the knot that binds us inseparably; nothing can part us.”

Having thus joined himself to them, ‘‘ Here,” he said, ‘‘ is the knot that binds us inseparably; nothing can part us.
translation: Translated by Thwaites's staff (Finlow Alexander, Percy Favor Bicknell, William Frederic Giese, Crawford Lindsay, William Price, Hiram Allen Sober; the translator of this document is not specified), The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, ed. Reuben Gold Thwaites, vol. 27, 1898
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with the page image (Thwaites vol. 27, p. 253, leaf 257) and p. 261: the OCR joins/splits 'ina', 'Iam', 'songsin', 'havea', 'Onon- tio' are printed 'in a', 'I am', 'songs in', 'have a', 'Onon-|tio' (line-break hyphen), so the text's spacing fixes are correct; no other differences. The cut skips the first nine presents; the quotation marks follow the page. Document LV is the Relation of 1644–45 by Barthélemy Vimont, superior at Quebec (dated Quebec, Oct. 1, 1645); the Three Rivers council was in July 1645.
