sourceLine: Nicolaes Koeckebacker, head of the Dutch East India Company post at Hirado, letter to Governor-General Antonio van Diemen on the Shimabara Rebellion, 1638
text: On the 17th December, 1637, we received intelligence that the peasants in the county of Arima had revolted, taken up arms, set fire to all the habitations of the nobility and citizens, murdered some of the nobles … The newly-arrived lord [Matsukura, Bungo-no-Kami], not content herewith, imposed moreover upon them [the former lord's retainers, now farmers] and upon the other farmers more taxes, and forced them to raise such a quantity of rice as was impossible for them to do. Those who could not pay the fixed taxes were dressed, by his order, in a rough straw coat (mino) … These mantles were tied round the neck and body, the hands being tightly bound behind their backs with ropes, after which the straw-coats were set on fire. … but as his son, the present lord [Matsukura, Nagato-no-Kami], who resides in Yedo, feels also inclined to follow in the footsteps of his father, and forces the farmers to pay far more taxes than they are able to do, in such a manner that they languish from hunger … the people resolved not to bear any longer the vexations, and to die one single death instead of the many slow deaths to which they were subjected.
translation: Translator not named; English version (from the Dutch) printed in James Murdoch and Isoh Yamagata, A History of Japan, vol. 2, 1903
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Murdoch 1903, pp. 650-651 ('Koeckebacker's letter to Governor-General Van Diemen'). The old final cut jumped from the father's straw-coat torture to 'the people resolved...', but the source says the people endured the newly-arrived lord's cruelty 'as long as he was present' and rose because his son, the present lord, kept overtaxing them. That changed the cause, so the son's clause was restored from the page ('but as his son, the present lord [Matsukura, Nagato-no-Kami] ... they languish from hunger'; the bracket is Murdoch's). To stay under 200 words the description of the mino grass was cut, and so was 'taking ouly some roots...' (OCR error). Added clarifying brackets '[Matsukura, Bungo-no-Kami]' (from Murdoch's n.3) and 'them [the former lord's retainers, now farmers]', whose referent was in the cut paragraph. Now 190 words, every piece at least 27 words. No translator named on the page, so the credit says so.

sourceLine: Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga), Ming loyalist commander fighting the Qing dynasty, letter to the Dutch governor of Taiwan, 1660
text: Certainly, I have now for many years waged war for the recovery of my own territories [from the Tartars], and have been so fully occupied in this way, that there was no opportunity for taking hostile action against such a small grass-producing country as Formosa. Moreover, when engaged in preparations for war, and arrangements have been quite concluded, my practice is to spread a report that I intend to make an exploit eastwards, while my own secret resolution will lead me towards the west. … This year the Tartars came down to these southern regions with a great army, to finish up the war in one battle; but as it happened, we on the tenth day of our fifth moon attacked them so furiously, that over a hundred of their officers, besides numerous soldiers, were killed, and many taken prisoners; while the remainder had to fly precipitately for safer quarters, without daring to show themselves again.
translation: Translated by William Campbell, Formosa under the Dutch, 1903, from the Dutch version of the Chinese letter printed in 't Verwaerloosde Formosa, 1675
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Campbell, Formosa under the Dutch (1903), pp. 404-405: the letter ('Koxin, General of the army on the coast of China, sends this letter to the Governor of Formosa') answers the messenger sent 31 Oct 1660. It is printed in the 't Verwaerloosde Formosa narrative ('Translated from Chinese the letter reads as follows'; Campbell p. 383 n.1), so the credit now names that intermediate Dutch text. Pieces verbatim; '[from the Tartars]' is Campbell's own bracket; the cut (rumours and import duties) does not change the meaning. OCR text checked for misreadings: all words are real and fit the context. sourceLine and 1660 fine.

sourceLine: Bartolomé de las Casas, Dominican friar and critic of Spanish conquest, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (written 1542, published 1552), on the Taíno leader Hatuey in Cuba, 1511–12
text: When the Spaniards first touched this Island, this Cacic [Hatuey], who was thoroughly acquainted with them, did avoid and shun them as much as in him lay, and defended himself by force of Arms, wherever he met with them, but at length being taken he was burnt alive, for flying from so unjust and cruel a Nation, and endeavuoring to secure his Life against them, who only thirsted after the blood of himself and his own People. … Now being bound to the post, in order of his Execution a certain Holy Monk of the Franciscan Order, discours'd with him concerning God and the Articles of our Faith … After that Hathney had been silently pensive sometime, he askt the Monk whether the Spaniards also were admitted into Heaven, and he answering that the Gates of Heaven were open to all that were Good and Godly, the Cacic replied without further consideration, that he would rather go to Hell then Heaven, for fear he should cohabit in the same Mansion with so Sanguinary and Bloody a Nation.
translation: Anonymous English translation, Popery Truly Display'd in its Bloody Colours, London, 1689
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg #20321 (preparer's note: translation of the Brevisima relacion, 1552; title page 'Popery Truly Display'd in its Bloody Colours', London, R. Hewson, 1689) — translation credit matches the page. Excerpt is the Hatuey passage on Cuba, contiguous apart from one '…' that spans only a paragraph break and one that drops a clause on the friar's promises of heaven; '[Hatuey]' is a pure insertion after 'Cacic' (source spells him 'Hathney'); 'endeavuoring' and 'Hathney' are as printed. Las Casas was a Dominican friar in 1542 (bishop only from 1543/44); written 1542, printed 1552; Hatuey's resistance and execution 1511–12. All consistent.

sourceLine: Bartolome de las Casas, Spanish Dominican friar and former colonist, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, on Hispaniola, written 1542, published 1552
text: … they [the Indians] began to consider by what wayes and means they might expel the Spaniards out of their Countrey, and immediately took up Arms. But, good God, what Arms, do you imagin? Namely such, both Offensive and Defensive, as resemble Reeds wherewith Boys sport with one another, more than Manly Arms and Weapons. Which the Spaniards no sooner perceived, but they, mounted on generous Steeds, well weapon'd with Lances and Swords, begin to exercise their bloody Butcheries and Strategems, and overrunning their Cities and Towns, spar'd no Age, or Sex, nay not so much as Women with Child, but ripping up their Bellies, tore them alive in pieces. They laid Wagers among themselves, who should with a Sword at one blow cut, or divide a Man in two; … nay farther, which should sheath his Sword in the Bowels of a Man with the quickest dispatch and expedition. … and if at any time it hapned, (which was rarely) that the Indians irritated upon a just account destroy'd or took away the Life of any Spaniard, they promulgated and proclaim'd this Law among them, that One Hundred Indians should dye for every individual Spaniard that should be slain.
translation: Anonymous English translation, Popery Truly Display'd in its Bloody Colours (London), 1689
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 20321 (the anonymous 1689 English translation "Popery Truly Display'd", from the 1552 Brevisima; preparer's note on the page). The excerpt began "Which the Spaniards no sooner perceived", where "Which" refers to the Indians taking up arms, a sentence that had been cut. Restored that passage from the page ("they began to consider ... immediately took up Arms. But, good God, what Arms ... more than Manly Arms and Weapons.") with the bracket [the Indians]. It also shows the contrast in weapons the author draws. Date and attribution correct. Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: Bartolomé de las Casas, Dominican friar and former encomienda holder who campaigned for Indigenous rights, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies, written 1542, published 1552
text: The Spaniards first assaulted the innocent Sheep, so qualified by the Almighty, as is premention'd, like most cruel Tygers, Wolves and Lions hunger-starv'd, studying nothing, for the space of Forty Years, after their first landing, but the Massacre of these Wretches … that of Three Millions of Persons, which lived in Hispaniola itself, there is at present but the inconsiderable remnant of scarce Three Hundred. Nay the Isle of Cuba, which extends as far, as Valledolid in Spain is distant from Rome, lies now uncultivated, like a Desert, and intomb'd in its own Ruins. … The Lucayan Islands on the North Side, adjacent to Hispaniola and Cuba, which are Sixty in number, or thereabout, … is now laid waste and uninhabited; and whereas, when the Spaniards first arriv'd here, about Five Hundred Thousand Men dwelt in it, they are now cut off, some by slaughter, and others ravished away by Force and Violence, to work in the Mines of Hispanioloa [Hispaniola], which was destitute of Native Inhabitants …
translation: Translated in Popery Truly Display'd in its Bloody Colours (London, 1689), translator not named
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 20321 (images), Preface of the 1689 translation. After "Cuba ... intomb'd in its own Ruins. …" the excerpt went on "whereas, when the Spaniards first arriv'd here, about Five Hundred Thousand Men dwelt in it", so the 500,000 seemed to be Cuba's. On the page they are the Lucayan Islands' (the Bahamas). Restored "The Lucayan Islands on the North Side, adjacent to Hispaniola and Cuba, which are Sixty in number, or thereabout, … is now laid waste and uninhabited; and"; the new "…" skips a list of other islands. Added a closing "…" because the excerpt ends mid-sentence. Attribution, dates and the credit (translator not named) correct.

sourceLine: Bartolomé de las Casas, Dominican friar and former encomienda holder who campaigned for Indigenous rights, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies, on Hispaniola, written 1542, published 1552
text: The Warlike Engagements being over, and the Inhabitants all swept away, they divided among themselves the Young Men, Women, and Children reserved promiscuously for that purpose, one obtained thirty, another forty, to this Man one hundred were disposed, to the other two hundred, and the more one was in favor with the domineering Tyrant (which they styled Governor) the more he became Master of, upon this pretence, and with this Proviso, that he should see them instructed in the Catholick Religion … they sent the Males to the Mines to dig and bring away the Gold, which is an intollerable labor; but the Women they made use of to Manure and Till the ground … The Men died in Mines, hunger starved and oppressed with labor, and the Women perished in the Fields, harrassed and broken with the like Evils and Calamities: Thus an infinite number of Inhabitants that formerly peopled this Island were exterminated and dwindled away to nothing by such Consumptions.
translation: Translated in Popery Truly Display'd in its Bloody Colours (London, 1689), translator not named
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 20321 (images), section on Hispaniola. Cuts skip Las Casas's comment on the masters' vices and the details of starvation; meaning kept. Attribution, dates and credit correct (the 1689 translation names no translator).

sourceLine: Paul Le Jeune, Jesuit missionary who wintered with the Montagnais (Innu) of Quebec, Relation of 1634, recording their answers to his questions
text: Thirdly: "What do these souls do when they arrive at their dwelling place?" "During the daytime, they are seated with their two elbows upon their two knees, and their heads between their two hands, the usual position of sick Savages; during the night, they go and come, they work, they go to the chase." "Oh, but they cannot see at all during the night," I rejoined. "Thou art an ignoramus, thou hast no sense," they answered; "souls are not like us, they do not see at all during the day, and see very clearly at night; their day is in the darkness of the night, and their night in the light of the day." … And when they see that I make sport of their dreams, they are astonished and ask me, "What does thou believe then, if thou dost not believe in thy dream?" "I believe in him who has made all things, and who can do all things." "Thou hast no sense, how canst thou believe in him, if thou hast not seen him?"
translation: Translated by John Cutler Covert (assisted by Mary Sifton Pepper), The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, ed. Reuben Gold Thwaites, vol. 6, 1897
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg #51262 (Thwaites vol. 6), Relation of 1634, ch. 4, English pp. 179–183. The leading bracket '[Le Jeune asked:]' stood in for the source word 'Thirdly:' (Le Jeune is numbering his questions), so the source word is restored; the sourceLine already says he records their answers to his questions, and he speaks in the first person ('I rejoined'). The long cut (the fourth question, on hunting souls, and other beliefs) is marked; 'What does thou believe' is as printed. Translation credit now names the translators listed on the volume's staff page: 'Translator from the French: John Cutler Covert; Assistant Translator from the French: Mary Sifton Pepper'. Relation closed at Quebec, August 7, 1634; Le Jeune wintered with the Montagnais 1633–34.

sourceLine: Lebna Dengel (King David), Christian emperor of Ethiopia, letter to King Manuel I of Portugal, written c. 1522 before news of Manuel's death (December 1521) reached Ethiopia, and carried back by the Portuguese embassy in 1526, as printed in Francisco Alvares's account of the embassy (1540)
text: Before this I had not seen any embassy from a Christian king, and now you are near to me, before all were Pagans and Moors, dirty sons of Mahomed, and others are slaves who do not know God; … Do you always write to me that we may assist one another. On the arrival of those that you sent to Masua, and also of those who may come in future, both to Masua and Dalaqua and the other ports, I will do what you have commanded, because thus I desire that we should both assist one another : and as your people will be there, I shall be there, because there are my lands : there are no Christians and churches there, and all are Moors and Pagans. I am pleased that your people should settle there at the extremities of my countries ; for the sake of this do you accomplish what you have at first begun.
translation: Translated by Lord Stanley of Alderley, Narrative of the Portuguese Embassy to Abyssinia during the Years 1520-1527 (Hakluyt Society), 1881
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org narrativeofportu00alvarich, pp. 389-395 (Stanley of Alderley, Hakluyt Society, 1881, named on the title page); the cuts keep the meaning. Date (flagged): the letter addresses Manuel as living. Alvares (ch. cxii, p. 299) records the arrival of letters announcing Manuel's death while the embassy was still in Ethiopia, between entries dated 1521 and 1526, and the emperor's separate letter to King John III (pp. 396-397) says he heard of Manuel's death "before we had despatched his ambassadors". So the Manuel letter was written between the embassy's arrival (1520) and that news (c. 1523), not in 1526, when it was carried back. Set year 1522 (c., the midpoint of 1520-1523) and reworded the sourceLine.

sourceLine: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan), Muslim scholar and diplomat from Fez who travelled in West Africa, The History and Description of Africa, book 7, on the kingdom of Bornu and its trade in horses for slaves with merchants from Barbary (North Africa, across the Sahara), written 1526 (adapted)
text: Whereupon the king of Borno sent for the merchants of Barbary, and willed them to bring him great store of horses; for in this country they use to exchange horses for slaves … Sometimes he bringeth not home slaves enough to satisfy the merchants: and otherwhiles they are constrained to await there a whole year together; for the king maketh invasions but every year once. … And yet the king seemeth to be marvellous rich; for his spurs, his bridles, platters, dishes, pots, and other vessels wherein his meat and drink are brought to the table, are all of pure gold: yea, and the chains of his dogs and hounds are of gold also. Howbeit this king is extremely covetous, for he had much rather pay his debts in slaves than in gold.
original: Whereupon the king of Borno sent for the merchants of Barbary, and willed them to bring him great store of horses : for in this countrey they vse to exchange horses for slaues … Sometimes he bringeth not home slaues enough to satisfie the merchants: and otherwhiles they are constrained to awaite there a whole yeere togither ; for the king maketh inuasions but euery yeere once, … And yet the king seemeth to be marueilous rich ; for his spurres, his bridles, platters, dishes, pots, and other vessels wherein his meate and drinke are brought to the table, are all of pure golde : yea, and the chaines of his dogs and hounds are of golde also. Howbeit this king is extreamely couetous, for he had much rather pay his debts in slaues than in gold.
translation: Translated by John Pory, 1600; edited by Robert Brown, The History and Description of Africa, vol. 3 (Hakluyt Society), 1896
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with archive.org historyanddescr01porygoog: its title page is "Vol. III", Hakluyt Society no. XCIV, 1896 (Pory 1600, ed. Robert Brown), so the vol. 3 credit is right even though the scan id says 01. Book 7 ("The Seventh Booke"), "Of the kingdome of Borno", pp. 833–834; page images (leaves 148–149) checked: the original matches the print word for word (this edition prints no long s), and the text differs only in spelling (countrey, vse, slaues, yeere, golde etc.). Cuts remove the price (15–20 slaves per horse), the merchants' waiting and Leo's own meeting with unpaid merchants; meaning kept. "Written 1526" matches the colophon "Written at Rome in the yeere of Christ 1526. and vpon the tenth of March". sourceLine now says the trade is with North African merchants across the Sahara, so it is not read as Atlantic trade (flagged); topics left as they were.

sourceLine: Richard Ligon, English royalist exile who helped manage a sugar plantation on Barbados 1647–1650, A True and Exact History of the Island of Barbados, 1657
text: …which had in it 500 Acres of Land, with a faire dwelling house, an Ingenio [sugar mill] plac’t in a roome of 400 foot square; a boyling house, filling roome, Cisterns, and Still-house … Houses for Negroes and Indian slaves, with 96 Negroes, and three Indian women, with their Children; 28 Christians, 45 Cattle for worke, 8 Milch Cowes, a dosen Horses and Mares, 16 Assinigoes [donkeys]. … In this plantation of 500 acres of land, there was imployed for sugar somewhat more then 200 acres; above 80 acres for pasture, 120 for wood, 30 for Tobacco, 5 for Ginger, as many for Cotton wool, and 70 acres for provisions; viz. Corne, Potatoes, Plantines, Cassavie, and Bonavist … The Iland is divided into three sorts of men, viz. Masters, Servants, and slaves. The slaves and their posterity, being subject to their Masters for ever, are kept and preserv’d with greater care then the servants, who are theirs but for five yeers, according to the law of the Iland.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 70489 (Ligon, A True & Exact History, London: Humphrey Moseley, 1657). Cuts skip buildings, the purchase terms and a list of fruits; the closing sentence is complete. The brackets [sugar mill] and [donkeys] clarify words. The role is correct: Ligon managed the plantation with Colonel Modyford for about three years from 1647.

sourceLine: Sejarah Melayu (Malay Annals), court chronicle of the Malacca sultanate compiled c. 1612, on the first Portuguese attack on Malacca
text: When the monsoon arrived, the capitan [captain of a Portuguese trading ship] returned to Goa, and reported to the vizier the greatness of Malaca, and its great population. Now the name of the great vizier was Alphonsus Albuquerco, and he began to covet it eagerly, when he heard how fine a country Malaca was. He accordingly ordered a fleet of seven ships and thirteen galleons to be fitted out ; and he appointed Gonsalvo Pereira to be captain-admiral to attack Malaca. When they reached Malaca they began to fire away with their cannon, and all the people of Malaca, were frightened when they heard the sound of their cannon, saying, “What sound is this like thunder ?” And the bullets came and struck the people who were on the land, and some had their necks severed, and some had their waists, and some their hands and their feet. The terror grew constantly worse and worse, and they said, “What is the name of this weapon which is so round ? It is not sharp, yet will it kill.”
translation: Translated by John Leyden, Malay Annals, 1821
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org b29336600, pp. 324-325 (Leyden, Malay Annals, 1821, translator named on the title page). "the capitan" had no referent in the excerpt; the page just before introduces him as the captain of "a Frangi vessel from Goa, to trade at Malaca". Added the bracket [captain of a Portuguese trading ship]. Date c. 1612: the preface dates the compilation to AH 1021 (AD 1612). The Annals' version of events (Albuquerque sending "Gonsalvo Pereira") is the chronicle's own and is kept as it stands.

sourceLine: Niccolao Manucci, Venetian who lived in India from 1653 and served Mughal princes as gunner and physician, Storia do Mogor, Part IV (written after August 1702), on the poll tax (jizya) imposed on Hindus in 1679
text: It was during the years 1678 and 1679 that Aurangzeb decided to impose a new tribute upon all the Hindus. … But all was in vain, and the king stood firm, still more so because it was his purpose to spread the Mahomedan religion among those people (the Hindus). He was of the opinion that he had found in this tax an excellent means of succeeding in converting them, besides … thereby replenishing his treasuries greatly, which were daily becoming depleted. … Begam Sahib, eldest sister of the king, a very generous princess, wanted to make a fresh appeal. With this intent she paid her brother a visit, and entreated most humbly that he would not go farther with this affair … ‘Just think, sire,’ said she, ‘that the lands of Hindustan are like a vast ocean; your majesty and all the other members of our royal family are like ships navigating its waters and ploughing through its waves. Where is there any sovereign prince who would desire to load with imposts the sea on which he sails? Who has ever seen the physician pay the patient?’
translation: Translated by William Irvine, Storia do Mogor, vol. 3, 1907
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Irvine, Storia do Mogor vol. 3 (John Murray, 1907), pp. 288-289. Date: the passage is in Part IV (Part IV begins p. 249; its preface is dated by Irvine to early 1701), and the paragraph immediately before it narrates 'the end of August, 1702' (Muhammad Sa'id at San Thome, p. 287), so 'written c. 1700' was wrong: sourceLine now 'Part IV (written after August 1702)', year 1702. Text: the cut after 'converting them' removed the rest of the same sentence, Manucci's second motive — 'besides thereby replenishing his treasuries greatly, which were daily becoming depleted' — leaving a religion-only reading; restored it from the page. The '…' between 'besides' and 'thereby' spans only footnotes 1-2 and the page head at the p. 288/289 break, not text (needed so the mechanical check matches). 'But all was in vain' follows a marked cut of the nobles' protest; acceptable. Translation credit correct.

sourceLine: King Manuel I of Portugal, letter to Ferdinand and Isabella of Castile announcing that Vasco da Gama's fleet had reached India, July 1499
text: Your Highnesses already know that we had ordered Vasco da Gama, a nobleman of our household, … with four vessels to make discoveries by sea, … And as the principal motive of this enterprise has been, with our predecessors, the service of God our Lord, and our own advantage, … it pleased Him in His mercy to speed them on their route. From a message which has now been brought to this city … we learn that they did reach and discover India … that they entered and navigated its sea, finding large cities, large edifices and rivers, and great populations, among whom is carried on all the trade in spices and precious stones, which are forwarded in ships … to Mecca, and thence to Cairo, whence they are dispersed throughout the world. … Moreover, we hope, with the help of God, that the great trade which now enriches the Moors of those parts, … shall, in consequence of our regulations (ordenanços) be diverted to the natives and ships of our own kingdom, so that henceforth all Christendom, in this part of Europe, shall be able, in a large measure, to provide itself with these spices and precious stones.
translation: Translated by E. G. Ravenstein, A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (Hakluyt Society), 1898
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 46440, Appendix A, letter I (Ravenstein 1898; dated July 1499; Ravenstein's italics mark words missing from one of the two printed versions and are genuine text). The excerpt joined "And as the principal motive ... and our own advantage, …" straight onto "we learn that they did reach ...", cutting the main clause ("it pleased Him in His mercy to speed them on their route") and making it read as if the motive caused the news. Restored the source words, and the opening sentence naming Vasco and Paulo da Gama so that "they" has a referent. The "…" after "advantage," skips only footnote marker [269]. [Nicolau Coelho] sits at footnote marker [270] and names the captain, per Ravenstein's introduction (letter written after "the arrival of Coelho's vessel on July 10"). Other cuts unchanged. Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: Peter Martyr d'Anghiera, Italian humanist at the Spanish court who questioned returning explorers and colonists, De Orbe Novo, First Decade, c. 1510
text: The bread made by the natives is found, by those who are accustomed to our wheat bread, to be insufficiently nourishing and therefore they lose their strength. The King consequently issued a recent decree, ordering that wheat should be sown in different places and at different seasons. The harvest produced nothing but straw, similar to twigs, and with little grain; although what there is, is large and well formed. This also applies to the pastures where the grass grows as high as the crops; thus the cattle become extraordinarily fat, but their flesh loses its flavour; their muscles become flabby, and they are, so to say, watery. With pigs it is just the contrary; for they are healthy and of an agreeable flavour. This is due doubtless to certain of the island's fruits they greedily devour. Pork is about the only kind of meat bought in the markets. The pigs have rapidly increased, but they have become wild since they are no longer kept by swineherds.
translation: Translated by Francis Augustus MacNutt, De Orbe Novo: The Eight Decades of Peter Martyr d'Anghera, 1912
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 12425 (MacNutt 1912, vol. 1). The passage is in the First Decade, Book X ("and Epilogue to the Decade"), continuous, with no cuts. Date c. 1510: in Book X Martyr says he is narrating "the principal events between the years 1500 and 1510", and the First Decade was first printed in 1511, so c. 1510 is reasonable.

sourceLine: Hans Mayr, German clerk aboard the fleet of Francisco de Almeida, Portuguese viceroy of India, account of the taking of Kilwa (East Africa), 1505
text: Immediately on their arrival the Grand-Captain, Dom Francisco d'Almeida, sent Bona Ajuta Veneziano to summon the king. … Then the captains, each in his best clothes, and full armour, went in his own boat to lie off the town in the hope that the king would decide to come out. The sheikh, however, sent a message to say that he could not come since he had guests, but, if required, he would send the tribute due to the King of Portugal. This message was brought by a party of five Moors, who were immediately seized. … As soon as the town had been taken without opposition, the Vicar-General and some of the Franciscan fathers came ashore carrying two crosses in procession and singing the Te Deum. They went to the palace, and there the cross was put down and the Grand-Captain prayed. Then everyone started to plunder the town of all its merchandise and provisions. … The fortress of Kilwa was built out of the best house there was there. All the other houses round it were pulled down. … Pero Ferreira was left in command of it with eighty men.
translation: Translated in Eric Axelson, South-East Africa 1488-1530, 1940, as reprinted in G. S. P. Freeman-Grenville, The East African Coast: Select Documents (London: Rex Collings), 1974, and given in the Internet Modern History Sourcebook
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1505mayr (source: Axelson, South East Africa, 1940, pp. 231-238, quoted in Freeman-Grenville, 1974). The excerpt went from the seizing of the king's messengers straight to "Then everyone started to plunder the town", leaving out the landing and capture of the town, so "Then" was misleading. Restored the source sentence that comes just before "Then everyone started" on the page ("As soon as the town had been taken without opposition, the Vicar-General and some of the Franciscan fathers came ashore ... and the Grand-Captain prayed."). Added the 1974 reprint year, which the page gives, to the credit. Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: The inspector-general of Chincheo (Zhangzhou/Quanzhou, Fujian), a Ming Chinese official, letter to Pedro de Acuña, Spanish governor of the Philippines, after the 1603 massacre of Chinese in Manila, 1605
text: We said that the land of Luzon was a wretched land of little importance, of old inhabited only by devils and snakes; and that, as a result of the immigration there a few years ago of so many Sangleys [Chinese merchants] to trade with the Castilians, the country has been enriched to the extent to which the said Sangleys have labored therein. They have built the walls, and made houses and gardens, and other things of great advantage to the Castilians. … If the Castilians show justice to the Chinese, send back the Sangleys who have survived the war, and pay the money due for the goods taken from the Sangleys, there will be amity between this kingdom and that, and merchant vessels will sail there every year.
translation: Translated by Henry B. Lathrop from a contemporary Spanish translation of the Chinese letter (Spanish translator not named), in E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., The Philippine Islands, 1493–1898, vol. 13, 1904
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with B&R vol. 13 (1904), "Letter from a Chinese official to Acuña": verbatim; "[Chinese merchants]" glosses Sangleys. Heading: "Translation of a letter from the inspector-general of Chincheo ... received in this year 1605, addressed to Don Pedro de Acuña"; dated 12th of the second month = March [1605]. The B&R text is an English version of a Spanish translation made at the time, so the credit now says so (as for the Chanchian letter); section note says "the second and third [are translated] by Henry B. Lathrop" - this letter is the second of the 1605 documents. Excerpt ends before the letter's threat of war if the Spaniards do not comply (not a cut, but worth knowing).

sourceLine: Cristóbal de Molina, Spanish priest in Cuzco who preached in Quechua, An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas, c. 1575, describing the Taki Onqoy movement of the 1560s
text: Many preachers went forth from among the Indians, who preached as well in the desert places as in the villages, declaring the resurrection of the huacas, and saying that they now wandered in the air, thirsty and dying of hunger, because the Indians no longer sacrificed nor poured out chicha to them. … The huacas, it was announced, were enraged with all those who had been baptized, and it was declared that they would all be killed unless they returned to the old belief and renounced the Christain faith. … Those who would return to the love of the huacas and live, were to fast for some days, not eating salt nor aji, nor coloured maize, nor any Spanish thing, nor entering churches, nor obeying the call of the priests, nor using their christian names. Henceforth the times of the Yncas would be restored, and the huacas would not enter into stones or fountains to speak, but would be incorporated in men whom they would cause to speak.
translation: Translated by Clements R. Markham, Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, 1873
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Markham, Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873), p. 61 (page image, leaf 97). 'Christain' is printed so (printer's error), and kept. Cuts drop the 'fields sown with worms' sentence and one on the prosperity promised to followers; meaning kept. Markham's introduction: Molina was priest of the hospital for natives at Cuzco and a master of Quechua, and the report was written for Bishop Artaun between 1570 and 1584; c. 1575 is a reasonable estimate within that span. The text itself dates the beginnings of the movement to 1560.

sourceLine: The sultan (king) of Mombasa, letter to Sayyid Ali, king of Malindi, after the Portuguese sack of Mombasa, as recorded by Hans Mayr, a German clerk with the Portuguese fleet, 1505
text: Now the King of Mombasa and the King of Malindi were at war, and many of their people had been killed on both sides, the cause of the war being the friendship of the King of Malindi with the King of Portugal. Eventually the King of Mombasa had been defeated by the King of Malindi, and for the present they were friends. So the King of Mombasa wrote the following letter to the King of Malindi: May God's blessing be upon you, Sayyid Ali! This is to inform you that a great lord has passed through the town, burning it and laying it waste. He came to the town in such strength and was of such cruelty, that he spared neither man nor woman, old nor young, nay, not even the smallest child. Not even those who fled escaped from his fury. He not only killed and burnt men but even the birds of the heavens were shot down. The stench of the corpses is so great in the town that I dare not go there; nor can I ascertain nor estimate what wealth they have taken from the town. I give you these sad news for your own safety.
translation: Translated in Eric Axelson, South-East Africa 1488-1530, 1940, as reprinted in G. S. P. Freeman-Grenville, The East African Coast: Select Documents (London: Rex Collings), 1974, and given in the Internet Modern History Sourcebook
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1505mayr. The cut removed "Eventually the King of Mombasa had been defeated by the King of Malindi, and for the present they were friends.", so the excerpt read "they were at war ... So the King of Mombasa wrote ...", a false link. Restored the sentence. The sourceLine already says the letter is as recorded by Hans Mayr. Credit: Axelson 1940 as quoted in Freeman-Grenville; added the 1974 year given on the page.

sourceLine: Montesquieu (Charles de Secondat), French nobleman, former magistrate in the Parlement of Bordeaux, and political philosopher, The Spirit of Laws, book 21, chapter 21, on European colonies, 1748
text: The colonies they [the nations of Europe] have formed are under a kind of dependence, of which there are but very few instances in all the colonies of the ancients; whether we consider them as holdings of the state itself, or of some trading company established in the state. The design of these colonies is to trade on more advantageous conditions than could otherwise be done with the neighbouring people, with whom all advantages are reciprocal. … Thus it is still a fundamental law of Europe that all commerce with a foreign colony shall be regarded as a mere monopoly, punishable by the laws of the country. … The disadvantage of a colony that loses the liberty of commerce is visibly compensated by the protection of the mother country, who defends it by her arms, or supports it by her laws.
translation: Translated by Thomas Nugent (1750), revised by J. V. Prichard; The Spirit of Laws, G. Bell & Sons, London, 1914 (as reproduced by the Constitution Society)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with constitution.org book 21, chapter 21 ('The Discovery of two new Worlds, and in what manner Europe is affected by it'). Words match. 'they' referred back to 'several nations' of Europe in the previous paragraph, so a clarifying bracket was added. The cuts (45 words: 'It has been established that the metropolis... alone shall trade in the colonies...'; 56 words on ancient precedent) do not change the meaning. Translation credit corrected to the 1914 G. Bell edition the site names, and role refined, as for the other Montesquieu document.

sourceLine: Montesquieu (Charles de Secondat), French nobleman, former magistrate in the Parlement of Bordeaux, and political philosopher, The Spirit of Laws, book 21, chapter 22, "Of the Riches which Spain drew from America", 1748
text: Gold and silver are either a fictitious or a representative wealth. The representative signs of wealth are extremely durable, and, in their own nature, but little subject to decay. But the more they are multiplied, the more they lose their value, because the fewer are the things which they represent. The Spaniards, after the conquest of Mexico and Peru, abandoned their natural riches, in pursuit of a representative wealth which daily degraded itself. … However, it was not long before the specie of Europe was doubled; this appeared from the price of commodities, which everywhere was doubled. … The king of Spain, who receives great sums from his custom-house at Cadiz, is in this respect only a rich individual in a state extremely poor.
translation: Translated by Thomas Nugent (1750), revised by J. V. Prichard; The Spirit of Laws, G. Bell & Sons, London, 1914 (as reproduced by the Constitution Society)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with constitution.org book 21, chapter 22 'Of the Riches which Spain drew from America' (the heading is right). The site's title page says the text is Nugent's translation as revised by J. V. Prichard, 'based on a public domain edition published in 1914 by G. Bell & Sons, Ltd., London'. The old credit's '1900' is not supported, so the credit was corrected. The first '…' marked only a paragraph break and was removed. The other cuts (on the Indians not knowing mercury; ~900 words of the doubling argument) keep the meaning. Role refined: Montesquieu had sold his office as président à mortier of the Parlement of Bordeaux in 1726, so in 1748 he was a former magistrate. Year 1748 (first edition, Geneva) is right.

sourceLine: Francis Moore, English clerk and factor for the Royal African Company on the Gambia River, 1730–35, Travels into the Inland Parts of Africa, 1738 (adapted)
text: Besides the Slaves which the Merchants bring down, there are many bought along the River. These are either taken in War as the former are, or else Men condemned for Crimes, or else People stolen, which is very frequent. … Since this Slave-Trade has been us'd, all Punishments are chang'd into Slavery; there being an Advantage on such Condemnations, they strain for Crimes very hard, in order to get the Benefit of selling the Criminal. Not only Murder, Theft and Adultery, are punish'd by selling the Criminal for a Slave, but every trifling Crime is punish'd in the same manner.
original: Besides the Slaves which the Merchants bring down, there are many bought along the River. Thefe are either taken in War as the former are, or elfe Men condemned for Crimes, or elfe People ftolen, which is very frequent. … Since this Slave-Trade has been us'd, all Punifhments are chang'd into Slavery j there being an Advantage on fuch Condemnations, they ftrain for Crimes very hard, in order to get the Benefit of felling the Criminal. Not only Murder, Theft and Adultery, are punifh*d by felling the Criminal for a Slave, but every trifling Crime is punilh'd in the fame manner.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with archive.org travelsintoinlan00moor (London: Edward Cave, 1738; "By Francis Moore, Factor several Years to the Royal African Company"; appointed Writer at James Fort, July 1730), p. 42; page image leaf 82 viewed. Word diff: spelling only; OCR fixes confirmed on the image: "felling" (twice) and "fame" are printed with long s ("ſelling", "ſame"), and "Slavery j" is "Slavery ;". (The OCR's "condemned" is printed "condemn'd"; the text's "condemned" is the modern spelling.) The cut removes the Company's claim that its servants consult the Alcade before buying people suspected of being stolen; meaning of the rest kept.

sourceLine: Antonio de Morga, Spanish judge of the royal Audiencia and lieutenant-governor in Manila (1595–1603), Events in the Philippine Islands (Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas), 1609
text: The purchase price is paid in silver and reals, for the Sangleys [Chinese merchants] do not want gold, or any other articles, and will not take other things to China. … This trade and commerce is so great and profitable, and easy to control—for it only lasts three months in the year, from the time of the arrival of the ships with their merchandise, until those vessels that go to Nueva España take that merchandise—that the Spaniards do not apply themselves to, or engage in, any other industry. … That trade has been very hurtful and prejudicial in this respect, as well as for the occupations and farm industries in which the natives used to engage. Now the latter are abandoning and forgetting those labors. Besides, there is the great harm and loss resulting from the immense amount of silver that passes annually by this way [of the trade], into the possession of infidels, which can never, by any way, return into the possession of the Spaniards.
translation: Translated by Alfonso de Salvio, Norman F. Hall and James A. Robertson, in E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, eds., History of the Philippine Islands by Antonio de Morga, 1907
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg #7001, Morga, History of the Philippine Islands (Blair & Robertson separate issue, 1907, vol. II = series vol. 16), ch. 8: all pieces verbatim; "[of the trade]" is the editors' bracket, "[Chinese merchants]" a gloss on Sangleys. Cuts (galleon lading; no husbandry or mining by Spaniards) keep the meaning; "in this respect" still points back to the retained statement that Spaniards engage in no other industry. Translation note: "This is made by Alfonso de Salvio, Norman F. Hall, and James Alexander Robertson". B&R preface: Morga sent out in 1595 as lieutenant-governor, later auditor; he left in 1603. Sucesos printed Mexico 1609.

sourceLine: Thomas Mun, London merchant and director of the English East India Company, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade, chapter 2, "The means to enrich the Kingdom, and to encrease our Treasure", written c. 1630, published 1664 (adapted)
text: Although a Kingdom may be enriched by gifts received, or by purchase taken from some other Nations, yet these are things uncertain and of small consideration when they happen. … The ordinary means therefore to encrease our wealth and treasure is by Forraign Trade, wherein wee must ever observe this rule; to sell more to strangers yearly than wee consume of theirs in value. For suppose that when this Kingdom is plentifully served with the Cloth, Lead, Tinn, Iron, Fish and other native commodities, we doe yearly export the overplus to forraign Countries to the value of twenty two hundred thousand pounds; by which means we are enabled beyond the Seas to buy and bring in forraign wares for our use and Consumptions, to the value of twenty hundred thousand pounds; By this order duly kept in our trading, we may rest assured that the Kingdom shall be enriched yearly two hundred thousand pounds, which must be brought to us in so much Treasure; because that part of our stock which is not returned to us in wares must necessarily be brought home in treasure.
original: Although a Kingdom may be enriched by gifts received, or by purchase taken from some other Nations, yet these are things uncertain and of small consideration when they happen. … The ordinary means therefore to encrease our wealth and treasure is by Forraign Trade, wherein wee must ever observe this rule; to sell more to strangers yearly than wee consume of theirs in value. For suppose that when this Kingdom is pletifully served with the Cloth, Lead, Tinn, Iron, Fish and other native commodities, we doe yearly export the overplus to forraign Countries to the value of twenty two hundred thousand pounds; by which means we are enabled beyond the Seas to buy and bring in forraign wares for our use and Consumption, to the value of twenty hundred thousand pounds; By this order duly kept in our trading, we may rest assured that this order duly kept in our trading, we may rest assured that the Kingdom shall be enriched yearly two hundred thousand pounds, which must be brought to us in so much Treasure; because that part of our stock which is not returned to us in wares must necessarily be brought home in treasure.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Checked against the scan behind the Wikisource transcription (Ashley's Economic Classics reprint of the 1664 text, Commons djvu p. 7, image viewed). The printed text reads 'By this order duly kept in our trading, we may rest assured that the Kingdom shall be enriched...'. The Wikisource page repeats 'we may rest assured that this order duly kept in our trading,', and the old excerpt cut around that, losing 'By this order duly kept in our trading'. The page also has 'pletifully' for printed 'plentifully' and 'Consumption' for printed 'Consumptions'. Now adapted: 'original' is the exact page text including the repeat, and 'text' is the printed wording (the repeat removed and the two transcription errors corrected, all confirmed on the page image; no other change). The first '…' still drops only the side-note 'Forraign Trade is the Rule of our Treasure.' The chapter title in sourceLine was wrong; it now uses the printed title.

sourceLine: Thomas Mun, London merchant and director of the English East India Company, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade, chapter 4, written c. 1630, published 1664
text: This Position [that exporting money in trade increases our treasure] is so contrary to the common opinion, that it will require many and strong arguments to prove it before it can be accepted of the Multitude, who bitterly exclaim when they see any monies carried out of the Realm; affirming thereupon that we have absolutely lost so much Treasure, and that this is an act directly against the long continued laws made and confirmed by the wisdom of this Kingdom in the High Court of Parliament, and that many places, nay Spain it self which is the Fountain of Mony, forbids the exportation thereof, some cases only excepted. … for all men do consent that plenty of mony in a Kingdom doth make the native commodities dearer, which as it is to the profit of some private men in their revenues, so is it directly against the benefit of the Publique in the quantity of the trade; for as plenty of mony makes wares dearer, so dear wares decline their use and consumption.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Checked the Wikisource text against its scan (W. J. Ashley's Economic Classics reprint of the 1664 text, Commons djvu pp. 19 and 24). Chapter IV begins 'This Position is so contrary...' and the excerpt matches the printed page word for word in both pieces. The bracket stands for the chapter title, 'The Exportation of our Moneys in Trade of Merchandize is a means to encrease our Treasure', and only clarifies 'This Position'. The ~1,180-word cut leaves the argument intact: the second piece is Mun's reason why hoarding money makes wares dearer and shrinks trade. Mun was an East India Company director from 1615. 'written c. 1630, published 1664' is right: the book was published after his death by his son.

sourceLine: Nahua (Aztec) accounts of the conquest of Mexico, recorded in Nahuatl in the decades after 1521, on the massacre at the festival of Toxcatl in 1520
text: On the second day they began to sing again, but without warning they were all put to death. The dancers and singers were completely unarmed. They brought only their embroidered cloaks, their turquoises, their lip plugs, their necklaces, their clusters of heron feathers, their trinkets made of deer hooves. Those who played the drums, the old men, had brought their gourds of snuff and their timbrels. The Spaniards attacked the musicians first, slashing at their hands and faces until they had killed all of them. The singers—and even the spectators—were also killed. This slaughter in the Sacred Patio went on for three hours. … The Sun [Pedro de Alvarado] had treacherously murdered our people on the twentieth day after the captain left for the coast. We allowed the Captain to return to the city in peace. But on the following day we attacked him with all our might, and that was the beginning of the war.
translation: Translated from Nahuatl into Spanish by Ángel María Garibay K. and from Spanish into English by Lysander Kemp, in Miguel León-Portilla, ed., The Broken Spears: The Aztec Account of the Conquest of Mexico, Beacon Press, 1962 (Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with the Fordham page (source note: León-Portilla, ed., The Broken Spears, Boston: Beacon Press, 1962, pp. 64–66, 129–131). Text matches; the cut drops the attack on temple workers and Motecuhzoma's protest; '[Pedro de Alvarado]' glosses 'The Sun' (Tonatiuh); the em dashes render the page's hyphens. The page names no translator; library records for the 1962 Beacon edition (archive.org catalogue entries brokenspearsazte00le, brokenspearsaz00leac) give Lysander Kemp as English translator of Visión de los vencidos, itself translated from Nahuatl by Garibay, so the credit now names both stages. The page does not say which Nahuatl text (Florentine Codex, Codex Aubin, etc.) the passage comes from, so the sourceLine stays generic; year 1560 is an estimate for accounts recorded between the 1520s and 1570s.

sourceLine: Nakuk Pech (baptized Don Pablo Pech), Maya noble and hereditary chief of Chac Xulub Chen in Yucatán, history of his town and of the conquest, c. 1562
text: …I, Nakuk Pech, was taken and given to Don Julian Doncel the Encomendero, the first lord of the town Chac Xulub Chen, the first Encomendero, and my hand was given him by the captain Don Francisco de Montejo, and I was given for a chief to Don Julian Doncel, in his hand, and I began to take tribute for the holy fathers. … when I entered the water and received baptism, I was called Don Pablo Pech; and I ceased to be called Nakuk Pech; we first … chiefs were created hidalgos by the captains when possession was first taken of this province, and we first paid tribute to the foreigners, and possession was given to us by God and the ruling king; and our descendants are hidalgos, and all our sons, until the time shall come when the world shall end … and I was also the first to receive the rod of the justicia, because I went to aid the Word of God and our great Lord the ruling king …
translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Maya Chronicles, 1882
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 20205 (Brinton 1882), Chronicle of Chac Xulub Chen, sec. 8-9. Brinton dates it "about 1562" (p. 189), which matches the year. "[we first]" put source words in brackets, as if an editor had added them. The page reads "we first [222]chiefs", where [222] is the print page number, so I made it "we first … chiefs", the bank's convention for skipping a page number. Added a closing "…" because the excerpt ends mid-sentence. No words changed.

sourceLine: Pope Nicholas V, papal bull Romanus Pontifex, granting rights in Africa to King Afonso V of Portugal and Prince Henry, 1455
text: … and war was waged for some years against the peoples of those parts in the name of the said King Alfonso and of the infante, and in it very many islands in that neighborhood were subdued and peacefully possessed, as they are still possessed together with the adjacent sea. Thence also many Guineamen and other negroes, taken by force, and some by barter of unprohibited articles, or by other lawful contract of purchase, have been sent to the said kingdoms. … we had formerly by other letters of ours granted among other things free and ample faculty to the aforesaid King Alfonso — to invade, search out, capture, vanquish, and subdue all Saracens and pagans whatsoever, and other enemies of Christ wheresoever placed, and the kingdoms, dukedoms, principalities, dominions, possessions, and all movable and immovable goods whatsoever held and possessed by them and to reduce their persons to perpetual slavery, and to apply and appropriate to himself and his successors the kingdoms, dukedoms, counties, principalities, dominions, possessions, and goods, and to convert them to his and their use and profit …
translation: Translated in Frances Gardiner Davenport, ed., European Treaties Bearing on the History of the United States and Its Dependencies to 1648 (Carnegie Institution of Washington), 1917
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with papalencyclicals.net (Davenport 1917 translation, named on the page). The second segment began "… granted among other things free and ample faculty ...", cutting its subject, so it was not clear that the Pope himself had granted the power to enslave. Restored the source words "we had formerly by other letters of ours" before "granted". Attribution and date (January 8, 1455) correct.

sourceLine: Pope Nicholas V, papal bull Romanus Pontifex, granting rights in Africa to King Afonso V of Portugal and Prince Henry, 1455
text: Moreover, since, some time ago, it had come to the knowledge of the said infante that never, or at least not within the memory of men, had it been customary to sail on this ocean sea toward the southern and eastern shores, … believing that he would best perform his duty to God in this matter, if by his effort and industry that sea might become navigable as far as to the Indians who are said to worship the name of Christ, and that thus he might be able to enter into relation with them, and to incite them to aid the Christians against the Saracens and other such enemies of the faith, … strengthened, however, always by the royal authority, he has not ceased for twenty-five years past to send almost yearly an army of the peoples of the said kingdoms with the greatest labor, danger, and expense, in very swift ships called caravels, to explore the sea and coast lands toward the south and the Antarctic pole.
translation: Translated in Frances Gardiner Davenport, ed., European Treaties Bearing on the History of the United States and Its Dependencies to 1648 (Carnegie Institution of Washington), 1917
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with papalencyclicals.net, which states the translation is Davenport, European Treaties (1917) pp. 20-26. Bull dated January 8, 1455. Cuts remove a clause on western ignorance of those shores and a clause on subduing pagans and preaching to them; the remaining sentence keeps its sense and grammar.

sourceLine: Otreouti (called 'Grangula'), Onondaga speaker, reply to Joseph-Antoine de La Barre, governor of New France, at La Famine in 1684, as retold by the French officer the Baron de Lahontan, who was with the expedition and said he set the speech 'in an European Dress', New Voyages to North-America, 1703 (adapted)
text: Do you hear, Onnontio, our Women had took up their Clubs; and the Children and the old Men, had visited your Camp with their Bows and Arrows, if our Warlike Men had not stop'd and disarm'd 'em, when Akouessan your Ambassador appear'd before my Village. But I have done, I'll talk no more of that. … You must know, Onnontio, we have robb'd no French-Men but those who supply'd the Illinese and the Oumamis (our Enemies) with Fusees, with Powder, and with Ball: These indeed we took care of, because such Arms might have cost us our life. … We are born Freemen, and have no dependance either upon the Onnontio [governor of New France] or the Corlar [governor of New York]. We have a power to go where we please, to conduct who we will to the places we resort to, and to buy and sell where we think fit. If your Allies are your Slaves or Children, you may e'en treat 'em as such, and rob 'em of the liberty of entertaining any other Nation but your own.

If your Allies are your ' Slaves or Children, you may e'en treat 'em as fuch, and rob ' 'em of the liberty of entertaining any other Nation but your ' own.
translation: Translator not named (English edition issued by Lahontan, London, 1703); reprinted in New Voyages to North-America, ed. Reuben Gold Thwaites, 1905
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with the page images (Thwaites reprint of the London 1703 English text, 1905, pp. 81–82, leaves 195–196). Text vs original: long-s spelling, 'I'll' (OCR ''11'), 'Onnontio' (OCR 'Onnontto'), 'conduct' (OCR 'condudl'), all confirmed on the images; the '…' marks in the original that the text drops only bridge the OCR's interleaving of the side-note 'Corlar is the Title of the Governor of New-York', which also supports the two bracketed glosses (Thwaites's footnote glosses Onontio as the governor of Canada). The cuts drop the Jesuit-brandy comparison and the sentence about bringing the English to the Lakes; meaning kept. sourceLine corrected: Lahontan's Preface says 'the thoughts of the Savages are set forth in an European Dress' and that his correspondent asked him 'not to make a literal Translation' of the Grangula's harangue, so 'as recorded by' overstated it; Lahontan narrates as a member of La Barre's camp ('we row'd', 'our Camp'). sourceLine: The Requerimiento (Requirement), drafted by the royal jurist Juan Lopez de Palacios Rubios for the Spanish Crown, to be read to Indigenous peoples before conquest, 1513 (adapted)
text: Wherefore, as best we can, we ask and require you that you consider what we have said to you, … and that you acknowledge the Church as the Ruler and Superior of the whole world … and the high priest called Pope, and in his name the King and Queen Doña Juana our lords, in his place, as superiors and lords and kings of these islands and this Terra-firma by virtue of the said donation, … If you do so, you will do well, … and we in their name shall receive you in all love and charity, … But, if you do not do this, and maliciously make delay in it, I certify to you that, with the help of God, we shall powerfully enter into your country, and shall make war against you … and shall subject you to the yoke and obedience of the Church and of their Highnesses ; we shall take you and your wives and your children, and shall make slaves of them, … and we protest that the deaths and losses which shall accrue from this are your fault, and not that of their Highnesses, or ours, nor of these cavaliers who come with us.
original: Wherefore, as best we can, we ask and require you that you consider what we have said to you, … and that you acknowledge the Church as the Ruler and Superior of the whole world … and the high priest called Pope, and in his name the King and Queen Dona Juana our lords, in his place, as superiors and lords and kings of these islands and this Terra-firma by virtue of the said donation, … If you do so, you will do well, … and we in their name shall receive you in all love and charity, … But, if you do not do this, and maliciously … make delay in it, I certify to you that, with the help of Grod, we shall powerfully enter into your country, and shall make war against you … and shall subject you to the yoke and obedience of the Church and of their Highnesses ; we shall take you and your wives and your children, and shall make slaves of them, … and we protest that the deaths and losses which shall accrue from this are your fault, and not that of their Highnesses, or ours, nor of these cavaliers who come with us.
translation: Translated by Arthur Helps, The Spanish Conquest in America, vol. 1, 1855
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org spanishconquesti01helpuoft, pp. 381-382 (Helps, The Spanish Conquest in America, vol. 1, London: Parker, 1855). (1) The bracket "[But if you refuse,]" replaced the cut clause "But, if you do not do this, and maliciously make delay in it, I certify to you that, with the help of God," (rule 5); restored it. The OCR reads "Grod" and puts the margin note "The Requisition" in mid-clause. I viewed the printed page (leaf n401, p. 382), which reads "help of God", so the document is now adapted: "original" has the OCR "Grod" and a "…" where the margin note falls; "text" has "God" and no ellipsis there, because no words are cut. (2) The first cut dropped the second half of the demand, that the hearers acknowledge "the high priest called Pope, and in his name the King and Queen Doña Juana our lords ... as superiors and lords and kings of these islands", and allow the friars to preach. Without it the demand reads as purely religious, so I restored it; the remaining "…" skips only Helps's Spanish gloss "(por Señora y Superiora del universo mundo)". "Doña" is as printed on p. 381 (OCR "Dona"). Added "(adapted)" to the sourceLine, as for the bank's other adapted documents. Attribution correct: p. 382 calls it the Requisition "drawn up by the learned Doctor Palacios Rubios". Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: Pedro Pizarro, Spanish conquistador and cousin of Francisco Pizarro, Relation of the Discovery and Conquest of the Kingdoms of Peru, 1571, describing the Inca siege of Cuzco led by Manco Inca in 1536
text: So numerous were the [Indian] troops who came here that they covered the fields, and by day it looked as if a black cloth had been spread over the ground for half a league around this city of Cuzco. At night there were so many fires that it looked like nothing other than a very serene sky full of stars. There was so much shouting and din of voices that all of us were astonished. … When they were all assembled, as I say, one morning they began to set fire to all parts of Cuzco, and, by means of this fire they were gaining many portions of the town, making palisades in the streets so that the Spaniards could not go out through them.
translation: Translated by Philip Ainsworth Means, Relation of the Discovery and Conquest of the Kingdoms of Peru, 1921
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Means's translation (Cortes Society, New York, 1921, vol. II, pp. 301–302). Title page of the Relation says it was signed in 1571 by Pedro Pizarro, 'a conqueror and settler'; Means's notes call him Francisco Pizarro's cousin. '[Indian]' is the translator's own bracket on the page, not an insertion. The single cut drops the sentence giving 200,000 besiegers; no change of meaning. Events: Manco Inca's siege of Cuzco, 1536.

sourceLine: William Penn, English Quaker and proprietor of Pennsylvania, letter to the Lenape (Delaware) leaders, sent with his commissioners, October 18, 1681
text: Now this great God hath been pleased to make me concerned in your part of the world, and the king of the country where I live hath given me a great province therein, but I desire to enjoy it with your love and consent, that we may always live together as neighbours and friends; … Now I would have you well observe, that I am very sensible of the unkindness and injustice that hath been too much exercised towards you by the people of these parts of the world, … which I hear hath been matter of trouble to you, and caused great grudgings and animosities, sometimes to the shedding of blood, which hath made the great God angry. But I am not such a man … I have great love and regard towards you, and I desire to win and gain your love and friendship by a kind, just, and peaceable life, … I shall shortly come to you myself, at what time we may more largely and freely confer and discourse of these matters; in the mean time I have sent my commissioners to treat with you about land, and a firm league of peace.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with CCEL primitivechristianity.vii (letter dated "London, the 18th of the 8th month, 1681", i.e. October 18, 1681, Old Style). (1) Removed a "…" between "in the world." and "Now I would", where the page has no cut. (2) The second cut removed Penn's central contrast, "But I am not such a man ... I desire to win and gain your love and friendship by a kind, just, and peaceable life", so the excerpt went from European injustice straight to sending commissioners about land. Restored "which I hear hath been matter of trouble ... peaceable life," and "I shall shortly come to you myself, at what time we may more largely and freely confer and discourse of these matters;", which "in the mean time" depends on. Written in English (translation null). Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: The English Parliament (Lords and Commons), the Petition of Right presented to King Charles I, 1628
text: Your subjects have inherited this freedom, that they should not be compelled to contribute to any tax, tallage, aid, or other like charge not set by common consent, in parliament. … Yet nevertheless of late divers commissions directed to sundry commissioners in several counties, with instructions, have issued; by means whereof your people have been in divers places assembled, and required to lend certain sums of money unto your Majesty, and many of them, upon their refusal so to do, have had an oath administered unto them not warrantable by the laws or statutes of this realm, and have been constrained to become bound and make appearance and give utterance before your Privy Council and in other places, and others of them have been therfore imprisoned, confined, and sundry other ways molested and disquieted. … They do therefore humbly pray your most excellent Majesty, that no man hereafter be compelled to make or yield any gift, loan, benevolence, tax, or such like charge, without common consent by act of parliament.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with the Wikisource text, sections I, II and the prayer (section X/XI). The first '…' spans only the section label 'II.'; the second skips sections III-IX (imprisonment, billeting, martial law) and the third piece is the prayer clause, cut at a semicolon; meaning intact. Excerpt begins mid-sentence ('…statutes of this realm, your subjects have inherited this freedom'), capital added, sense unchanged. sourceLine: Philip II, king of Spain, royal decree (cédula) to the viceroy and Audiencia of New Spain about Diego Díaz del Castillo, son of the conquistador Bernal Díaz, Madrid, 1565
text: Diego Diaz del Castillo has presented me an account of how Bernal Diaz del Castillo, his father, was one of the first explorers and conquerors of that City of Mexico and of New Spain … In consideration of these, and of the fact that he was the son of such a conqueror, poor, and in need, our former viceroy of that land, Don Luis de Velasco, commanded that he be given in our name a gratuity of one hundred and fifty dollars in common gold … it is our determined will that you appoint and prefer him, as a son of a conqueror, to one of the corregimientos and positions made mention of above in the said provinces of Tlascala, Tepeaca, Chalco, Cholula, Jilotepeque, or to any other position which may be very good, honorable, and profitable. … for by appointing him to offices and other positions in our service he may serve us and be honored and benefited. And in other appointments in that land you will bear this order in mind and appoint like persons to them.
translation: Translated in Charles W. Hackett, ed., Historical Documents Relating to New Mexico, Nueva Vizcaya, and Approaches Thereto, vol. 1, 1923
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 17C-spanishbios (source: Hackett, Historical Documents Relating to New Mexico..., Carnegie Institution, 1923, vol. 1). The cedula is dated "Madrid, April 1, 1565. I THE KING." Cuts skip the list of Bernal Diaz's campaigns and the Council's grant of 300 pesos; meaning kept. Fordham's own bracket "[But he wanted even more!]" is not in the excerpt.

sourceLine: King Philip III of Spain, royal decree regulating trade between the Philippines and New Spain (the Manila galleon), 31 December 1604 (adapted)
text: The king my lord and father (may he rest in peace!) by various decrees prohibited trade and commerce of the Western Indias with the Philipinas Islands and China generally, to obviate the loss that resulted therefrom to these kingdoms and to their trade and commerce. … Although it has been ordered by other decrees at various times that these should be observed and complied with, I have been informed that this has not been done, and that the quantity allowed has been and is being greatly exceeded in the amount taken each year, with the knowledge and permission of my viceroys, audiencias, and governors—goods to the extent of more than two millions of ducats being registered and openly sent, besides what is secretly shipped. All this money finally makes it [sic] way into infidel kingdoms, whereby their power is increased; and from this have resulted great losses to our exchequer and to the commerce of these kingdoms with the Western Indias. … I have decided that for the present the trade and commerce of the said Philipinas Islands with Nueva España should be maintained according to the ordinances.

sourceLine: Miles Philips, English sailor on John Hawkins's slaving voyage of 1567–1568, later a prisoner in New Spain, account written after his return in 1582 (adapted)
text: … passing the time upon the coast of Guinea, until the twelfth of January, we obtained by that time the number of 150. Negroes. And being ready to depart from the Sea coast, there was a Negro sent as an Ambassador to our General, from a King of the Negroes, … desiring our General to grant him succour and aid against those his enemies, which … our General granted unto, … and the said King which had requested our aid, did join his force with ours, so that thereby our General assaulted, and set fire upon a Town of the said King his enemies, … there were taken prisoners to the number of eight or nine hundred, which our General ought to have had for his share: howbeit the Negro King which requested our aid, falsifying his word and promise, secretly in the night conveyed himself away with as many prisoners as he had in his custody: but our General notwithstanding finding himself to have now very near the number of 500. Negroes thought it best without longer abode to depart with them, and such merchandise as he had from the coast of Africa, towards the West Indies …
original: … passing the time vpon the coast of Guinea, until the twelfth of Ianuary, we obteined by that time the number of 150. Negros. And being ready to depart from the Sea coast, there was a Negro sent as an Ambassadour to our Generall, from a King of the Negros, … desiring our Generall to grant him succour and ayde against those his enemies, which … our Generall granted vnto, … and the said King which had requested our ayde, did ioyne his force with ours, so that thereby our Generall assaulted, and set fire vpon a Towne of the said King his enemies, … there were taken prisoners to the number of eight or nine hundreth, which our Generall ought to haue had for his share: howbeit the Negro King which requested our ayde, falsifying his word and promise, secretly in the night conueyed himselfe away with as many prisoners as he had in his custodie: but our Generall notwithstanding finding himselfe to haue nowe very neere the number of 500. Negros thought it best without longer abode to depart with them, and such marchandize as hee had from the coast of Africa, towards the West Indies …

sourceLine: Miles Philips, English sailor left in New Spain in 1568 and handed out as a servant to Spanish gentlemen, account written after his return in 1582 (adapted)
text: The gentlemen that thus took us for their servants or slaves, did new apparel us throughout, with whom we abode, … for in that country no Spaniard will serve one another, but they are all of them attended and served by Indians weekly, and by Negroes which be their slaves during their life. … Afterwards many of us were by our masters appointed to go to sundry of their Mines where they had to do, and to be as overseers of the Negroes and Indians that laboured there. In which mines many of us did profit and gain greatly: for first we were allowed three hundred Pesos a man for a year, which is threescore pound sterling and besides that the Indians and Negroes which wrought under our charge, upon our well using and entreating of them, would at times as upon Saturdays when they had left work, labour for us, and blow as much silver as should be worth unto us 3 marks or thereabouts … Sundry weeks we did gain so much by this means besides our wages, that many of us became very rich, and were worth three thousand, or four thousand Pesos …
original: The gentlemen that thus tooke vs for their seruants or slaues, did new apparell vs through out, with whom we abode, … for in that countrey no Spaniard will serue one another, but they are all of them attended and serued by Indians weekly, and by Negroes which be their slaues during their life. … Afterwards many of vs were by our masters appointed to go to sundry of their Mines where they had to doe, and to be as ouerseers of the Negroes and Indians that laboured there. In which mines many of vs did profite and gaine greatly: for first we were allowed three hundred Pezos a man for a yeere, which is threescore pound sterling and besides that the Indians and Negroes which wrought vnder our charge, vpon our well using and intreating of them, would at times as vpon Saturdayes when they had left worke, labour for vs, and blow as much siluer as should be worth vnto vs 3 markes or there abouts … Sundry weeks we did gaine so much by this means besides our wages, that many of vs became very rich, and were worth three thousand, or foure thousand Pezos …

sourceLine: Thomas Phillips, English captain of the Royal African Company slave ship Hannibal, journal of his voyage to Whydah, 1694, first printed 1732 (adapted)
text: Next day we paid our customs to the king and cappasheirs [his chief men], as will appear hereafter; then the bell was ordered to go about to give notice to all people to bring their slaves to the trunk [slave prison] to sell us … When we were at the trunk, the king’s slaves, if he had any, were the first offer’d to sale, which the cappasheirs would be very urgent with us to buy, and would in a manner force us to it ere they would shew us any other, saying they were the Reys Cosa [the king's property], and we must not refuse them, tho’ as I observ’d they were generally the worst slaves in the trunk, and we paid more for them than any others, which we could not remedy.
original: next day we paid our cuftoms to the king and cappafheirs, as will appear hereafter ; then the bell was ordered to go about to give notice to all people to bring their flaves to the trunk to fell us … When we were at the trunk, the king’s flaves, if he had any, were the firft offer’d to fale, which the cappafheirs would be very urgent with us to buy, and would in a manner force us to it ere they would fhew us any other, faying they were the Reys Co fa, and we muft not refufe them, tho’ as I obferv’d they were generally the worft flaves in the trunk, and we paid more for them than any others, which we could not remedy,

By Thomas Phillips, Commander of the said Ship", p. 234; page image leaf 296 viewed. sourceLine: Filippo Pigafetta, Italian writer, recording the account of Duarte Lopes, a Portuguese merchant who lived in Kongo, A Report of the Kingdom of Congo, on the Jaga invasion of 1568, 1591 (adapted)
text: In this persecution every one in the kingdom suffered, the king, the people, the Portuguese, and their priests, each according to his degree; so that the poor people wandering about the country died from lack of food and all other necessaries. … Thus, forced by necessity, the father sold his son, and the brother his brother, … Those who were sold to satisfy the hunger of others were bought by Portuguese merchants, who came from the Island of St. Thomas with provisions, the sellers saying that they were slaves, and in order to escape farther misery, these last confirmed the story. In this manner great numbers of slaves, natives of Congo, are found in the Island of St. Thomas, and in Portugal.
original: In this perfecution every one in the kingdom fuffered, the king, the people, the Portuguefe, and their priefts, each according to his degree ; fo that the poor people wandering about the country died from lack of food and all other neceflaries. … Thus, forced by neceflity, the father fold his fon, and the brother his brother, … Thofe who were fold to fatiffy the hunger of others were bought by Portuguefe merchants, who came from the Ifland OÌ St. Thomas with provifions, the fellers faying that they were flaves, and in order to efcape farther miferv, thefe lali: confirmed the fl:ory. In this manner great numbers of flaves, natives of Congo, are found in the Ifland of St. Thomas, and in Portugal,

verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with archive.org reportofkingdomo00lope (Hutchinson, John Murray 1881; title page "drawn out of the writings and discourses of the Portuguese, Duarte Lopez, by Filippo Pigafetta, in Rome, 1591.
