sourceLine: Filippo Pigafetta, Italian writer, setting down the account of Duarte Lopes, a Portuguese merchant who lived in the Kingdom of Kongo 1578–1583, A Report of the Kingdom of Congo, 1591 (adapted)
text: The whole plain is fruitful and cultivated, having verdant meadows and large trees, and produces grain of various kinds. The best grain is called Luco, which is like mustard seed, but larger. This is ground in a handmill, and from the white flour excellent bread is made, and such as is not even inferior to corn [wheat], although only the latter is used in the celebration of mass. … Here is also the best white grain, called mazza di Congo, that is, grain of Congo, and maize, which is of so little value that they give it to pigs, rice being likewise little thought of. Maize is known as mazza Manputo, that is, Portugal grain.

The beft grain is called Luco, which is like muftard feed, but larger. This is ground in a handmill, and from the white flour excellent bread is made, and fuch as is not even inferior to corn, although only the latter is ufed in the celebration of mafs. … Here is alfo the beft white grain, called mazza di Congo, that is, grain of Congo, and maize, which is of fo little value that they give it to pigs, rice being likewife little thought of. Maize is known as mazza Manputo, that is, Portugal grain.

sourceLine: Powhatan (Wahunsenacawh), paramount chief of the Powhatan people of Virginia, speech to John Smith in January 1609, as recorded in Smith's Generall Historie of Virginia (1624)
text: Yet Captaine Smith, sayth the King, some doubt I have of your comming hither, that makes me not so kindly seeke to relieve you as I would: for many doe informe me, your comming hither is not for trade, but to invade my people, and possesse my Country, who dare not come to bring you Corne, seeing you thus armed with your men. … What will it availe you to take that by force you may quickly have by love, or to destroy them that provide you food. What can you get by warre, when we can hide our provisions and fly to the woods? whereby you must famish by wronging us your friends. … Let this therefore assure you of our loves, and every yeare our friendly trade shall furnish you with Corne; and now also, if you would come in friendly manner to see us, and not thus with your guns and swords as to invade your foes.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 56347 (Smith, Generall Historie, 1624, in the MacLehose 1907 reprint of the 1624 text). The excerpt joins two of Powhatan's speeches from the same January 1609 visit ("Powhatans reply and flattery" and "Powhatans discourse of peace and warre"), separated by narrative and marked by "…"; the last cut skips the "Thinke you I am so simple" passage. Meaning kept. The sourceLine says honestly that the speech is as recorded by Smith in 1624. Translation null is right, since the words are Smith's English rendering.

sourceLine: Powhatan (Wahunsenacah), paramount chief of the Powhatan peoples of Virginia, speech to John Smith in 1609, as recorded by Smith's companions (this section by Anas Todkill) in The Proceedings of the English Colonie in Virginia, 1612 (adapted)
text: What will it avail you to take that perforce, you may quietly have with love, or to destroy them that provide you food? What can you get by war, when we can hide our provision and fly to the woods, whereby you must famish, by wronging us your friends? And why are you thus jealous of our loves, seeing us unarmed, and both do, and are willing still to feed you with that you cannot get but by our labours? Think you I am so simple not to know it is better to eat good meat, lie well, and sleep quietly with my women and children, laugh and be merry with you, have copper, hatchets, or what I want, being your friend; than be forced to fly from all, to lie cold in the woods, feed upon acorns, roots and such trash, and be so hunted by you that I can neither rest, eat nor sleep …
original: What will it availe you to take that perforce, you may quietly haue with loue, or to destroy them that provide you food ? What can you get by war, when we can hide our provision and flie to the woodes, whereby you must famish, by wronging vs your friends ? And whie are you thus iealous of our loues, seeing vs vnarmed, and both doe, and are willing still to feed you with that you cannot get but by our labours ? Think you I am so simple not to knowe it is better to eate good meate, lie well, and sleepe quietly with my women and children, laugh and be merrie with you, haue copper, hatchets, or what I want, being your friend ; then bee forced to flie from al, to lie cold in the woods, feed vpon acorns roots and such trash, and be so hunted by you that I can neither rest eat nor sleepe …
translation: Powhatan's words as rendered in English by the colonists (no interpreter named); The Proceedings of the English Colonie in Virginia, Oxford, 1612, reprinted in Travels and Works of Captain John Smith, ed. Edward Arber, new ed. A. G. Bradley, 1910

sourceLine: Jean-François Paul de Gondi, Cardinal de Retz, coadjutor archbishop of Paris and a leader of the Fronde, Memoirs (written c. 1675), on the tax quarrels of 1647
text: Emeri, Superintendent of the Finances, and in my opinion the most corrupt man of the age, multiplied edicts as fast as he could find names to call them by. … In August, 1647, there was a mighty clamour against the tariff edict imposing a general tax upon all provisions that came into Paris, which the people were resolved to bear no longer. But the gentlemen of the Council being determined to support it, the Queen consulted the members deputed from Parliament, when Cardinal Mazarin, a mere ignoramus in these affairs, said he wondered that so considerable a body as they were should mind such trifles,—an expression truly worthy of Mazarin. However, the Council at length imagining the Parliament would do it, thought fit to suppress the tariff themselves by a declaration, in order to save the King’s credit. … Thereupon they [the Council] trumped up a declaration which had been registered two years before for the establishment of the Chamber of Domain, which was a terrible charge upon the people … The people mutinied, went in crowds to the Palace, and used very abusive language to the President de Thore, Emeri’s son.
translation: Anonymous English translation, 1723; Project Gutenberg text (Historic Court Memoirs series), whose wording matches the 1896 London reprint by H. S. Nichols, “reprinted from a translation dated 1723”
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with the Gutenberg text (Book II) and the 1896 H. S. Nichols edition (archive.org cu31924028186421, pp. 71-72), whose wording matches. The last cut skipped the Council's five new edicts and its revival of the Chamber of Domain declaration, so 'The people mutinied…' read as a reaction to the suppressed tariff; in the source the mutiny follows the Chamber of Domain declaration, 'a terrible charge upon the people'. Restored that clause from the page ('Thereupon they [the Council] trumped up a declaration… a terrible charge upon the people'; bracket only names the referent of 'they'); 187 words. Translation: the Gutenberg page names no translator or edition; the 1896 Nichols reprint's publisher's note says it 'is reprinted from a translation dated 1723' and its text matches the excerpt word for word, but the Gutenberg file (Historic Court Memoirs series) is not that 1896 printing (its preface modernises names, e.g. 'Philippe' for 'Philip'), so the credit was reworded. sourceLine: Jean-François Paul de Gondi, Cardinal de Retz, coadjutor archbishop of Paris and a leader of the Fronde, Memoirs (written c. 1675), on the Day of the Barricades, August 1648
text: On the 26th of August, 1648, the worthy Broussel, councillor of the Grand Chamber, and Rene Potier, Sieur de Blancmenil, President of the Inquests, were both arrested by the Queen’s officers. … The Chancellor, hemmed in on every side, narrowly escaped with his life to the Hotel d’O, which the people broke open, rushed in with fury … The news of this occurrence ran like wild-fire through the whole city. Men and women were immediately up in arms, and mothers even put daggers into the hands of their children. In less than two hours there were erected above two hundred barricades, adorned with all the standards and colours that the League had left entire. All the cry was, “God bless the King!” sometimes, “God bless the Coadjutor!” and the echo was, “No Mazarin!” … The Court minions of the two last centuries knew not what they did when they reduced that effectual regard which kings ought to have for their subjects into mere style and form; for there are, as you see, certain conjunctures in which, by a necessary consequence, subjects make a mere form also of the real obedience which they owe to their sovereigns.
translation: Anonymous English translation, 1723; Project Gutenberg text (Historic Court Memoirs series), whose wording matches the 1896 London reprint by H. S. Nichols, “reprinted from a translation dated 1723”
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with the Gutenberg text (Book II) and the 1896 Nichols edition pp. 89-90. The first cut (~4,000 words) joined Broussel's arrest (26 August) directly to 'The news of this occurrence ran like wild-fire… In less than two hours there were erected above two hundred barricades', but in the source 'this occurrence' is the next day's attack on the Chancellor, whom the people chased into the Hotel d'O. sourceLine: Sir Thomas Roe, English ambassador to the Mughal emperor Jahangir, letter to the East India Company, 1616 (adapted)
text: For a fort, at my first arrival I received it as very necessary; but experience teaches me we are refused it to our advantage. If he [the Mughal emperor] would offer me ten, I would not accept one. … A war and traffic are incompatible. By my consent, you shall no way engage yourselves but at sea, where you are like to gain as often as to lose. It is the beggaring of the Portugal, notwithstanding his many rich residences and territories, that he keeps soldiers that spends it; yet his garrisons are mean. He never profited by the Indies, since he defended them. Observe this well. It hath been also the error of the Dutch, who seek plantation here by the sword. … Let this be received as a rule that if you will profit, seek it at sea, and in quiet trade; for without controversy it is an error to affect garrisons and land wars in India.
original: For a Fort, at my first arriuall I receiued it as very Necessarie ; but experience teaches mee wee are refusd it to our aduantage. If hee would offer mee ten, I would not accept one. … A warr and trafique are incompatible. By my consent, you shall no way engage your selues but at sea, wher you are like to gayne as often as to loose. It is the beggering of the Portugall, notwithstanding his many rich residences and territoryes, that hee keepes souldiers that spendes it ; yet his garrisons are meane. He neuer Profited by the Indyes, since hee defended them. Obserue this well. It hath beene also the error of the Dutch, who seeke Plantation heere by the Swoord. … Lett this bee receiued as a rule that if you will Profitt, seeke it at Sea, and in quiett trade ; for without controuersy it is an error to affect Garrisons and Land warrs in India.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Adapted: compared text with original word by word against archive.org embassysirthoma01fostgoog, pp. 343-344 (Foster, Embassy of Sir Thomas Roe, vol. II, 1899; letter to the East India Company dated 24 November 1616). Only spelling is modernised. "If he would offer me ten" has no referent in the excerpt: it is the Mughal emperor, who refused the fort. Added the bracket [the Mughal emperor] in "text".

sourceLine: Mary Rowlandson, English colonist taken captive when Native forces attacked Lancaster, Massachusetts, in February 1676 during King Philip’s War, narrative of her captivity, 1682
text: I cannot but remember how the Indians derided the slowness, and dullness of the English army, in its setting out. For after the desolations at Lancaster and Medfield, as I went along with them, they asked me when I thought the English army would come after them? I told them I could not tell. "It may be they will come in May," said they. Thus did they scoff at us, as if the English would be a quarter of a year getting ready. … It was thought, if their corn were cut down, they would starve and die with hunger, and all their corn that could be found, was destroyed, and they driven from that little they had in store, into the woods in the midst of winter; and yet how to admiration did the Lord preserve them for His holy ends, and the destruction of many still amongst the English! strangely did the Lord provide for them; that I did not see (all the time I was among them) one man, woman, or child, die with hunger.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg #851 (the 'second Addition, Corrected and amended', 1682). Excerpt joins items 2 and 4 of her closing list of 'remarkable passages of providence'; the cut is all of item 3 (the Baquaug river crossing) and is marked; no change of meaning. Attack on Lancaster dated 'tenth of February 1675' in the text (Old Style = 1676), as the sourceLine gives; published 1682.

sourceLine: Christian peasant rebels besieged in Hara Castle during the Shimabara Rebellion, letter shot by arrow into the besiegers’ lines and addressed to the attendants of the shogun’s commissioner, February 1638
text: For the sake of our people we have now resorted to this castle. You will, no doubt, think that for the sake of conquering countries and acquiring houses we have done this; but such is by no means the case. It is simply because the Christian sect is not tolerated as a distinct sect, as you know. … Because they [the faithful] will not change their religion, they incur various kinds of severe punishments, being inhumanly subjected to shame and extreme suffering, till at last, for their devotion to the Lord of Heaven, they are tortured to death. … Should we continue to live as hitherto, and the above laws not be repealed, we must incur all sorts of punishments hard to be endured; we must, our bodies being weak and sensitive, sin against the infinite Lord of Heaven; and from solicitude for our brief lives incur the loss of what we highly esteem. These things fill us with grief beyond our capacity. Hence we are in our present condition. It is not the result of a corrupt doctrine.
translation: Translator not named; English version printed in James Murdoch and Isoh Yamagata, A History of Japan, vol. 2, 1903
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Murdoch 1903, p. 660 n.13: letter text verbatim, dated '4th of 1st month of 15th year of Kanyei (February 17th, 1638). Addressed to the attendants on the Imperial Commissioner' -- sourceLine (Feb. 1638, shogun's commissioner) fine. Cut 1 removes 'Frequent prohibitions ... For these there is no escape'; '[the faithful]' is a pure insertion naming 'they' (those who value the future life). Cut 2 removes the passage on recanters and the rising. Neither changes the argument. Murdoch does not say who translated it, so the credit now says 'translator not named'.

sourceLine: Shivaji, Maratha ruler, letter to the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb protesting the jizya tax on non-Muslims, 1679 (drafted in Persian by his secretary Nila Prabhu; some historians attribute the letter to Rana Raj Singh of Mewar)
text: It has recently come to my ears that, on the ground of the war with me having exhausted your wealth and emptied your treasury, your Majesty has ordered that money under the name of jaziya should be collected from the Hindus and the imperial needs supplied with it. … Your peasants are down-trodden; the yield of every village has declined—in the place of one lakh [of Rupees] only one thousand, and in the place of a thousand only ten are collected, and that too with difficulty. When Poverty and Beggary have made their homes in the palaces of the Emperor and the Princes, the condition of the grandees and officers can be easily imagined. … How can the royal spirit permit you to add the hardship of the jaziya to this grievous state of things? … If it be a mosque, the call to prayer is chanted in remembrance of Him. If it be a temple, the bell is rung in yearning for Him only.
translation: Translated by Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times, 2nd ed., 1920
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times, 2nd ed. (Longmans, 1920), ch. XIII §8, pp. 366-370 ('About the middle of this year [1679] Shivaji sent to Aurangzib a… letter of protest against the jaziya, which was drafted by Nila Prabhu in eloquent Persian'; translation cited from Sarkar's History of Aurangzib iii. 325-329). '[of Rupees]' is Sarkar's own bracket. Cuts (praise of Akbar/Jahangir/Shah Jahan; army/merchants lament; infamy and Quran passages) do not change meaning; 'Him' in the last piece is plainly God. Sarkar's edition does not raise the Rana Raj Singh attribution, and the letter itself names 'Rana Raj Singh, who is the head of the Hindus' in the third person; the sourceLine's caveat ('some historians attribute the letter to Rana Raj Singh of Mewar') is honest and kept. Sarkar calls Nila Prabhu 'the accomplished Persian draftsman (munshi)'; 'secretary' is a fair gloss. Confirmed.

sourceLine: Sidi Ali Reis, Ottoman admiral stranded in Gujarat (India) after a sea battle with the Portuguese, The Mirror of Countries, 1557, on events of 1554
text: … one of the nobles, Nasir-ul-Mulk, had refused to take the oath of allegiance, and had raised the banner of sovereignty on his own behalf. … called in the aid of the Governor of the Portuguese at Goa, promising that in return for his services the harbors on the coast of Gujarat, … should be thrown open to the Portuguese, while he would retire to the land of the interior. … One day, being at the house of Imad-ul-Mulk, I met the infidel [Portuguese] envoy, and our host addressed him in this way, "We have need of the Sultan of Turkey. Our ships touch the ports of his Empire, and if we were not free to do so, it would be bad for us. Moreover, he is the Padishah of the Islamitic world, and it is not seemly that we should be expected to deliver up his Admiral to you."
translation: Translated by A. Vambery, The Travels and Adventures of the Turkish Admiral Sidi Ali Reis (London: Luzac), 1899, as reprinted without the translator's name in Charles F. Horne, ed., The Sacred Books and Early Literature of the East, vol. 6, 1917
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Fordham 16CSidi1 credits only Horne 1917. Compared it with Vambery's 1899 translation (archive.org india.history.resource.111193; title page "Translated from the Turkish, with notes, by A. Vambery. London: Luzac & Co. 1899"): the Nasir-ul-Mulk passage and Imad-ul-Mulk's speech are word for word the same. So the translator is established (flagged item) and named in the credit. Added [Portuguese] after "the infidel", because the excerpt cut the earlier passage where the Portuguese demand his surrender. Date: The Mirror of Countries, 1557, on events of 1554 (AH 961-962), correct.

sourceLine: William Snelgrave, English slave-ship captain who traded at Whydah and visited the camp of King Agaja of Dahomey in 1727, A New Account of Some Parts of Guinea and the Slave-Trade, 1734 (adapted)
text: It has been the Custom among the Negroes, time out of Mind, and is so to this day, for them to make Slaves of all the Captives they take in War. Now, before they had an Opportunity of selling them to the white People, they were often obliged to kill great Multitudes, when they had taken more than they could well employ in their own Plantations, for fear they should rebel, and endanger their Masters' Safety. … First, it is evident, that abundance of Captives, taken in War, would be inhumanly destroyed, was there not an Opportunity of disposing of them to the Europeans.
original: It has been the Cuſtom among the Negroes, time out of Mind, and is ſo to this day, for them to make Slaves of all the Captives they take in War. Now, before they had an Opportunity of ſelling them to the white People, they were often obliged to kill great Multitudes, when they had taken more than they could well employ in their own Plantations, for fear they ſhould rebel, and endanger their Maſters Safety. … Firſt, It is evident, that abundance of Captives, taken in War, would be inhumanly deſtroyed, was there not an Opportunity of diſpoſing of them to the Europeans.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with archive.org bim_eighteenth-century_a-new-account-of-some-pa_snelgrave-william_1734 (London 1734), Book on "The manner how the Negroes become Slaves", pp. 158 and 160; page images leaves 181 and 183 viewed. The OCR reads long s correctly here; text differs from original only by long s, "Masters'" apostrophe and capitalisation. The cut (c. 430 words) removes Snelgrave's other "heads" (crimes, debt, selling children), the 70,000-a-year export figure and his preface to the "following Reasons" in justification of the trade; "First, ..." is the first of those reasons. Meaning kept. Attribution (captain, Whydah, Agaja's camp 1727, 1734 title) is right.

sourceLine: Raimondo di Soncino, envoy of the Duke of Milan at the English court, dispatch to the Duke on John Cabot's voyage for Henry VII, December 18, 1497
text: Perhaps amidst so many occupations of your Excellency it will not be unwelcome to learn how this Majesty has acquired a part of Asia without drawing his sword. In this kingdom there is a certain Venetian named Zoanne Caboto, of gentle disposition, very expert in navigation, who, seeing that the most serene Kings of Portugal and Spain had occupied unknown islands, meditated the achievement of a similar acquisition for the said Majesty. Having obtained royal privileges securing to himself the use of the dominions he might discover, the sovereignty being reserved to the Crown, he entrusted his fortune to a small vessel with a crew of 18 persons, and set out from Bristo, a port in the western part of this kingdom. … This Messer Zoanne has the description of the world on a chart, and also on a solid sphere which he has constructed, and on which he shows where he has been …
translation: Translated for the Hakluyt Society in Clements R. Markham, ed., The Journal of Christopher Columbus, 1893, as given in the Internet Modern History Sourcebook
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1497cabot-3docs (second despatch, 18 December 1497; page says the texts are from the Hakluyt Society edition of Columbus's Journal, i.e. Markham 1893, and the despatch was "translated ... for the Hakluyt Society"). Soncino was the Milanese envoy in London. The excerpt ended on a semicolon in mid-sentence; changed it to " …". No words changed.

sourceLine: Raimondo di Soncino, envoy of the Duke of Milan at the English court, dispatch to the Duke on John Cabot's plans, December 18, 1497
text: But Messer Zoanne has set his mind on higher things, for he thinks that, when that place has been occupied, he will keep on still further towards the east, where he will be opposite to an island called Cipango, situated in the equinoctial region, where he believes that all the spices of the world, as well as the jewels, are found. … He further says that he was once at Mecca, whither the spices are brought by caravans from distant countries; … And it is said that before long his Majesty will arm some ships for him, and will give him all the malefactors to go to that country and form a colony, so that they hope to establish a greater depot of spices in London than there is in Alexandria.
translation: Translated for the Hakluyt Society in Clements R. Markham, ed., The Journal of Christopher Columbus, 1893, as given in the Internet Modern History Sourcebook
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Fordham 1497cabot-3docs, second despatch. Cuts skip Cabot's argument about the spice caravans and the earth's roundness; meaning kept. Attribution, date and translation as for soncino-1497-cabot-rivalry.

sourceLine: States General of the United Netherlands, Charter of the Dutch West India Company, 3 June 1621
text: And we find by experience, that without the common help, assistance, and interposition of a General Company, the people designed from hence for those parts cannot be profitably protected and mantained in their great risque from pirates, extortion and otherwise, which will happen in so very long a voyage. … That, moreover, the aforesaid Company may, in our name and authority, within the limits herein before prescribed, … make contracts, engagements and alliances with the princes and natives of the countries comprehended therein, and also build any forts and fortifications there, to appoint and discharge Governors, people for war, and officers of justice, and other public officers, for the preservation of the places, keeping good order, police and justice, and in like manner for the promoting of trade.
translation: Translator not named; English text from Ebenezer Hazard, Historical Collections, vol. 1 (Philadelphia, 1792), as reprinted in Francis Newton Thorpe, ed., The Federal and State Constitutions, Colonial Charters, and Other Organic Laws, vol. 1 (US Government Printing Office), 1909
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Avalon (source: Thorpe 1909) and with Thorpe vol. 1 pp. 59–61 on archive.org (federalstatecons01thor). Thorpe's printed text itself repeats 'make contracts, engagements and alliances with the limits herein before prescribed,' in article II. The old excerpt cut out both the repeat and the genuine limit 'within the limits herein before prescribed'. The limit is restored, and the '…' now covers only the repeated words. Neither Avalon nor Thorpe names a translator; Thorpe's footnote gives the text as from Hazard's Historical Collections (1792), vol. I, pp. 121–131. So the credit now says honestly that the translator is not named. The first cut (~580 words of monopoly limits) does not change the meaning. Date 3 June 1621 is right.

sourceLine: Senior councillors of the Tokugawa shogunate, sentence signed at Edo and read at Nagasaki to the envoys sent from Portuguese Macao to ask for the reopening of trade, 1640
text: The crimes committed by these men during a long series of years in promulgating the Christian faith contrary to the decrees of the Shogun are very numerous, and exceedingly serious; last year [1639] the Shogun has, under the gravest penalties, forbidden any one to sail from Macao to Japan, and he has decreed that in case any vessel disregard this prohibition, the said vessel shall be burned, and all her crew and passengers put to death without exception. … It is decreed that the vessel shall be burned, and that the chiefs of the embassy with all their suite shall be put to death, in order that the bruit of this example may reach Macao and even the country of Europe … We mean, however, that the lowest among the crew be spared and sent back to Macao. If by any chance whatsoever — from stress of weather or from any other cause — any Portuguese vessel put into a Japanese harbour, no matter where, all on board of her shall be put to death to the last man.
translation: Translated in James Murdoch and Isoh Yamagata, A History of Japan, vol. 2, 1903 (from the European accounts of the episode by the Jesuit Cardim and others, not the Japanese original)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Murdoch 1903, pp. 665-667. Attribution: Murdoch says the sentence was 'drawn up and signed by all the senior members of the Shogun's Government on July 21st' in Edo and read by an interpreter at Nagasaki at the commissioners' order (Aug. 1640), so sourceLine changed from 'Commissioners of the Tokugawa shogunate'. Translation: Murdoch's footnote 1 p. 665 names the 'chief original authorities' as Father Cardim (Jesuit, Macao) and the Spaniard Magisu, used by Charlevoix and Pages, so the credit now says it is from European accounts, not the Japanese text. '[1639]' is Murdoch's own bracket (OCR '[1639J'). Text: the second cut had dropped the sentence's own qualification 'We mean, however, that the lowest among the crew be spared and sent back to Macao.' (p. 667), leaving 'all her crew ... put to death without exception' unqualified; restored it from the page (174 words).

sourceLine: Treaty of Tordesillas, agreed by representatives of Ferdinand and Isabella of Castile and Aragon and King John II of Portugal, 1494
text: That, whereas a certain controversy exists between the said lords, their constituents, as to what lands, of all those discovered in the ocean sea up to the present day, the date of this treaty, pertain to each one of the said parts respectively; therefore, for the sake of peace and concord, … they, their said representatives, … covenanted and agreed that a boundary or straight line be determined and drawn north and south, from pole to pole, on the said ocean sea, from the Arctic to the Antarctic pole. This boundary or line shall be drawn straight, as aforesaid, at a distance of three hundred and seventy leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, … And all lands, both islands and mainlands, found and discovered already, or to be found and discovered hereafter, by the said King of Portugal and by his vessels on this side of the said line and bound determined as above, toward the east, … on the eastern side of the said bound provided the said bound is not crossed, shall belong to, and remain in the possession of, and pertain forever to, the said King of Portugal and his successors.
translation: Translated in Frances Gardiner Davenport, ed., European Treaties Bearing on the History of the United States and Its Dependencies to 1648 (Carnegie Institution of Washington), 1917
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Avalon (source: Davenport, European Treaties, 1917, named on the page), article I. Three fixes, all restoring source words: (1) the first cut removed the subject, leaving "… covenanted and agreed" with no one agreeing; restored "they, their said representatives, acting in their name and by virtue of their powers herein described,"; (2) removed a "…" between "Antarctic pole." and "This boundary", where nothing is cut; (3) restored "and bound determined as above, toward the east, in either north or south latitude, on the eastern side of the said bound provided the said bound is not crossed," because without it "on this side of the said line" does not say which side goes to Portugal. Attribution and date (June 7, 1494) correct. Trimmed to the 200-word limit after verification with "…" cuts at clause or sentence boundaries; the passages the verifier restored were kept, and every remaining segment is a substring of the verified text.

sourceLine: The Twelve Articles of the peasants of Swabia, manifesto of the German Peasants’ War, 1525
text: In the second place, it is clear that the peasants demand that this Gospel be taught them as a guide in life, and they ought not to be called disobedient or disorderly. … First, it is our humble petition and desire, as also our will and resolution, that in the future we should have power and authority so that each community should choose and appoint a pastor, and that we should have the right to depose him should he conduct himself improperly. The pastor thus chosen should teach us the Gospel pure and simple, without any addition, doctrine or ordinance of man. … We will that for the future our church provost, whomsoever the community may appoint, shall gather and receive this tithe. From this he shall give to the pastor, elected by the whole community, a decent and sufficient maintenance for him …
translation: Translated by the editors, James Harvey Robinson and Merrick Whitcomb, in Translations and Reprints from the Original Sources of European History, vol. 2, no. 6 (Period of the Early Reformation in Germany), University of Pennsylvania Press; this printing undated
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Translations and Reprints vol. 2 no. 6, pp. 25-27 (archive.org translationsrepr02univiala; leaves 163-165): piece 1 is the preface ('In the second place…'), piece 2 the First Article, piece 3 the Second Article; cuts are between whole sentences and do not change meaning. The excerpt ended mid-sentence at 'maintenance for him' (source continues 'and his [im und den seynen], as shall seem right to the whole community'), so a closing '…' was added. Translation: the headnote says 'In the translation the editors have availed themselves so far as possible of the partial translation… in Gieseler's Ecclesiastical History', and the vol. 2 contents (leaf 7) name the editors of no. 6 as James Harvey Robinson and Merrick Whitcomb; credit now names them. The scan carries no date (title page leaf 5 undated; archive.org catalogues it '[1897?-1907?]', and no. 4 in the same volume cites an 1898 book), so the unsupported '1897' was replaced by 'this printing undated'. Attribution (Swabian peasants' manifesto, 1525) and year fine.

sourceLine: The Twelve Articles of the peasants of Swabia, manifesto of the German Peasants’ War, 1525
text: It has been the custom hitherto for men to hold us as their own property, which is pitiable enough, considering that Christ has delivered and redeemed us all, without exception, by the shedding of his precious blood, the lowly as well as the great. Accordingly, it is consistent with Scripture that we should be free and wish to be so. Not that we would wish to be absolutely free and under no authority. … We are thus ready to yield obedience according to God's law to our elected and regular authorities in all proper things becoming to a Christian. We, therefore, take it for granted that you will release us from serfdom, as true Christians, unless it should be shown us from the Gospel that we are serfs. … In the eighth place, we are greatly burdened by holdings which cannot support the rent exacted from them. The peasants suffer loss in this way and are ruined; and we ask that the lords may appoint persons of honor to inspect these holdings, and fix a rent in accordance with justice, so that the peasant shall not work for nothing, since the laborer is worthy of his hire.
translation: Translated by the editors, James Harvey Robinson and Merrick Whitcomb, in Translations and Reprints from the Original Sources of European History, vol. 2, no. 6 (Period of the Early Reformation in Germany), University of Pennsylvania Press; this printing undated
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Translations and Reprints vol. 2 no. 6, pp. 27-29 (Third and Eighth Articles). The first cut removed the Article's own qualification right after 'we should be free and wish to be so' — 'Not that we would wish to be absolutely free and under no authority… We are thus ready to yield obedience according to God's law to our elected and regular authorities' — so the excerpt read as a demand for freedom from all authority. Restored those two source sentences (copied from the page; 195 words now). The second cut (Articles 4-7) is fine. Translation credit corrected as for the companion document (editors Robinson and Whitcomb named; printing undated, '1897' not supported by the scan).

sourceLine: Antonio Vázquez de Espinosa, Spanish Carmelite friar who spent much of his life in Spanish America and travelled from Mexico to Peru in 1612–1622, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, written 1628–1629, on the city of Cuzco
text: The city has a large population, with over 3,000 Spaniards, many knights and nobles, encomenderos, descendants of the earliest pioneers in that Kingdom, together with many other Spaniards of honorable, distinguished, and middle class, and mestizos, sons of Spaniards and Indian women … from among whom have arisen very valiant and courageous warriors, servants of His Majesty who suffer great trials at all crises—all these form a … very illustrious republic. In this imperial city there is a large Indian population, nobility and commoners, comprising over 14,000 residents, not counting many others who come in from the adjoining provinces to render service in the city, plus large numbers of Negro slaves and mulattoes whom the city residents keep for their service in the city and on their farms, for they have cattle ranches, sugar mills, vineyards, and fields of wheat, corn, and other cereals and crops, and troops of mules for traffic to Lima and other points.
translation: Translated by Charles Upson Clark, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections vol. 102, 1942
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org smithsonianmisce1021942smit, sec. 1599, pp. 597-598 (Clark, Smithsonian Misc. Coll. vol. 102, 1942). The first "…" cuts only "here called Montañeses" (OCR "Montafieses"); the second skips only the page break and running head (flagged). Clark's introduction says the work was "written in 1628 or 1629" (corrected 1629), and that Vazquez travelled between Mexico (1612) and Peru and returned to Spain about 1622; this supports the sourceLine and year.

sourceLine: Antonio Vázquez de Espinosa, Spanish Carmelite friar who spent much of his life in Spanish America and travelled from Mexico to Peru in 1612–1622, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, written 1628–1629, on Cartagena and Lima
text: The city [Cartagena] contains more than 1,500 Spanish residents, not counting mestizos, mulattoes, free Negroes and other categories, and the population is increasing … There is another company of free creole colored men, with a Captain appointed by His Majesty and 600 soldiers, as good as Spaniards and in their very image. These are employed in the handling of the artillery and other matters in His Majesty’s service, like trench and fascine work. … [In Lima] there are 32 municipal companies, not counting 22 appointed by the Viceroy to enroll men … and there are 3 of mulattoes and 2 of free Negroes, persons who are necessary and important for the work …
translation: Translated by Charles Upson Clark, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections vol. 102, 1942
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org smithsonianmisce1021942smit, sec. 912 and 915 (Cartagena, pp. 309-310) and p. 457 (Lima defences, "information arriving from Lima this present year, 1629, and written in 1627"). "[In Lima]" is a correct clarifying bracket: the companies are raised by "the city's residents" and the Viceroy at Lima. Date as for the Cuzco excerpt.

sourceLine: Antonio Vázquez de Espinosa, Spanish Carmelite friar who spent much of his life in Spanish America and travelled from Mexico to Peru in 1612–1622, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, written 1628–1629, on the mita (forced labour draft) for the silver mines of Potosí
text: These Indians [drafted for the mita] are sent out every year under a captain whom they choose in each village or tribe, for him to take them and oversee them for the year each has to serve; every year they have a new election, for as some go out, others come in. This works out very badly, with great losses and gaps in the quotas of Indians, the villages being depopulated; and this gives rise to great extortions and abuses on the part of the inspectors toward the poor Indians, ruining them and thus depriving the caciques and chief Indians of their property and carrying them off in chains because they do not fill out the mita assignment, which they cannot do … These mita Indians earn each day, or there is paid each one for his labor, 4 reals. Besides these there are others not under obligation, who are mingados or hire themselves out voluntarily: these each get from 12 to 16 reals, and some up to 24, according to their reputation of wielding the pick and knowing how to get the ore out.
translation: Translated by Charles Upson Clark, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections vol. 102, 1942
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org smithsonianmisce1021942smit, sec. 1652-1653, pp. 623-624. "These Indians" referred to the 13,300 mita Indians of the cut opening paragraph; added the bracket [drafted for the mita]. Cuts keep the meaning. Date as for the Cuzco excerpt.

sourceLine: Antonio Vázquez de Espinosa, Spanish Carmelite friar who travelled through Peru in the 1610s, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, c. 1629
text: These Indians are sent out every year under a captain whom they choose in each village or tribe, for him to take them and oversee them for the year each has to serve; every year they have a new election, for as some go out, others come in. This works out very badly, with great losses and gaps in the quotas of Indians, the villages being depopulated; and this gives rise to great extortions and abuses on the part of the inspectors toward the poor Indians, ruining them and thus depriving the caciques and chief Indians of their property and carrying them off in chains because they do not fill out the mita assignment, which they cannot do, for the reasons given and for others which I do not bring forward. … These 13,300 [mita workers] are divided up every 4 months into 3 mitas, each consisting of 4,433 Indians, to work in the mines on the range and in the 120 smelters in the Potosi and Tarapaya areas.
translation: Translated by Charles Upson Clark, Compendium and Description of the West Indies (Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections, vol. 102), 1942
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Smithsonian Misc. Coll. vol. 102 (1942), paras 1652-1653 (p. 624-625): verbatim. The "…" omits only the paragraph number "1653."; "[mita workers]" is a pure gloss. Title page: "translated by Charles Upson Clark", Smithsonian, 1 Sept. 1942. sourceLine: John Winthrop, governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, journal entries for November 1633 to January 1634
text: A great mortality among the Indians. Chickatabot, the sagamore of Naponsett, died, and many of his people. The disease was the small pox. … John Sagamore died of the small pox, and almost all his people; (above thirty buried by Mr. Maverick … of Winesemett in one day). The towns in the bay took away many of the children; but most of them died soon after. … Divers of them, in their sickness, confessed that the Englishmen's God was a good God; and that, if they recovered, they would serve him. … Hall and the two others, who went to Connecticut November 3, came now home, having lost themselves and endured much misery. They informed us, that the small pox was gone as far as any Indian plantation was known to the west, and much people dead of it, by reason whereof they could have no trade. At Naragansett, by the Indians' report, there died seven hundred; but, beyond Pascataquack, none to the eastward.
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org winthropsjournal00wint (Hosmer's edition, vol. 1), pp. 111-118. The last segment began "They informed us", whose referent had been cut; restored the source sentence "Hall and the two others, who went to Connecticut November 3, came now home, having lost themselves and endured much misery." The "…" after "Mr. Maverick" skips only a page break and running head. Dates (November 1633 to January 20, 1634) correct.

sourceLine: The Annals of the Cakchiquels, history of the Kaqchikel Maya kingdom of Guatemala kept by the Xahila family of Kaqchikel nobles; this part written by a family member who lived through the events, entries for c. 1530–1548, written before 1560
text: During this year frightful imposts were levied; they paid gold and silver before the face of Tunatiuh [Pedro de Alvarado], and there were demanded as tribute five hundred men and five hundred women to go to the gold washings; all the people were busy seeking gold. … All that, yes, all that, we ourselves witnessed, O my children. … The prince Don Jorge was appointed by the sole command of Tunatiuh. There was no council held nor assembly to confirm him. Tunatiuh gave his orders to the princes and they obeyed him; for, truly, he made himself feared. … In the course of the year the President Cerrado [Alonso López de Cerrato] arrived … When he arrived he condemned the Castilians; he set free the slaves and prisoners of the Castilians, diminished by one-half the imposts, put an end to forced labor, and obliged the Castilians to pay all for their work, little or great. This Prince Cerrado truly solaced the afflictions of our nation; for I, myself, O my children, was a witness of the many miseries which we endured.
translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Annals of the Cakchiquels, 1885
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 20775 txt, sec. 165-166 and 177 (Brinton 1885). The brackets [Pedro de Alvarado] for Tunatiuh and [Alonso López de Cerrato] for "President Cerrado" are correct identifications that clarify names, which rule 5 allows (Tonatiuh was the Nahua name for Alvarado; Cerrato became president of the Audiencia of Guatemala in 1548). Cuts skip entries; the sourceLine gives the span "c. 1530-1548". Date and authorship as for xahila-1559-plague.

sourceLine: The Annals of the Cakchiquels, history of the Kaqchikel Maya kingdom of Guatemala kept by the Xahila family of Kaqchikel nobles; this part written by a family member who lived through the events, entries for 1556–1557, written before 1560
text: There were then three rulers, the Prince Ramirez, the Doctor Mercia and Louaisa. They held court at Panchoy. In the 14th month of the year, after this day of Sanctiago, there came an order from Ramirez. He imposed a tribute on members of the nobility among the people. He also made provision for the surplusage of the tribute. There had never been a surplus under the chiefs; it was known to be stolen, but no one knew by whom. The maize tax was reduced and that of roast fowls, and none of the chiefs could steal anything from the surplus. … Twenty days after the promulgation of the order of Ramirez, the Book of the Doctrina was published, on the day of Saints, a Monday; but many would not accept the Doctrina, but refused it. … Don Juan Juarez and Francisco Pez Martin were chosen as Alcaldes, to issue orders. (Note by a later writer: These were the first Alcaldes, and with them began the elections.)
translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Annals of the Cakchiquels, 1885
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 20775, sec. 183-184 (Brinton 1885): Philip II's accession (1556), the Ramirez tribute order, the Doctrina, and the alcaldes of 1557. sourceLine: The Annals of the Cakchiquels, history of the Kaqchikel Maya kingdom of Guatemala kept by the Xahila family of Kaqchikel nobles; this part written by a family member who lived through the events, describing the epidemic of 1519–1521, written before 1560
text: In the course of the fifth year the pestilence began, O my children. First there was a cough, then the blood was corrupted, and the urine became yellow. The number of deaths at this time was truly terrible. The Chief Vakaki Ahmak died, and we ourselves were plunged in great darkness and great grief, our fathers and ancestors having contracted the plague, O my children. … Truly the number of deaths among the people was terrible, nor did the people escape from the pestilence. … The ancients and the fathers died alike, and the stench was such that men died of it alone. Then perished our fathers and ancestors. Half the people threw themselves into the ravines, and the dogs and foxes lived on the bodies of the men. The fear of death destroyed the old people, and the oldest son of the king died at the same time as his young brother. Thus did we become poor, O my children, and thus did we survive, being but a little child—and we were all that remained.
translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Annals of the Cakchiquels, 1885
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 20775 (Brinton, Annals of the Cakchiquels, 1885), sec. 127-130. Cuts skip intervening year entries and deaths; meaning kept. The sourceLine avoids the dispute by saying it was written by a family member who lived through the events, which both views support. sourceLine: Francis Xavier, Jesuit missionary, letter from Japan to the Jesuits at Goa, 1551, describing events in Satsuma in 1549–50
text: But the bonzes admonished the prince [the lord of Satsuma] (who is very powerful, the lord of several towns), that if he allowed his people to embrace the Christian religion, his whole dominion would be destroyed, and the ancestral gods of the country, which they call pagodas, would come to be despised by the natives. For the law of God was contrary to the law of Japan, and it would therefore result that any who embraced that law would repudiate the holy founders of the ancient law of their forefathers, which could not be done without great ruin to the town and realm. Let him look, therefore, with reverence on those most holy men who had been the legislators of Japan, and, considering that the law of God was opposed and hostile to the law of his fathers, let him issue an edict forbidding, under penalty of death, that any one in future should become a Christian. The prince was moved by this discourse of the bonzes, and issued the edict as they had requested.
translation: Translated in Henry James Coleridge, The Life and Letters of St. Francis Xavier, 1872 (2nd ed. 1890), as modernised in the Internet Modern History Sourcebook
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Fordham 1551xavier3.asp ('Letter from Japan, to the Society of Jesus at Goa, 1551'); Satsuma passage (bonzes persuade the lord of Satsuma to forbid conversion): continuous, verbatim; bracket is a pure insertion naming the lord ('the prince'/'the king' in the source). Page source note: Henry James Coleridge, ed., Life and Letters of St. Francis Xavier, 2d ed., 1890, vol. II, pp. 295-301, 'modernized by Prof. Arkenberg' -- matches the credit (Coleridge's 1st ed. 1872). Letter opens 'Last year ... I wrote to you from Cagoxima', so 1551 and the 1549-50 Satsuma dating hold.

sourceLine: Francis Xavier, Jesuit missionary, letter from Japan to the Jesuits at Goa, 1551, describing his reception by the lord of Yamaguchi
text: The king [the lord of Yamaguchi] was very much delighted both with the letters and with the presents, and that he might reward us, he offered us a great amount of gold and silver. These gifts we sent back, and then asked him that, if he desired to make some acceptable present to the strangers who had come to his city, he would give us leave to announce the law of God to his people, saying that nothing could possibly be more pleasing to us than such a gift. This he granted us with the greatest goodwill. He accordingly affixed edicts in the most crowded places of the city, declaring that it was pleasing to him that the law of heaven should be announced in his dominions; and that it was lawful for any, who desired, to embrace it. At the same time, he assigned an empty monastery for us to inhabit.
translation: Translated in Henry James Coleridge, The Life and Letters of St. Francis Xavier, 1872 (2nd ed. 1890), as modernised in the Internet Modern History Sourcebook

sourceLine: Francis Xavier, Jesuit missionary, letter to the Society of Jesus in Europe after two years in Japan, 1552
text: The Japanese are led by reason in everything more than any other people, and in general they are all so insatiable of information and so importunate in their questions that there is no end either to their arguments with us, or to their talking over our answers among themselves. They did not know that the world is round, they knew nothing of the course of the sun and stars, so that when they asked us and we explained to them these and other like things, such as the causes of comets, of the lightning and of rain, they listened to us most eagerly, and appeared delighted to hear us, regarding us with profound respect as extremely learned persons. This idea of our great knowledge opened the way to us for sowing the seed of religion in their minds.
translation: Translated in Henry James Coleridge, The Life and Letters of St. Francis Xavier, 1872 (2nd ed. 1890), as modernised in the Internet Modern History Sourcebook
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Fordham 1552xavier4.asp ('Letter from Japan, to the Society of Jesus in Europe, 1552'; Coleridge, 2d ed. 1890, vol. II, pp. 331-350, modernised by Arkenberg): passage continuous and verbatim, no cuts or brackets. sourceLine: Xu Guangqi, Ming scholar-official, mathematician and Christian convert, memorial to the Wanli emperor defending the Jesuits accused by the Board of Rites, 1616
text: Knowing full well that the arts and sciences of the foreigners are in a high degree correct, your majesty's humble servant earnestly begs of his sacred Intelligence, the illustrious honor of issuing a manifesto in their behalf, so as to render his own felicity eternal, and give great tranquility to ten thousand generations. … As your servant for years past has been thus accustomed to engage in discussions and investigations with these courtiers [the Jesuit missionaries], he has become well acquainted with them, and knows that they are not only in deportment and in heart wholly free from aught which can excite suspicion, but that they are indeed worthies and sages; that their doctrines are most correct; their regimen most strict; their learning most extensive; their knowledge most refined; their hearts most true; their views most steady; and that among the people of their own nations, there is not one in a thousand so accomplished, or one in ten thousand so talented as these men.
translation: Translator not named; English version printed in The Chinese Repository, March 1850, as modernised by Jerome S. Arkenberg (Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Fordham 1617hsukuang.asp ('Memorial to Fra Matteo Ricci, 1617'; source note: Chinese Repository, March 1850, pp. 118-126, modernised by Arkenberg; no translator named, so credit made explicit). Pieces verbatim; cut removes the Board of Rites report and Xu's own involvement, meaning intact. Added '[the Jesuit missionaries]' after 'these courtiers' (no referent for 'courtiers' in the excerpt). Date: the memorial answers the 1616 accusations by Shen Que of the (Nanjing) Board of Rites; it is Xu's 'Bianxue zhangshu' of Wanli 44 = 1616 (zh.wikipedia 'Nanjing jiao'an' dates the incident and Xu's memorial, quoting this very passage, to 1616; Pantoja was expelled at the end of that year). The Sourcebook's '1617' is the later date; year and sourceLine set to 1616 (id left unchanged).

sourceLine: Xu Guangqi, Ming scholar-official and Christian convert, memorial to the Wanli emperor proposing how the Jesuits should be examined, 1616
text: 1st. Let all the courtiers [the Jesuit missionaries], whose names have been included in the memorials, be called to the capital; and let a selection be made of your majesty's ministers both in and out of the capital; let all these jointly translate the standard works that have been brought from the West; let subjects be taken up in detail—what is said on serving Heaven and loving man, what relates to natural and moral philosophy, to the systems of civil government, to astronomy, to mathematics, to physic and medicine, to agriculture and irrigation, to political economy, &c.; and let a distinct treatise be prepared on each of these; and then let his majesty command the ministers of his own palace, in general assembly, to decide whether they are correct or erroneous. And if indeed they be subversive of the cardinal virtues and opposed to the classics, involving wicked doctrines and sinister means, then let the said courtiers be immediately dismissed and expelled; and your majesty's servant will willingly abide the punishment appointed for those who aid and abet the deceivers of his majesty.
translation: Translator not named; English version printed in The Chinese Repository, March 1850, as modernised by Jerome S. Arkenberg (Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Same Fordham page; first of Xu's 'three modes of examination', continuous and verbatim (180 words). sourceLine: Shaykh Zainuddin Makhdum, Muslim scholar of Malabar (south-west India), Tuhfat al-Mujahidin, a history of the Portuguese ("Franks") in Malabar, c. 1583
text: Subsequently, however, they [the Muslims of Malabar] were guilty of ingratitude towards God, forgetting the blessings that they enjoyed; going astray, and becoming divided into schisms. On this account, therefore, did God bring down upon them the people of Europe, the Franks, Christians by religion (whom may Almighty God confound !), who began to oppress the Mahomedans, and to bring ruin amongst them ; being guilty of actions the most diabolical and infamous, such indeed as are beyond the power of description … seizing their ships ; … profaning the sanctuaries of their mosques ; ever striving to make the professors of Islamism apostates from their creed, and worshippers of their crucifixes, and seeking, by bribes of money, to induce them to this apostacy. … these Franks sallying forth in the directions of Guzerat, the Conkan, and Malabar, and towards the coast of Arabia, would there lie in wait for the purpose of intercepting vessels … How many noble Seids, too, and learned and worthy men, did they not imprison and persecute even unto death ! How many Moslems, both men and women, did they not compel to embrace Christianity !
translation: Translated by M. J. Rowlandson, Tohfut-ul-Mujahideen: An Historical Work in the Arabic Language (Oriental Translation Fund), 1833
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with archive.org TohfutUlMujahideen, pp. 103-107 (Rowlandson 1833). The other cuts skip items in a list; meaning kept. Date as for zainuddin-1583-pepper-lands. sourceLine: Shaykh Zainuddin Makhdum, Muslim scholar of Malabar (south-west India), Tuhfat al-Mujahidin, a history of the Portuguese in Malabar, c. 1583
text: … a party from on board left the ships, and proceeded by land to Calicut. At this city they [the Franks] remained for some months, employing themselves in gathering information of the statistics and condition of the several countries of Malabar ; but, on this occasion, they abstained from engaging in trade, and at the expiration of the above period returned to their own country in Europe … the occasion of this visit of the Franks to Malabar was, according to their own accounts, in quest of pepper lands, they being greatly desirous of establishing a trade in that spice; because, at this time, they could only procure it from those who brought it from the original exporters of the article from Malabar.
translation: Translated by M. J. Rowlandson, Tohfut-ul-Mujahideen: An Historical Work in the Arabic Language (Oriental Translation Fund), 1833

sourceLine: The Zamorin, Hindu ruler of Calicut, letter to King Manuel I of Portugal, its substance as reported in the journal of Vasco da Gama's first voyage (attributed to Alvaro Velho), August 1498
text: When the king heard that we had sailed for Portugal, and that he was thus no longer able to carry his point, he thought of undoing the evil he had done. … At the same time he forwarded a letter to the captain, which had been written for him by Diogo Dias with an iron pen upon a palm-leaf, as is the custom of the country, and which was intended for the King of Portugal. The tenor [the general sense, not the exact words] of this letter was as follows:— “Vasco da Gama, a gentleman of your household, came to my country, whereat I was pleased. My country is rich in cinnamon, cloves, ginger, pepper, and precious stones. That which I ask of you in exchange is gold, silver, corals and scarlet cloth.”
translation: Translated by E. G. Ravenstein, A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (Hakluyt Society), 1898
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 46440 (Ravenstein 1898). sourceLine: Gomes Eanes de Zurara, royal chronicler of Portugal, Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea, on Prince Henry urging Gil Eannes to sail past Cape Bojador (which Eannes passed in 1434), 1453
text: Now the Infant always received home again with great patience those whom he had sent out, as Captains of his ships, in search of that land, never upbraiding them with their failure, … "You cannot find", said the Infant, "a peril so great that the hope of reward will not be greater, and in truth I wonder much at the notion you have all taken on so uncertain a matter--for even if these things that are reported had any authority, however small, I would not blame you, but you tell me only the opinions of four mariners, who come but from the Flanders trade or from some other ports that are very commonly sailed to, and know nothing of the needle or sailing-chart. … Go forth, then, and heed none of their words, but make your voyage straightway, inasmuch as with the grace of God you cannot but gain from this journey honour and profit."
translation: Translated by Charles Raymond Beazley and Edgar Prestage, The Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea, vol. 1 (Hakluyt Society), 1896
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 35738, ch. IX. Date of event 1434 matches ch. IX ("in the next year" after 1433). Translation correct.

sourceLine: Gomes Eanes de Zurara, royal chronicler of Portugal, Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea, on the reasons of Prince Henry the Navigator, 1453
text: The fourth reason was because during the one and thirty years that he had warred against the Moors, he had never found a Christian king, nor a lord outside this land, who for the love of our Lord Jesus Christ would aid him in the said war. Therefore he sought to know if there were in those parts any Christian princes, in whom the charity and the love of Christ was so ingrained that they would aid him against those enemies of the faith. … The fifth reason was his great desire to make increase in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ and to bring to him all the souls that should be saved … For I that wrote this history saw so many men and women of those parts turned to the holy faith, that even if the Infant had been a heathen, their prayers would have been enough to have obtained his salvation.
translation: Translated by Charles Raymond Beazley and Edgar Prestage, The Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea, vol. 1 (Hakluyt Society), 1896
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 1: Compared with Gutenberg 35738, ch. VII, reasons four and five. Cuts drop only the theological elaboration of the fifth reason; meaning kept. Attribution, date, translation (Beazley & Prestage 1896, named on the page) correct.

sourceLine: Gomes Eanes de Zurara, royal chronicler of Portugal, Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea, on the reasons of Prince Henry the Navigator, 1453
text: And because the said Lord Infant wished to know the truth of this [the land beyond Cape Bojador],--since it seemed to him that if he or some other lord did not endeavour to gain that knowledge, no mariners or merchants would ever dare to attempt it--(for it is clear that none of them ever trouble themselves to sail to a place where there is not a sure and certain hope of profit)--and seeing also that no other prince took any pains in this matter, he sent out his own ships against those parts, to have manifest certainty of them all. And to this he was stirred up by his zeal for the service of God … And this was the first reason of his action. The second reason was that if there chanced to be in those lands some population of Christians, or some havens, into which it would be possible to sail without peril, many kinds of merchandise might be brought to this realm, which would find a ready market, … and also the products of this realm might be taken there, which traffic would bring great profit to our countrymen.
translation: Translated by Charles Raymond Beazley and Edgar Prestage, The Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea, vol. 1 (Hakluyt Society), 1896

sourceLine: Gomes Eanes de Zurara, royal chronicler of Portugal writing for Prince Henry, Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea, on the division of African captives at Lagos in 1444, written 1453
text: But what heart could be so hard as not to be pierced with piteous feeling to see that company? For some kept their heads low and their faces bathed in tears, looking one upon another; others stood groaning very dolorously, looking up to the height of heaven, fixing their eyes upon it, crying out loudly, as if asking help of the Father of Nature; others struck their faces with the palms of their hands, throwing themselves at full length upon the ground; others made their lamentations in the manner of a dirge, after the custom of their country. And though we could not understand the words of their language, the sound of it right well accorded with the measure of their sadness. … and then was it needful to part fathers from sons, husbands from wives, brothers from brothers. No respect was shewn either to friends or relations, but each fell where his lot took him.
translation: Translated by Charles Raymond Beazley and Edgar Prestage, The Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea, vol. 1 (Hakluyt Society), 1896
verifiedNote: Reviewed by verifier 2: Compared with Gutenberg 35738 (Beazley & Prestage, Hakluyt Society vol. 1, preface dated October 1896), ch. XXV pp. 81–82. Text is verbatim; the one cut (40 words) only removes the arrival of the officials who made the division and does not change the meaning. Attribution: the chronicle is headed "written by command of ... the Infant Don Henry" and was finished in 1453 (Introduction, Feb. 18, 1453); Zurara was then in charge of the Royal Library as successor to the chronicler Fernão Lopes. The edition does not print the year 1444 itself; 1444 is the standard date of Lançarote's expedition (chs. XVIII–XXV, after Nuno Tristão's 1443 voyage).
